docs.title: The assistant
docs.description: Operate Flagon by asking. The assistant acts as you, runs reads immediately, and proposes every change for you to confirm.
docs.body:
The **assistant** is Flagon's built-in AI agent. Anything you can do in the
dashboard, you can do by asking it, and anything it can do, you can also do
yourself: it is an accelerant, never a requirement. It works through the same
[tool registry](/docs/ai/tools) as the [MCP server](/docs/ai/mcp), and every tool
calls the same permission-checked operation as the [API](/docs/api/using-the-api),
so the assistant gains each new capability as it is built.

## Where to find it

- The organization dashboard (`app.flagon.io/<org>`) leads with it: the first
  thing on the page is the prompt.
- **Ask AI** in the top bar opens the assistant panel from any page in the
  organization.
- In the command menu (`Ctrl K`, or `Cmd K` on macOS), **Shift+Enter** hands
  whatever you typed to the assistant.

A conversation is scoped to the organization you are in: its usage is metered
against that organization, and its tools can act only there. Flagon does not
store conversations on the server: the panel sends the conversation so far with
each message, and clearing the panel discards it.

## How it behaves

- **It acts as you.** Every tool runs with your identity and your organization
  membership, so the assistant can never do anything you could not do yourself.
  Row-level security and role checks apply exactly as they do in the dashboard.
- **It stays in this organization.** A tool call that names a different
  organization is refused with `403`, before it runs or is proposed. Restoring a
  deleted organization (`restore_organization`) addresses the organization by id
  rather than by the one you are in, so the assistant refuses it outright; use
  your personal **Settings > Organizations** page or MCP for that. To work in another organization, switch to it in
  Flagon and ask there.
- **The organization's security policy applies.** If the organization requires
  two-factor authentication or single sign-on and your session does not satisfy
  it, sending a message or confirming an action fails with `403`, the same as
  any other request to that organization. See
  [Two-factor authentication](/docs/platform/two-factor) and
  [Single sign-on](/docs/platform/sso).
- **Reads run, changes are proposed.** Read-only tools (listing projects,
  reading the audit log, searching the docs) run immediately. Any tool that
  changes data is returned as a **proposal** instead of running.
- **It is scoped to Flagon.** The assistant only has Flagon tools and a system
  prompt that confines it to operating Flagon. Ask it about something unrelated
  and it politely declines and steers back to what it can do.
- **It reads the docs.** For "how does this work" questions it searches this
  documentation with `search_docs` and reads pages with `get_doc`, and names the
  page it used, rather than answering from memory. Pages marked
  `visibility: internal` (none today; the handbook is public) are available to
  the assistant too, because it always acts for a signed-in user.

## Confirming changes

Human-in-the-loop is the default. When the assistant wants to change something,
the panel shows a card for each proposed action, such as
**Confirm: Create project "billing-api" in "acme"**, with a **Confirm** button.
Nothing happens until you press it; then Flagon runs exactly the proposed tool
with exactly the proposed input, as you. If the action fails, you get the same
error the API would return (for example `403` or `409`).

```text
 you: "create a project called billing-api"
   │
   ▼
 assistant ──► read tools run now (list_projects ...)
   │
   ▼
 proposal: create_project { org: "acme", name: "billing-api" }
   │
   ▼
 you press Confirm ──► tool runs as you ──► result in the panel
```

The panel's mode picker offers two settings:

| Mode | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| **Ask before editing** (default) | Every proposed change waits for you to press **Confirm**. |
| **Automatically edit** | Proposed changes run as soon as the assistant proposes them, for this conversation. |

**Automatically edit** is a convenience in the dashboard, not a bypass: each
change still goes through the same confirm step on the server, still runs as you,
and is still subject to your permissions.

See [Work with the assistant](/docs/guides/work-with-the-assistant) for
examples.

## Providers and models

The model is configuration, not code. The assistant talks to a **provider**
through one interface, and three ship with Flagon:

| Provider | Selected when | Default model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Anthropic** | `FLAGON_AI_PROVIDER=anthropic`, or `auto` with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` set | `claude-haiku-4-5` |
| **OpenAI-compatible** | `FLAGON_AI_PROVIDER=openai`, or `auto` with `FLAGON_AI_BASE_URL` or `FLAGON_AI_API_KEY` set | `gpt-4o-mini` |
| **Mock** | `FLAGON_AI_PROVIDER=mock`, or `auto` with nothing configured | offline, deterministic |

`FLAGON_AI_PROVIDER` defaults to `auto`, which prefers Anthropic, then an
OpenAI-compatible endpoint, then the mock. The OpenAI-compatible provider works
with any server that speaks the Chat Completions API: OpenAI itself, hosted
open-weight models (OpenRouter, Together, Groq), or a model you run yourself with
Ollama or vLLM for a flat cost. `FLAGON_AI_MODEL` overrides the model for any
provider. The mock needs no key and no network, so the assistant works in local
development out of the box. Pinning `FLAGON_AI_PROVIDER` to `anthropic` or
`openai` without its credentials, or naming an unknown provider, stops the API
at startup with a clear error rather than failing on every message. If a
configured key is later rejected by the provider (`401` or `403` upstream), the
assistant answers `503` with `the AI agent is not configured`.

The system prompt is a swappable file: point `FLAGON_AI_SYSTEM_PROMPT_FILE` at a
Markdown document to replace the built-in prompt without recompiling. See
[AI runtime](/docs/architecture/ai-runtime) for how the loop works and
[Configuration](/docs/reference/configuration) for every setting.

## Metering and limits

Every assistant turn and every confirmed action is recorded against the
organization, and each organization has a rolling daily limit: 100 calls per 24
hours by default (`FLAGON_AI_DAILY_LIMIT`). The limit is checked before each
message and before each confirmed action runs. When it is reached, both fail
with `429 Too Many Requests` (`AI usage limit reached for this organization`)
until older calls age out; everything else in Flagon keeps working. See [Usage and AI limits](/docs/platform/usage).

## Limits of the assistant

- It is available only in the dashboard, with your signed-in session. The
  `/ai/messages` operation does not accept access tokens; external agents use
  [MCP](/docs/ai/mcp) instead.
- One message runs at most six model round trips (read tools included) before the
  assistant replies.
- It has no tools for access tokens, your password, emails, sessions, or account
  deletion. Those stay in **Settings** by design.

## Related

- [Tool reference](/docs/ai/tools)
- [MCP server](/docs/ai/mcp)
- [Work with the assistant](/docs/guides/work-with-the-assistant)
- [AI safety](/docs/security/ai-safety)
- [Usage and AI limits](/docs/platform/usage)

docs.title: MCP server
docs.description: Connect an external agent to mcp.flagon.io to read Flagon's docs anonymously, or to operate your organizations with an access token.
docs.body:
Flagon runs a **Model Context Protocol** (MCP) server, so an external agent (an
assistant in your editor, Claude Desktop, Cursor, or your own agent) can work
with Flagon directly. It exposes the same [tool registry](/docs/ai/tools) as the
in-product [assistant](/docs/ai/assistant), and every tool calls the same
permission-checked operation as the [API](/docs/api/using-the-api): one registry,
three front doors.

## Endpoint and transport

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| URL | `https://mcp.flagon.io` (the root and `/mcp` both work) |
| Also served at | `https://api.flagon.io/mcp` |
| Transport | Streamable HTTP, `POST` only. Each request is one JSON-RPC 2.0 message and gets one JSON response; there is no server-sent event stream, and `GET` returns `405 Method Not Allowed`. |
| Protocol version | `2024-11-05` |
| Methods | `initialize`, `ping`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`. Notifications (messages without an `id`) are accepted with `202 Accepted`. Anything else returns error `-32601`. |

On the `mcp.flagon.io` host the MCP endpoint is the whole site: every other path
returns `404`, so the public hostname never exposes the rest of the API. A
self-hosted instance chooses its MCP hostname with `FLAGON_MCP_HOST`; without it,
only the `/mcp` path is served.

## Anonymous and authenticated access

What an MCP client can see depends on whether it presents an
[access token](/docs/platform/access-tokens).

| | Anonymous (no token) | Authenticated (`Authorization: Bearer flagon_...`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tools listed | `search_docs` and `get_doc` only | The docs tools, plus every tool the token's scopes allow |
| Docs reachable | Public pages only | Public and internal pages (no page is internal today) |
| Acts as | Nobody | The token's principal: you for a personal token, the org's service principal for an organization token |

Anonymous callers never learn that other tools exist: calling one returns
`unknown tool`. With a token, `tools/list` shows exactly the tools that token can
run. A full-access token sees every tool; a scoped token sees only the tools whose
scope it holds (parent scopes imply their children, as in the API). Your role
still applies on top, so a tool can be listed and still fail with a permission
error when you run it.

Organization security policies apply too. When a tool names an organization
that requires two-factor authentication, a personal token whose user has not
enabled it gets a tool error (`this organization requires two-factor authentication; ...`). When the organization requires single sign-on, a
personal token works only if its user has signed in through one of the
organization's identity providers at least once; organization owners are exempt
from the SSO requirement. Organization access tokens are exempt from both. See
[Two-factor authentication](/docs/platform/two-factor) and
[Single sign-on](/docs/platform/sso).

Unlike the in-product assistant, MCP has no conversation organization: a token
acts in every organization its principal can reach, and `restore_organization`
is available (to personal tokens; organization tokens can't restore
organizations).

A token that is present but invalid, revoked, or expired is **rejected**, not
silently treated as anonymous, so a rotated token shows up as an error instead of
a mysteriously shorter tool list.

## Connecting a client

Configure your client with the URL `https://mcp.flagon.io` and, for operational
tools, an `Authorization` header carrying your token. Client configuration
formats differ; see [Connect an MCP client](/docs/guides/connect-an-mcp-client)
for specific clients.

To check the connection by hand:

```bash
curl -X POST https://mcp.flagon.io \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list"}'
```

And to call a tool:

```bash
curl -X POST https://mcp.flagon.io \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/call",
       "params": {"name": "list_projects", "arguments": {"org": "acme"}}}'
```

A tool result is one text content block holding the JSON result. A failed tool
returns `isError: true` with a caller-safe message (internal details are logged on
the server, never returned).

## Mutating tools run immediately

<Callout type="warn" title="No confirmation step over MCP">

Over MCP, a mutating tool such as `delete_project` **executes as soon as it is
called**. Flagon does not hold it for confirmation the way the in-product
assistant does. Confirming actions is your MCP client's job: turn on its tool
approval setting if it has one, and give the token only the scopes the agent
needs.

</Callout>

The [Tool reference](/docs/ai/tools) marks which tools change data. A read-only
token (for example `read:org` and `read:project`) cannot reach any mutating tool,
which is the simplest way to let an agent look without touching.

## Errors

MCP errors come back as JSON-RPC errors with HTTP status `200`, except for a
few HTTP-level refusals that happen before the JSON-RPC message is read: `405`
on a non-`POST` request, `413` when the body is larger than the API's request
cap (`FLAGON_MAX_BODY_BYTES`, 4 MiB by default), and `429` with a `Retry-After`
header when the token (or, without a token, your IP address) exceeds the API's
per-principal rate limit.

| Code | Message | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-32700` | `parse error` | The body is not valid JSON-RPC. |
| `-32601` | `method not found: ...` | The method is not one of the four supported. |
| `-32602` | `unknown tool: ...` | No such tool, or an anonymous caller asked for an authenticated one. Also `invalid params` when the `params` object itself can't be decoded. |
| `-32001` | `invalid or expired token` | The bearer token is unknown, expired, or revoked. If Flagon can't check the token at all (for example its database is unavailable), you get an HTTP `503` problem response instead, so a valid token is never reported as bad. |
| `-32003` | `this token is missing the scope required for ...` | The token is valid but lacks the tool's scope. |

A tool that runs and fails (bad arguments, a missing project, a permission or
policy refusal) is not a JSON-RPC error: it is a normal result with
`isError: true` and the caller-safe message as its text.

## Usage and limits

MCP calls run no model on Flagon's side, so they do not count toward the
organization's [AI usage limit](/docs/platform/usage). They are ordinary
permission-checked operations, and every change an MCP tool makes is recorded in
the organization's [audit log](/docs/platform/audit-log), with the connection's
IP address and your client's user agent.

## Related

- [Tool reference](/docs/ai/tools)
- [Connect an MCP client](/docs/guides/connect-an-mcp-client)
- [Access tokens](/docs/platform/access-tokens)
- [Tool registry](/docs/architecture/tool-registry)
- [Assistant and MCP troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting/assistant-and-mcp)

docs.title: Tool reference
docs.description: Every tool the assistant and the MCP server expose, with the API operation behind it, the scope it requires, and whether it changes data.
docs.body:
The in-product [assistant](/docs/ai/assistant) and the [MCP server](/docs/ai/mcp)
draw from **one tool registry** (`api/internal/ai`). Every operational tool is the
front door for one real, permission-checked [API](/docs/api/using-the-api)
operation and calls the same service method, so the three front doors cannot
drift. CI enforces the pairing: an API operation that users can call without a
matching tool, or a tool whose scope or read/write nature differs from its
operation, fails the build. This page lists the whole registry: 60 tools.

## How to read the tables

- **API** is the operation the tool runs. Its request and response shapes are in
  the [OpenAPI spec](/docs/api/openapi).
- **Scope** is the [token scope](/docs/platform/access-tokens#scopes) the tool
  requires over MCP, the same scope as its API operation. Parent scopes imply
  their children (`admin:org` covers `write:org` and `read:org`). The in-product
  assistant uses your session, so only your role applies there.
- **Changes data** marks mutating tools. The assistant never runs these on its
  own: it **proposes** them and runs them after you confirm. Over MCP they run as
  soon as they are called, so your client is responsible for confirmation.
- Scopes are a ceiling, never a grant. Every tool also checks your role: for
  example, the SSO and audit tools work only for org owners and admins, whatever
  the token holds.
- Organization tools take the organization's slug as an `org` argument, and
  project and team tools add the project or team slug. The account and
  notification tools act on you and take no organization.
- Any tool call that names an organization first passes that organization's
  [security policy](/docs/platform/two-factor): if it requires two-factor
  authentication or single sign-on and your sign-in does not satisfy it, the call
  fails with 403, on both the assistant and MCP.
- The in-product assistant is confined to the organization its conversation
  belongs to. A call that names any other organization is refused with 403, and
  `restore_organization` (which addresses a deleted organization by id) is
  refused from the assistant entirely; use your personal **Settings >
  Organizations** page for it. MCP has no
  conversation, so a token acts in every organization its user can reach.

## Account and organizations

| Tool | What it does | API | Scope | Changes data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `whoami` | Your account (id, email) and the organizations you belong to. | `GET /me` | `read:user` | |
| `list_organizations` | List your organizations with your role in each. | `GET /orgs` | `read:org` | |
| `create_organization` | Create an organization you own; the slug is derived from the name if omitted. | `POST /orgs` | `admin:org` | Yes |
| `update_organization` | Rename an organization (owners and admins). The slug does not change. | `PATCH /orgs/{slug}` | `write:org` | Yes |
| `leave_organization` | Leave an organization. The only owner cannot leave. | `POST /orgs/{slug}/leave` | `admin:org` | Yes |
| `delete_organization` | Soft-delete an organization for every member (owners only). Restorable for 30 days. | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}` | `admin:org` | Yes |
| `list_deleted_organizations` | List organizations you owned that were deleted in the last 30 days, with `id` and `purge_at`. | `GET /deleted-orgs` | `read:org` | |
| `restore_organization` | Restore a deleted organization by id, optionally under a new `slug` (owners only, within 30 days). MCP only: the assistant refuses it. | `POST /deleted-orgs/{id}/restore` | `admin:org` | Yes |
| `get_org_security` | Read the security policy: 2FA requirement, SSO requirement, base permission. | `GET /orgs/{slug}/security` | `read:org` | |
| `set_org_security` | Change the security policy (`enforce_two_factor`, `require_sso`, `base_permission`). Only the fields you pass change. | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/security` | `write:org` | Yes |

## Single sign-on

| Tool | What it does | API | Scope | Changes data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `list_sso_providers` | List the org's OIDC and SAML providers (owners and admins). Secrets are never returned. | `GET /orgs/{slug}/sso/providers` | `read:org` | |
| `get_sso_provider` | Read one provider by its provider ID. Secrets are never returned. | `GET /orgs/{slug}/sso/providers/{provider}` | `read:org` | |
| `create_sso_provider` | Add an OIDC or SAML provider. Its client secret or private key is write-only. | `POST /orgs/{slug}/sso/providers` | `write:org` | Yes |
| `update_sso_provider` | Change a provider's domain, issuer, or settings, or replace its secret. | `PATCH /orgs/{slug}/sso/providers/{provider}` | `write:org` | Yes |
| `delete_sso_provider` | Remove a provider; sign-in through it stops at the next attempt. | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/sso/providers/{provider}` | `write:org` | Yes |

## Members and invitations

| Tool | What it does | API | Scope | Changes data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `list_members` | List the organization's members and their roles. | `GET /orgs/{slug}/members` | `read:org` | |
| `add_member` | Add an existing Flagon user by email or username. | `POST /orgs/{slug}/members` | `write:org` | Yes |
| `set_member_role` | Change a member's organization role, by user id. | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/members/{userId}/role` | `write:org` | Yes |
| `remove_member` | Remove a member from the organization, by user id. | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/members/{userId}` | `write:org` | Yes |
| `list_invitations` | List pending invitations. | `GET /orgs/{slug}/invitations` | `read:org` | |
| `invite_member` | Invite someone by email as a `member` (default) or `admin`; owners can't be invited. Adds them directly if they already have an account. Otherwise the API emails the invitation and the result reports `email_sent` (`false` when the server only logs email or delivery failed; never the invitation token). | `POST /orgs/{slug}/invitations` | `write:org` | Yes |
| `revoke_invitation` | Revoke a pending invitation by id. | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/invitations/{id}` | `write:org` | Yes |

## Projects

| Tool | What it does | API | Scope | Changes data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `list_projects` | List the organization's projects, with optional search and a cursor for paging. | `GET /orgs/{slug}/projects` | `read:project` | |
| `list_deleted_projects` | List projects deleted in the last 30 days, each with its `purge_at` (org owners and admins). | `GET /orgs/{slug}/deleted-projects` | `read:project` | |
| `get_project` | Read one project, including its README. | `GET /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}` | `read:project` | |
| `create_project` | Create a project; the slug is derived from the name if omitted. | `POST /orgs/{slug}/projects` | `write:project` | Yes |
| `update_project` | Edit a project's name, slug, description, README, or repository URL. Only the fields you pass change. | `PATCH /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}` | `write:project` | Yes |
| `delete_project` | Soft-delete a project (owner tier); its slug is freed. | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}` | `admin:project` | Yes |
| `restore_project` | Restore a project deleted in the last 30 days by its slug (owner tier). Pass `new_slug` if a live project has taken the old slug. | `POST /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/restore` | `admin:project` | Yes |

## Project access

| Tool | What it does | API | Scope | Changes data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `list_project_members` | List a project's explicit collaborators and their roles. | `GET /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/members` | `read:project` | |
| `add_project_member` | Give an organization member a role on a project. | `POST /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/members` | `admin:project` | Yes |
| `set_project_member_role` | Change a collaborator's project role, by user id. | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/members/{userId}/role` | `admin:project` | Yes |
| `remove_project_member` | Remove a collaborator, dropping them to their org-level access. | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/members/{userId}` | `admin:project` | Yes |
| `list_project_teams` | List the teams a project is shared with and their roles. | `GET /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/teams` | `read:project` | |
| `add_project_team` | Grant a team a role on a project. | `POST /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/teams` | `admin:project` | Yes |
| `set_project_team_role` | Change a team's role on a project. | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/teams/{team}/role` | `admin:project` | Yes |
| `remove_project_team` | Remove a team's access to a project. | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/teams/{team}` | `admin:project` | Yes |
| `list_project_owners` | List a project's owners (users and teams). | `GET /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/owners` | `read:project` | |
| `add_project_owner` | Make a user or team an owner of a project (owner tier). | `POST /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/owners` | `admin:project` | Yes |
| `remove_project_owner` | Remove a project owner (owner tier). | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/owners/{type}/{principalId}` | `admin:project` | Yes |

## Teams

| Tool | What it does | API | Scope | Changes data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `list_teams` | List the organization's teams with member counts. | `GET /orgs/{slug}/teams` | `read:team` | |
| `get_team` | Read one team by slug. | `GET /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}` | `read:team` | |
| `create_team` | Create a team (org owners and admins); you become its first maintainer. | `POST /orgs/{slug}/teams` | `write:team` | Yes |
| `update_team` | Edit a team's name, slug, or description. | `PATCH /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}` | `write:team` | Yes |
| `delete_team` | Delete a team (org owners and admins); its grants stop having effect. | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}` | `admin:team` | Yes |
| `list_team_members` | List a team's members and their team roles. | `GET /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/members` | `read:team` | |
| `list_team_projects` | List the projects a team can reach and its role on each. | `GET /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/projects` | `read:team` | |
| `add_team_member` | Add an organization member to a team as maintainer or member. | `POST /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/members` | `write:team` | Yes |
| `set_team_member_role` | Make a team member a maintainer or a regular member. | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/members/{userId}/role` | `write:team` | Yes |
| `remove_team_member` | Remove someone from a team. | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/members/{userId}` | `write:team` | Yes |

## Audit log

| Tool | What it does | API | Scope | Changes data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `list_audit_events` | Read the organization's audit log, newest first (owners and admins). | `GET /orgs/{slug}/audit` | `read:org` | |
| `get_audit_config` | Read whether actor IP addresses are disclosed in the log (owners and admins). | `GET /orgs/{slug}/audit/config` | `read:org` | |
| `set_audit_config` | Turn actor IP disclosure on or off (owners and admins); the change is audited. | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/audit/config` | `write:org` | Yes |

## Notifications

| Tool | What it does | API | Scope | Changes data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `list_notifications` | List your notifications, unread first. | `GET /notifications` | `notifications` | |
| `count_unread_notifications` | Count your unread notifications. | `GET /notifications/unread-count` | `notifications` | |
| `mark_notification_read` | Mark one notification read, by id. | `POST /notifications/{id}/read` | `notifications` | Yes |
| `mark_notification_unread` | Mark one notification unread, by id. | `POST /notifications/{id}/unread` | `notifications` | Yes |
| `mark_all_notifications_read` | Mark every notification read. | `POST /notifications/read-all` | `notifications` | Yes |

## Documentation

The documentation tools are the only **public** tools: they are read-only, touch
no tenant data, and need no token. They are the only tools an anonymous MCP
client sees.

| Tool | What it does | API | Scope | Changes data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `search_docs` | Search the documentation (and, for authenticated callers, internal pages). Returns ranked slugs, titles, and snippets; default 5 results. | none | none | |
| `get_doc` | Read one documentation page in full by slug, such as `platform/projects`. | none | none | |

Pages marked `visibility: internal` (none today; the handbook is public) are served
only to authenticated callers. There is nothing to configure.

| Caller | Pages |
| --- | --- |
| Anonymous MCP client | Public pages only |
| MCP client with an access token | Public and internal pages |
| In-product assistant | Public and internal pages |

The public HTTP routes (`/docs`, `/docs/search`, `/docs/page`) serve the same
corpus, public pages only.

## Not available as tools

A few capabilities deliberately have no tool:

- **Access tokens.** Minting and revoking tokens is dashboard-only, so a
  credential can never create more credentials. See
  [Access tokens](/docs/platform/access-tokens).
- **Your account.** Password, emails, sessions, profile edits, and account
  deletion are managed in **Settings**, so a token or an agent cannot take over
  the account behind it.
- **Internal operations.** Accepting an invitation, SSO provisioning, and the
  sign-in service's SSO configuration reads run only with Flagon's internal
  credential.

## Related

- [The assistant](/docs/ai/assistant)
- [MCP server](/docs/ai/mcp)
- [Tool registry architecture](/docs/architecture/tool-registry)
- [Scopes reference](/docs/reference/scopes)

docs.title: Authentication and scopes
docs.description: How a request proves who it is with a flagon_ access token, and how scopes and roles decide what it may do.
docs.body:
Every Flagon API request that touches your data is made by a **principal**: a
person, or an organization's service principal. You prove which one with an
**access token** sent as a bearer token. The API then applies two limits: the
token's **scopes** (which operations it may call) and the principal's **role**
(what that person or service may do in each organization). The stricter of the
two always wins, and enforcement fails closed.

## Send a token

Access tokens start with `flagon_` and go in the `Authorization` header:

```bash
curl https://api.flagon.io/me \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"
```

A missing, unknown, revoked, or expired token is rejected with `401` and the
detail `invalid or expired token`. If the API cannot check a token because a
dependency such as its database is unavailable, it answers `503` instead; retry
later, and keep the token. The API stores only a SHA-256 hash of each
token, so a token is shown once, when you create it, and cannot be recovered
later.

## Two kinds of token

| | Personal access token | Organization access token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prefix | `flagon_pat_` | `flagon_oat_` |
| Acts as | You, in every organization you belong to | A service principal that is a member of one organization |
| Bounded by | Your role in each organization | The role chosen when the token was created: `admin`, `member`, or `viewer` |
| Created in | **Settings > Personal access tokens** | The organization's **Settings > API tokens** |
| Who can create | Any signed-in user, for themselves | Organization owners and admins |

An organization access token creates a dedicated service user inside that
organization with the role you pick, so its activity shows up in the
[audit log](/docs/platform/audit-log) under the token's name rather than a
person's. It stops working if its organization is deleted.

Tokens are created and revoked only in the dashboard. The token-management
operations accept the dashboard's own credential and never an access token, so
a token cannot mint, list, or widen tokens. The same is true of the assistant's
endpoints under `/ai/*`: to drive the assistant from outside the dashboard, use
the [MCP server](/docs/ai/mcp), which accepts access tokens.

## Expiry

When you create a token you choose an expiry: 7, 30 (the default), or 90 days,
a custom date, or no expiration. Over the API the dashboard sends either
`expires_in_days` (`0` means no expiry) or an absolute `expires_at`, which must
be in the future (otherwise `422`). An expired token is rejected with `401`.
Each successful use records a `last_used_at` time you can see in the token list.

## Scopes

When you create a token you either grant **full access** (the token is limited
only by its principal's role) or pick scopes from a grouped checklist. Scopes are
hierarchical: a parent implies its children, so `admin:org` also grants
`write:org` and `read:org`.

| Group | Scopes, broadest first |
| --- | --- |
| Account | `admin:user` > `user` > `read:user` |
| Organization | `admin:org` > `write:org` > `read:org` |
| Projects | `admin:project` > `write:project` > `read:project` |
| Teams | `admin:team` > `write:team` > `read:team` |
| Notifications | `notifications` |

Every token-reachable operation maps to exactly one required scope. A scoped
token calling an operation it does not cover gets `403` with the detail `this
token is missing the scope required for this operation`. An operation that has no
scope mapping is unreachable by any scoped token. The complete list of scopes and
the operations each one gates is in the [scopes reference](/docs/reference/scopes).

## Roles still apply

A scope says which operations a token may call. It never grants more than the
principal could do. A full-access personal token held by an organization member
still cannot change the organization's security settings, because members
cannot. That request fails with `403` (`you don't have permission to do that`).
See the [roles matrix](/docs/reference/roles-matrix) for who can do what.

An organization access token's service principal is not a person, so a few
account-level operations refuse it with `403` whatever its scopes: creating an
organization, leaving one, listing or restoring deleted organizations, and
syncing a profile.

## Organization security policy

When an organization requires two-factor authentication or single sign-on, the
API checks it on every request that touches that organization, including token
requests:

- A **personal access token** works only if its owner has two-factor
  authentication enabled (when 2FA is required) and has signed in through one of
  the organization's SSO providers at least once (when SSO is required;
  organization owners are exempt). Otherwise the request fails with `403` and a
  detail that says what to fix.
- An **organization access token** is exempt from both requirements: it has no
  interactive sign-in, and only the organization's owners and admins, who are
  subject to the policy, can create it.

See the [roles matrix](/docs/reference/roles-matrix)
for the full rules.

## Rate limits

Each access token has its own request budget: 50 requests per second sustained,
bursts of up to 300, per API instance. Over it, requests fail with `429` and a
`Retry-After` header. See [Limits](/docs/reference/limits).

## Tenant isolation

Row-level security in Postgres applies to every query a token drives, so a
token cannot read another organization's rows even if a handler had a bug.
Organizations you are not a member of answer `404`, not `403`.

## Endpoints that need no token

Two reads are public by design:

- `GET /users/<username>`: a user's public profile.
- `GET /invitations/<token>`: the invitation landing page lookup, where the
  unguessable invitation token is itself the credential.

The documentation, roadmap, and changelog routes (`/docs`, `/roadmap`,
`/changelog`) and the health probes are also public. They are outside the
OpenAPI spec; see [OpenAPI and clients](/docs/api/openapi).

## One vocabulary, every front door

The same scope means the same thing whether a request arrives over REST, from
the in-product [assistant](/docs/ai/assistant), or over [MCP](/docs/ai/mcp).
Every agent and MCP [tool](/docs/ai/tools) carries the same scope as the API
operation it fronts, and an MCP client authenticated with a scoped token sees
only the tools its scopes cover.

## Related

- [Scopes reference](/docs/reference/scopes)
- [Roles matrix](/docs/reference/roles-matrix)
- [Access tokens](/docs/platform/access-tokens)
- [Errors](/docs/api/errors)
- [Call the API from CI](/docs/guides/call-the-api-from-ci)

docs.title: Errors
docs.description: How the API reports failures as RFC 9457 problem details, and what each status code means.
docs.body:
Flagon uses conventional HTTP status codes: `2xx` means the request succeeded,
`4xx` means something about the request needs to change, and `5xx` means
something failed on the server. Every error response has the same shape, so a
client can handle all of them with one code path.

## The error shape

Errors are **problem details** (RFC 9457) with the content type
`application/problem+json`:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://api.flagon.io/schemas/ErrorModel.json",
  "title": "Not Found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "project not found"
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `title` | The standard phrase for the status (`Not Found`, `Conflict`, ...). Stable for a given status. |
| `status` | The HTTP status code, repeated in the body. |
| `detail` | A human-readable explanation of this occurrence. Safe to show to a user. |
| `errors` | Optional. A list of individual problems, each with a `message` and, for validation failures, the `location` (for example `body` or `body.name`) and the offending `value`. |
| `$schema` | A link to the JSON Schema of the error body (`ErrorModel`), which is also in the [OpenAPI spec](/docs/api/openapi), so generated clients get a typed error model. |

Branch on `status`, not on the text of `detail`. The wording of a message can
improve over time; the status for a given condition does not change.

## Request ids and server errors

Every response, success or failure, carries an `X-Request-Id` header. The API
generates a random id, or keeps the one you send in `X-Request-Id` when it is 8
to 128 characters of letters, digits, `.`, `_`, and `-` (so the dashboard can
propagate its own id across the hop).

Server-side failures (`5xx`) never include internal error text such as SQL,
hostnames, or upstream provider responses. The body keeps only `title`,
`status`, and a generic `detail` such as `could not create project`; the
underlying cause is written to the server log together with the request id.
When you report a failure, quote the `X-Request-Id` value so an operator can find
the matching log line.

```bash
curl -i https://api.flagon.io/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"
# HTTP/2 200
# x-request-id: 3f9c1a0e5b7d4c2a9e8f6b1d0c3a5e7f
```

## Status codes

| Status | When you see it |
| --- | --- |
| `400 Bad Request` | The body could not be parsed, for example malformed JSON. The `errors` list carries the parser's message. Also returned when confirming an assistant action that names an unknown or non-executable tool. |
| `401 Unauthorized` | No credential, or one that is not valid: a missing bearer token, or an access token that is unknown, revoked, or expired. An organization access token also stops working when its organization is deleted. |
| `402 Payment Required` | The action needs a paid plan. Today this is creating, or restoring, a second organization you own: the free plan includes one owned organization. |
| `403 Forbidden` | You are authenticated but not allowed. Common causes: your **token is missing the scope** the operation requires; your **role** does not permit the action (a member changing the organization's security policy or reading the audit log, or a project `read` collaborator editing a project they can see); the organization **requires two-factor authentication or single sign-on** and you do not meet it (the `detail` says what to fix); turning on a 2FA or SSO requirement you do not meet yourself; an **organization access token** calling an operation that needs a human (creating, leaving, or restoring an organization, or listing deleted organizations); or the assistant being asked to act in an organization other than its conversation's. Accepting an invitation that was sent to a different email address is also a `403`. |
| `404 Not Found` | The resource does not exist, **or you cannot see it**. Organizations you do not belong to, their projects and teams, and projects inside your organization that you have no role on, return `404` rather than `403` (for reads and changes alike), so the API never confirms that something exists outside your reach. Restoring a project or organization deleted more than 30 days ago is also a `404`. |
| `409 Conflict` | The request conflicts with current state: a slug or username that is already taken, a user who is already a member or collaborator, a pending invitation that already exists, a change that would leave an organization without an owner (including the only owner trying to leave), changing your own membership through the member endpoints, or restoring a deleted organization or project whose slug was taken meanwhile (pass a new `slug`). |
| `410 Gone` | An invitation that has expired. Invitations are valid for seven days. |
| `413 Content Too Large` | The request body is too large. API operations accept up to 1 MiB; the server also enforces a global cap (`FLAGON_MAX_BODY_BYTES`, 4 MiB by default) on every route, including the MCP endpoint. See [Limits](/docs/reference/limits). |
| `422 Unprocessable Entity` | The request was readable but not valid: it failed schema validation (the `errors` list says which fields and why), or failed a domain rule such as an unknown role, an empty name, an unknown scope, an expiry in the past, or an invalid base permission. An invalid or tampered **pagination cursor** is also a `422` (see [Pagination](/docs/api/pagination)). |
| `429 Too Many Requests` | One of two limits. **Rate limit**: you sent requests faster than the per-caller rate limit allows; the response has a `Retry-After` header (in seconds) and a `detail` like `rate limit exceeded; retry after 2s`. Wait that long and retry. **AI quota**: the organization has used its daily AI allowance (`detail` is `AI usage limit reached for this organization`, no `Retry-After`); only the assistant's endpoints return this, and it clears as the 24-hour window rolls. See [Limits](/docs/reference/limits). |
| `500 Internal Server Error` | An unexpected failure on the server. The body carries a generic `detail` only; quote the `X-Request-Id` header when reporting it. The request may be retried. |
| `503 Service Unavailable` | Something the request needs is not available: the assistant is not configured (`the AI agent is not configured`: no model provider, a missing API key, or the provider rejected the key), the assistant could not record usage for a turn (the turn fails closed rather than going unmetered), the audit log is not available on this deployment, the API could not check an access token (for example, its database is down; the token itself may be fine, so retry rather than replacing it), or `GET /readyz` cannot reach the database. |

## Validation errors

When a request fails schema validation, the response lists every problem at
once, so a client can surface them all in one pass:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://api.flagon.io/schemas/ErrorModel.json",
  "title": "Unprocessable Entity",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "validation failed",
  "errors": [
    {
      "message": "expected required property name to be present",
      "location": "body",
      "value": {}
    }
  ]
}
```

## One mapping, every front door

Each domain condition maps to exactly one status in one table
(`api/internal/service/errors.go`), and every front door uses it. The same
mistake produces the same error whether you call the REST API directly, go
through the dashboard, or confirm an action proposed by the
[assistant](/docs/ai/assistant): confirming an assistant action returns the
underlying operation's real status (a `403` for a missing permission, a `409`
for a taken slug), not a generic failure.

Tools called over [MCP](/docs/ai/mcp) report failures the MCP way instead: a
tool result flagged `isError` whose text is the same caller-safe message, rather
than an HTTP status.

## Related

- [Using the API](/docs/api/using-the-api)
- [Authentication and scopes](/docs/api/authentication)
- [Pagination and search](/docs/api/pagination)
- [Troubleshooting API errors](/docs/troubleshooting/api-errors)

docs.title: Expanding responses
docs.description: Inline a related object in the same response with the expand[] query parameter instead of making a second request.
headings: The project with its organization inlined. -g stops curl treating [] as a glob.
docs.body:
Flagon objects reference each other: a project belongs to an organization, an
audit event has an actor. By default a response returns a **reference** to a
related object (an id such as `org_id`), not the whole object, so payloads stay
small and predictable. When you need the related object too, ask for it with the
**`expand[]`** query parameter instead of making a second request.

## Supported expansions

Expansion is opt-in per operation. Today one operation supports it:

| Operation | Relation | What it adds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /orgs/<org>/projects/<project>` (`get-project`) | `organization` | An `organization` object next to `org_id`: `id`, `name`, `slug`, your `role`, `enforce_two_factor`, `require_sso`, `created_at`. |

The delete project operation (`DELETE /orgs/<org>/projects/<project>`) shares
`get-project`'s input, so the [OpenAPI spec](/docs/api/openapi) lists an
`expand[]` parameter on it too, but it does not expand anything today. More relations will be added operation by
operation, following this same convention.

## How it works

Add an `expand[]` parameter naming the relation. The expanded object appears
alongside the reference it came from:

```bash
# The project alone (org_id only):
curl "https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/projects/billing-api" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"

# The project with its organization inlined. -g stops curl treating [] as a glob.
curl -g "https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/projects/billing-api?expand[]=organization" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"
```

```json
{
  "id": "75919af9-2064-4bcd-998d-5b63eb411de6",
  "org_id": "fcda53fb-3ab8-4b53-9f7f-fca413901062",
  "name": "Billing API",
  "slug": "billing-api",
  "organization": {
    "id": "fcda53fb-3ab8-4b53-9f7f-fca413901062",
    "name": "Acme",
    "slug": "acme",
    "role": "owner",
    "enforce_two_factor": false,
    "require_sso": false,
    "created_at": "2026-09-17T16:14:22.59927Z"
  }
}
```

(Other project fields are omitted here for brevity.)

To ask for several relations, repeat the parameter or separate names with commas
inside one value. Both forms are equivalent:

```text
?expand[]=organization&expand[]=another_relation
?expand[]=organization,another_relation
```

The parameter name must be `expand[]` with the brackets (URL-encoded as
`expand%5B%5D` if your client needs it). A bare `expand=organization` is not
read.

## Rules

- **Opt-in.** Nothing is expanded unless you ask, and the reference id is always
  present whether or not you expand it.
- **Never widens access.** An expanded object is loaded with the same identity
  and permission checks as a direct request for it. If that load fails, the
  whole request fails with that error rather than returning a partial object.
- **Unknown names are ignored.** Names are trimmed and lowercased, and a name an
  operation does not support is skipped silently, so asking for a relation a
  given endpoint does not know is harmless.

## Related

- [Using the API](/docs/api/using-the-api)
- [Pagination and search](/docs/api/pagination)
- [OpenAPI and clients](/docs/api/openapi)
- [Projects](/docs/platform/projects)

docs.title: OpenAPI and clients
docs.description: Where to get Flagon's generated OpenAPI 3.1 spec, how to regenerate it from the code, how to build a typed client, and which routes are deliberately outside it.
headings: which runs: cd api && go run ./cmd/genspec
which runs make openapi, then (in app/):
What the spec does and does not tell you
docs.body:
Flagon's OpenAPI document is generated from the Go source, never written by
hand. Every operation is registered with [huma](https://huma.rocks) in
`api/internal/server`, and huma derives the paths, parameters, request bodies,
response schemas, and error model from those registrations. The spec cannot
describe an endpoint that does not exist, and a new endpoint appears in it the
moment it is registered.

## Get the spec

The running API serves the spec live, with no authentication:

| URL | Format |
| --- | --- |
| `https://api.flagon.io/openapi.json` | OpenAPI 3.1, JSON |
| `https://api.flagon.io/openapi.yaml` | OpenAPI 3.1, YAML (`application/openapi+yaml`) |

```bash
curl -s https://api.flagon.io/openapi.json | jq '.paths | keys'
```

`GET /` on the API also returns both URLs (`openapi_url`, `openapi_yaml_url`)
alongside a `<operation_id>_url` entry for every documented operation. A
self-hosted deployment serves the same routes from its own origin.

The document's `info` block is `{"title": "Flagon API", "version": "0.0.0"}`.
Every operation has a stable `operationId` (`list-projects`, `create-project`,
`get-project`, ...), which is also the name the [scopes reference](/docs/reference/scopes)
uses.

## Regenerate it from the code

In a checkout of the repository:

```bash
make openapi
# which runs: cd api && go run ./cmd/genspec
```

This writes `openapi/openapi.json` at the repo root. The file is gitignored: it
is a build artifact, and the committed source of truth is the Go code. Pass
`-out` to `genspec` to write somewhere else.

`genspec` builds the spec with no database attached (`server.Spec()` in
`api/internal/server`), and every operation is registered whether or not its
backing store is configured, so the offline file and the live `/openapi.json`
describe the same operations. An operation whose store is missing on a given
deployment answers `503` at request time instead of disappearing from the spec.

## Generate a typed client

Because the spec is exact, generate clients from it rather than hand-writing
request and response types. The Flagon dashboard does exactly this with
[openapi-typescript](https://openapi-ts.dev): its API types in
`app/src/lib/api/schema.gen.ts` are generated from the spec, and every shape the
app uses is an alias of a generated schema, so a renamed or removed field is a
type error in the app.

```bash
make api-types
# which runs make openapi, then (in app/):
#   openapi-typescript ../openapi/openapi.json -o src/lib/api/schema.gen.ts
```

CI regenerates the spec and the types on every change and fails if the
committed `schema.gen.ts` differs, so the dashboard can never drift from the
API.

For your own TypeScript client, point openapi-typescript at the live spec:

```bash
npx openapi-typescript https://api.flagon.io/openapi.json -o flagon.gen.ts
```

```ts
import type { components, paths } from "./flagon.gen";

type Project = components["schemas"]["Project"];
type ListProjects =
  paths["/orgs/{slug}/projects"]["get"]["responses"]["200"]["content"]["application/json"];
```

Any OpenAPI 3.1 generator works the same way for other languages.

## What the spec does and does not tell you

- **Authentication is not declared in the spec.** It has no security schemes, so
  generated clients will not add a header for you. Send
  `Authorization: Bearer <token>` yourself on every call. See
  [Authentication and scopes](/docs/api/authentication).
- **Some documented operations are not reachable with an access token.** The
  spec lists every registered operation, including those only the dashboard can
  call: token management (`/me/tokens`, `/orgs/<org>/tokens`), the assistant
  (`/ai/messages`, `/ai/actions/execute`), invitation acceptance
  (`/invitations/<token>/accept`), and the internal routes under `/internal/`,
  `/me/profile`, and `/me/deleted`. An access token, even a full-access one, gets `401` on
  these. The
  [scopes reference](/docs/reference/scopes) lists exactly which operations a
  token can reach.
- **`QUERY` list operations are not in the spec.** Every paginated list also
  accepts the HTTP `QUERY` method at the same path (`query-projects`,
  `query-members`, ...). OpenAPI 3.1 has no field for `QUERY`, so these are
  registered as hidden operations: routed, validated, and scope-checked, but not
  documented in the spec. See [Pagination and search](/docs/api/pagination).

## Routes deliberately outside the spec

The spec is the product's **operational** contract: operations on your Flagon
resources. Content about Flagon and infrastructure probes are served by the same
process but registered directly on the router, so they never appear in it:

| Route | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /` | The JSON index of operation URLs. |
| `GET /healthz` | Liveness: `200` whenever the process is up. |
| `GET /readyz` | Readiness: `200` when Postgres is reachable, `503` with the reason otherwise. |
| `GET /internal/rls-check` | The tenant-isolation self-test: `200` when row-level security holds, `503` otherwise. |
| `GET /docs` | Every public documentation page. |
| `GET /docs/nav` | The docs navigation compiled from the `meta.json` files. |
| `GET /docs/search?q=&limit=` | Ranked search over public pages (`limit` defaults to 5). |
| `GET /docs/page?slug=` | One public page by slug, for example `slug=api/openapi`. |
| `GET /roadmap` | The public roadmap: items, stages, and teams. |
| `GET /changelog` | Every changelog entry, newest first. |
| `POST /mcp` | The [MCP server](/docs/ai/mcp) (JSON-RPC). On the dedicated MCP host it is served at `/`. |

The content routes are public, return plain JSON (not problem details), and
answer `503` when their corpus failed to load. They still carry an
`X-Request-Id` header and count toward the rate limit; only `/healthz` and
`/readyz` are exempt from it. They serve only public pages:
internal documentation never leaves the API through them. Prometheus metrics are
served on a separate private port (`METRICS_PORT`, default `9091`) at
`/metrics`, never on the public listener.

## Related

- [Using the API](/docs/api/using-the-api)
- [Scopes reference](/docs/reference/scopes)
- [Pagination and search](/docs/api/pagination)
- [MCP server](/docs/ai/mcp)
- [Content corpora](/docs/architecture/content-corpora)

docs.title: Pagination and search
docs.description: How list endpoints search on the server and page with opaque keyset cursors, Link headers, and the HTTP QUERY method.
headings: First page of projects whose name or slug contains "api":
Querying with a body: the QUERY method
docs.body:
Every paginated list in Flagon shares one convention: results are **searched on
the server** and returned a page at a time, and the next page is reached through
an opaque **cursor** that the API hands you in a `Link` header. A client that can
page one list can page them all.

## Which lists paginate

| Lists | Parameters |
| --- | --- |
| Projects, deleted projects (organization owners and admins only; each row has a `purge_at`), organization members, pending invitations, teams, team members, a team's projects, project collaborators, project teams, project owners | `q`, `limit`, `cursor` (this page) |
| The audit log (`GET /orgs/<org>/audit`) | `q`, `action`, `actor`, `limit`, `cursor` (see "The audit log" below) |
| Notifications (`GET /notifications`) | `limit` only: default 30, values above 100 are clamped to 100, `0` or a negative value means 30; no cursor |
| Organizations, deleted organizations, access tokens, SSO providers | Not paginated: the whole list in one response |

## Parameters

| Param | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `q` | Free-text search, matched case-insensitively against the resource's human columns (a project's name and slug; a person's name, email, and username; an invitation's email). Omit it for no filter. |
| `limit` | Page size. Defaults to 30; values above 100 are clamped to 100; `0` or a negative value means the default. |
| `cursor` | The opaque cursor from the previous page's `Link` header. Omit it for the first page. |

```bash
# First page of projects whose name or slug contains "api":
curl "https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/projects?q=api&limit=20" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"
```

## Following the Link header

The rows come back in the body (`{"projects": [...]}`), and when more exist the
response carries a `Link` header (RFC 8288) with `rel="next"`:

```http
Link: </orgs/acme/projects?cursor=WyJiaWxsaW5nIGFwaSIsIjc1OTE5YWY5LTIwNjQtNGJjZC05OThkLTViNjNlYjQxMWRlNiJd&limit=20&q=api>; rel="next"
Link: </schemas/ProjectsOutputBody.json>; rel="describedBy"
```

Two things to know when you parse it:

- **Pick the `rel="next"` link.** Every response also carries a
  `rel="describedBy"` link to its JSON Schema, so a response can have more than
  one `Link` header.
- **The next URL is a path**, relative to the API's base URL. Resolve it against
  `https://api.flagon.io` (or your self-hosted origin) before requesting it.

The next URL already carries your `q` and `limit`, so you only ever echo back
what Flagon gave you. When there is no `rel="next"` link, you are on the last
page.

```bash
url="/orgs/acme/projects?limit=100"
while [ -n "$url" ]; do
  curl -s -D headers.txt "https://api.flagon.io$url" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN" | jq -r '.projects[].slug'
  url=$(grep -i '^link:' headers.txt | grep 'rel="next"' | sed -E 's/.*<([^>]*)>.*/\1/')
done
```

## Why keyset cursors

Pagination is **keyset**, not page numbers: each page resumes strictly after the
last row of the previous one, ordered by a stable key the database computes (for
projects, the lowercased name and then the id). Deep pages stay as fast as the
first, and rows are never skipped or repeated when data changes underneath you.
The trade-off is that there is **no total count and no page count**: you page
until there is no next link, rather than jumping to "page 7".

- **The cursor is opaque.** Echo it back; do not parse or build it. Its format
  can change without notice.
- **A cursor belongs to its query.** Keep `q` the same while you page. Changing
  the search means starting again from the first page.
- **A malformed or tampered cursor** is rejected with `422` and the detail
  `invalid pagination cursor`.

## Querying with a body: the QUERY method

Long searches can be sent with the HTTP `QUERY` method instead of `GET`. `QUERY`
is a safe, read-only method that carries its parameters in the request body.
Every list in the first row of the table above accepts it at the same path, with
the same three fields in a JSON body:

```bash
curl -X QUERY https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/projects \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"q": "api", "limit": 20}'
```

The response is identical to the `GET` form, including the `Link` header. To
fetch the next page, either follow the `Link` URL with `GET`, or send another
`QUERY` with the cursor from it in the body (`"cursor": "..."`).

`QUERY` is optional; the dashboard uses `GET`. OpenAPI 3.1 has no field for the
`QUERY` method, so these operations (`query-projects`, `query-members`, and so
on) are routed and validated but do not appear in the generated spec. Each one
requires the same scope as its `GET` twin.

## The audit log

`GET /orgs/<org>/audit` pages the same way (newest events first, a `Link` header
with `rel="next"`, `limit` default 30 and clamped to 100, `0` or a negative
value meaning 30) and adds two filters:

| Param | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `q` | Search across the summary, action, actor, and location. |
| `action` | Only these [action keys](/docs/reference/audit-actions). Repeat it for several: `?action=project.created&action=project.deleted`. |
| `actor` | Only events by this user id. |

It has no `QUERY` form. See [Audit log](/docs/platform/audit-log).

## Rules

- **Search is always server-side.** There is no "fetch everything and filter"
  path; `q` does the work in the database.
- **Paging never widens access.** You only ever see rows you could already read,
  and the `QUERY` form requires the same scope as the `GET` form.

## Related

- [Using the API](/docs/api/using-the-api)
- [Expanding responses](/docs/api/expanding-responses)
- [Errors](/docs/api/errors)
- [Limits](/docs/reference/limits)

docs.title: Using the API
docs.description: The base URL, authentication, request and response conventions, errors, pagination, and where the generated OpenAPI spec lives.
headings: The spec is generated from the code
docs.body:
Flagon is API-first: every capability in the product is an HTTP operation in the
Go API before it is anything else. The dashboard, the in-product assistant, and
the MCP server are all clients of the same operations, so anything you can do by
clicking you can also do with `curl`, a script, or a generated client.

This page is the overview. Each convention links to a page with the details.

## Base URL

The hosted API is served at `https://api.flagon.io`. A self-hosted deployment
serves the same API from wherever you run `flagon-server serve` (port `8080` by
default; see [Configuration](/docs/reference/configuration)).

Paths are not versioned: there is no `/v1` prefix. Most resources live under an
organization, addressed by its slug:

```text
https://api.flagon.io/orgs/<org>/projects
https://api.flagon.io/orgs/<org>/projects/<project>/members
```

`GET /` returns a JSON index of every documented operation, keyed as
`<operation_id>_url` (for example `list_projects_url`), plus `openapi_url` and
`openapi_yaml_url`. Two probes sit outside the spec: `GET /healthz` (the process
is up) and `GET /readyz` (the database is reachable; `503` with the reason when
it is not).

## Make your first request

Create a personal access token in the dashboard under **Settings > Personal
access tokens**, export it, and ask the API who you are:

```bash
export FLAGON_TOKEN=flagon_pat_...

curl https://api.flagon.io/me \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"
```

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://api.flagon.io/schemas/MeOutputBody.json",
  "user": {
    "id": "b5e00dae-b1b8-4e4b-9f75-b4afd5b16a4f",
    "email": "you@example.com",
    "created_at": "2026-09-17T16:11:37.91393Z",
    "two_factor_enabled": true
  },
  "orgs": [
    {
      "id": "fcda53fb-3ab8-4b53-9f7f-fca413901062",
      "name": "Acme",
      "slug": "acme",
      "role": "owner",
      "enforce_two_factor": false,
      "require_sso": false,
      "created_at": "2026-09-17T16:14:22.59927Z"
    }
  ]
}
```

Then list the projects in one of those organizations:

```bash
curl "https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/projects?limit=20" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"
```

## Authentication

Every operation except two public reads needs a bearer token. Access tokens
start with `flagon_pat_` (personal, acts as you) or `flagon_oat_`
(organization, acts as a service principal inside one org), and each carries
either full access or a set of [scopes](/docs/reference/scopes). A token can
never exceed what its principal's role allows.

Some operations are never reachable with an access token: minting, listing, and
revoking tokens, and the assistant's own endpoints (`/ai/*`). Those are called
only by the dashboard, so a leaked token cannot mint more tokens. See
[Authentication and scopes](/docs/api/authentication).

## Requests

- **JSON in, JSON out.** Send bodies as `Content-Type: application/json`. Field
  names are `snake_case` (`repository_url`, `expires_in_days`).
- **Resources are addressed by slug** where they have one: `/orgs/acme`,
  `/projects/billing-api`, `/teams/platform`. Members and collaborators are
  addressed by user id (`/members/<userId>`). A deleted organization is restored
  by id (`POST /deleted-orgs/<id>/restore`), because its old slug may belong to
  a new organization by then.
- **Slugs are derived when omitted.** Create operations that take a `slug`
  (organizations, projects, teams) derive it from `name` when you leave it out:
  lowercased, with every run of other characters collapsed to one hyphen.
- **`PATCH` is partial.** Fields you omit are left unchanged; sending `slug`
  renames the resource.
- **Timestamps** are RFC 3339 strings, in requests (`expires_at`) and responses.
- **Bodies are capped.** API operations accept up to 1 MiB, and the server
  caps every route at 4 MiB by default (`FLAGON_MAX_BODY_BYTES`). A larger body
  is rejected with `413`.
- **Request ids.** You may send your own `X-Request-Id` (8 to 128 characters of
  letters, digits, `.`, `_`, and `-`) to correlate a request with your logs;
  otherwise the API generates one.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/projects \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "Billing API", "description": "Subscriptions and invoices"}'
```

The response is `201 Created` with the new project, whose slug is `billing-api`.

## Responses

- **Status codes.** Creates return `201`; everything else that succeeds returns
  `200`, including deletes.
- **Single objects are returned bare**, for example a project's fields at the
  top level. **Lists are wrapped** in an object keyed by the resource:
  `{"projects": [...]}`, `{"members": [...]}`, `{"events": [...]}`.
- **Deletes return a body**: the deleted resource (projects, organizations) or
  `{"ok": true}`.
- **Every response carries an `X-Request-Id` header.** Quote it when you
  report a failure; the server logs the underlying cause of any `5xx` under that
  id, and never puts internal error text in the response body.
- **Every JSON body carries a `$schema` link** to the JSON Schema that describes
  it, and the response has a matching `Link: <...>; rel="describedBy"` header.
  Ignore both if you do not need them.
- **References, not embedded objects.** A project carries `org_id`, not the
  organization. Ask for the object inline with
  [`expand[]`](/docs/api/expanding-responses).

## Errors

Failures are RFC 9457 problem details (`application/problem+json`) with
`title`, `status`, `detail`, and, for validation failures, an `errors` list.
Resources you cannot see return `404`, never `403`, so the API does not confirm
that something exists outside your reach; `403` means you can see the resource
but are not allowed to do that to it. See [Errors](/docs/api/errors).

## Rate limits

Each principal (a signed-in user, an access token, or the client IP for
unauthenticated requests) may make 50 requests per second sustained, in bursts of
up to 300, on each API instance. Over that, the API answers `429 Too Many
Requests` with a `Retry-After` header in seconds; wait and retry. Self-hosted
deployments tune this with `FLAGON_RATE_LIMIT` and `FLAGON_RATE_BURST`. The
assistant also has a separate per-organization daily allowance, which returns
`429` without `Retry-After`. See [Limits](/docs/reference/limits).

## Lists and pagination

Every paginated list takes `q` (search), `limit` (1 to 100, default 30), and an
opaque `cursor`, and returns the next page's URL in a `Link: <...>; rel="next"`
header. The same lists also accept the HTTP `QUERY` method with those fields in
a JSON body. See [Pagination and search](/docs/api/pagination).

## The spec is generated from the code

The OpenAPI 3.1 document is generated from the Go handlers, never written by
hand, and served live at `https://api.flagon.io/openapi.json` and
`/openapi.yaml`. Generate typed clients from it; see
[OpenAPI and clients](/docs/api/openapi).

## Related

- [Authentication and scopes](/docs/api/authentication)
- [Errors](/docs/api/errors)
- [OpenAPI and clients](/docs/api/openapi)
- [Scopes reference](/docs/reference/scopes)
- [Limits](/docs/reference/limits)

docs.title: AI runtime
docs.description: How the in-product assistant runs inside the Go API, from provider selection and the system prompt through org confinement, the tool loop, proposals, and per-organization metering.
headings: The system prompt is a swappable skill file
docs.body:
The assistant in the dashboard is not a separate service. It runs inside the Go
API (`api/internal/ai`), next to the operations it calls, and it uses the same
[tool registry](/docs/architecture/tool-registry) the MCP server does. This page
covers the runtime around that registry: which model answers, what instructions it
gets, how a turn executes, how changes wait for your confirmation, and how usage
is counted and capped per organization.

Two ideas shape the design. The **model is the brain and the tools are the
hands**: the model only has to pick a tool and fill in its arguments, and the
tool does the work through the permission-checked service layer. And the model is
**configuration, not code**: you can swap providers, including a model you host
yourself, without rebuilding Flagon.

```text
   Ask AI panel                                  Provider (from config)
        │ messages + org_id                   ┌────────────────────────┐
        ▼                                     │ anthropic              │
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐      │ openai-compatible      │
 │ POST /ai/messages   (internal auth) │      │ mock (offline)         │
 └──────────────────┬──────────────────┘      └────────────▲───────────┘
                    ▼                                      │
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐                   │
 │ 1. Caller is a member of org_id? 404│                   │
 │ 2. Org 2FA and SSO policy met?   403│                   │
 │ 3. Org under its daily limit?    429│                   │
 └──────────────────┬──────────────────┘                   │
                    ▼                                      │
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐    Complete()     │
 │ 4. Agent loop, up to 6 model calls  ├───────────────────┘
 │    other org named -> refused       │
 │    read tool       -> run, feed back│
 │    mutating tool   -> proposal      │
 └──────────────────┬──────────────────┘
                    ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ 5. Record usage in ai_usage      503│
 └──────────────────┬──────────────────┘
                    ▼
   reply + proposals  ->  you confirm  ->  POST /ai/actions/execute
```

## Providers

A **provider** is the adapter to a language model. The interface in
`api/internal/ai/provider.go` has two methods: `Complete`, which sends a system
prompt, the conversation, and the tool definitions and returns content blocks,
a stop reason, and token usage; and `DefaultModel`. The block model (text,
`tool_use`, `tool_result`) is shared by every backend, so the agent loop never
knows which one is running.

| Backend | File | Default model | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Anthropic | `anthropic.go` | `claude-haiku-4-5` | Messages API over plain HTTP, 60 second timeout. |
| OpenAI-compatible | `openai.go` | `gpt-4o-mini` | Chat Completions with function calling, 120 second timeout. Base URL defaults to `https://api.openai.com/v1`; point it at OpenRouter, Together, Groq, vLLM, or Ollama. The API key may be empty for keyless local servers. |
| Mock | `mock.go` | `mock` | Offline and deterministic. Matches keywords such as "create" or "list" to tools, so the assistant works with no keys and no network. |

### Selecting a provider

`buildProvider` in `api/cmd/flagon-server/main.go` passes the settings to
`ai.SelectProvider` (`api/internal/ai/select.go`), which reads `FLAGON_AI_PROVIDER`:

- `auto` (the default, also used when unset): Anthropic if `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is
  set, otherwise the OpenAI-compatible backend if `FLAGON_AI_API_KEY` or
  `FLAGON_AI_BASE_URL` is set, otherwise the mock. `auto` never fails.
- `anthropic`, `openai`, or `mock` pin that backend. A pinned backend without its
  credentials is a startup error: `anthropic` needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, and
  `openai` needs an API key or a base URL (a keyless local server). The server
  refuses to boot rather than fail on every turn.
- Any other value is a startup error too.

If the chosen backend turns out to have no usable key at request time, or the
provider answers `401` or `403`, the turn fails with `503` ("the AI agent is not
configured") rather than an opaque `500`.

`FLAGON_AI_MODEL` overrides the model for whichever backend is chosen.
`OPENAI_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_BASE_URL` are accepted as fallbacks for the
OpenAI-compatible settings. The server logs the chosen provider and model at
startup, and logs a warning when it is running on the mock. The full list of
settings is on [Configuration](/docs/reference/configuration).

## The system prompt is a swappable skill file

The instructions the model receives live in `DefaultSystemPrompt` in
`api/internal/ai/agent.go`. In short, they tell the model that it only helps with
Flagon and should decline anything else, that tools run as the current user, that
questions about how Flagon works should be answered from `search_docs` and
`get_doc` rather than memory, and that changes are proposed and must never be
described as done.

Set `FLAGON_AI_SYSTEM_PROMPT_FILE` to a path and the server loads that file
instead, at startup. An unreadable file logs a warning and keeps the built-in
prompt; an empty file is ignored the same way. This is the cheapest lever for
tuning behavior, especially on small or self-hosted models that lean heavily on
clear instructions, and it needs a restart, not a rebuild.

## A turn, step by step

The dashboard's Ask AI panel posts to the app route `/api/ai/messages`, and the
app forwards to the API's `POST /ai/messages` with its internal token and the
verified user id. Access tokens cannot call this endpoint; it is app-only. The
request body carries the organization id and the conversation so far as plain
text messages. The API stores no conversation history of its own.

1. **Membership.** The handler (`api/internal/server/ai.go`) confirms the caller
   belongs to `org_id` and resolves its slug, or the request fails with `404`. The
   check exists because `org_id` decides which organization is metered: without
   it, a caller could name a foreign org, pass the quota check (row-level security
   would count zero calls), and get an unrecorded turn.
2. **Org policy.** `service.CheckOrgAccess` applies the org's 2FA and SSO
   requirements to the conversation, exactly as for any `/orgs/{slug}` request, or
   the request fails with `403`.
3. **Quota.** The meter counts the org's rows in `ai_usage` from the last 24 hours
   and rejects the turn with `429` if the count has reached the limit.
4. **The loop.** The agent calls the provider with the system prompt, every tool
   definition in the registry, and the messages, allowing up to 1024 output tokens
   per call. If the model stops to call tools, each call is handled in turn:
   - an unknown tool name returns an error result to the model;
   - a call that would act outside the conversation's org (an `org` argument
     naming another org, or a `CrossOrg` tool such as `restore_organization`) is
     refused with an error result, before it is run or proposed;
   - a **read** tool runs immediately as the user, and its JSON result goes back
     to the model;
   - a **mutating** tool is not run. It becomes a proposal, and the model is told
     the action is waiting for confirmation.

   The loop repeats until the model stops asking for tools or it has made six
   model calls. Internal documentation is readable in this conversation, because
   it always acts for a signed-in user.
5. **Record.** The turn's total input and output tokens are written to `ai_usage`
   as one row. If that write fails, the whole turn fails with `503` ("AI usage
   could not be recorded"). This is deliberate: an unrecorded turn would not count
   against the quota, and unmetered AI is exactly what the quota exists to prevent.

The response contains the model's final text, the list of proposals, and the token
totals.

Tool errors are sanitized before the model sees them. A classified error (for
example "you don't have permission to do that") passes through; anything else is
logged and replaced with a generic message, so internal details never enter the
conversation.

## Proposals and confirmation

A **proposal** is a mutating tool call held for a person to approve. It carries
the tool name, the exact input the model chose, and a summary sentence produced by
the tool's `Summarize` function, such as `Delete project "billing" in "acme"`. The
summary is generated by code from the input, not written by the model.

Confirming a proposal posts the tool name and input to `POST /ai/actions/execute`
(also app-only). The API checks membership of `org_id` and the org's access policy
again. `Execute` then runs the tool only if it exists and is marked `Mutating`
(anything else is `400`), only if it stays inside the conversation's org (`403`
otherwise), and only if the org still has quota (`429` otherwise). The tool runs as
the signed-in user through the service layer, so the store's role checks,
row-level security, and audit recording all apply exactly as if you had clicked
the button in the UI, and the audit entry records the end user's IP, country, and
user agent forwarded by the app. Errors come back with the same status the
matching REST operation would return (`403`, `404`, `409`, `422`).

The confirmation step lives in the dashboard. The Ask AI panel has two modes:
**Ask before editing** (the default) shows each proposal with a confirm button,
and **Automatically edit** makes the browser post every proposal to
`/ai/actions/execute` as soon as the turn returns, for the rest of that
conversation. The mode is held in the page's memory and resets to Ask when the
page reloads. The API cannot tell the two apart: in both cases the change runs
only because the browser asked for it, as the signed-in user.

A successful action writes an `ai_usage` row with model `action:<tool>` and zero
tokens. A failure to write that row is logged but does not fail the response,
because the change has already committed and reporting it as failed would invite
a duplicate retry.

## Metering

Usage lives in the `public.ai_usage` table (migration `0004_ai_usage.sql`):
organization, user, model, input and output tokens, and a timestamp. Row-level
security is forced on it, so a user can read and write usage only for
organizations they belong to.

The meter (`api/internal/ai/meter.go`) caps **calls per organization per rolling
24 hours**, where one call is one row: an assistant turn (however many model calls
it made) or one confirmed action. The cap is `FLAGON_AI_DAILY_LIMIT`, default
`100`. `0` disables the cap and should never be used in production. The same
limit applies to every organization today; per-plan limits are not built yet, and
the dashboard's Usage page is a "Coming soon" preview that does not read this
table. See [Usage](/docs/platform/usage).

Two things are worth knowing:

- The limit is checked before a turn starts and again before a confirmed action
  runs, so an org at its limit cannot confirm proposals it already has until the
  window rolls forward.
- `org_id` scopes reach as well as metering. The conversation is confined to that
  organization: a tool call naming another org is refused, so usage is always
  metered against the org the work happens in. To work in another org, switch to
  it in the dashboard.

MCP calls are not metered here: no model runs on Flagon's side for them, since the
external client brings its own.

## Staying on topic

The assistant is scoped to Flagon by two things: it is given only Flagon tools,
and the system prompt instructs it to decline anything unrelated. There is no
separate classifier, so how strictly off-topic requests are refused depends on the
model following its instructions. What does not depend on the model is the
ceiling: every tool acts as the user, so the assistant cannot read or change
anything the user could not. See [AI safety](/docs/security/ai-safety).

## Related

<Cards>
  <Card title="Tool registry" href="/docs/architecture/tool-registry" description="The one registry behind the assistant, MCP, and the REST API." />
  <Card title="Assistant" href="/docs/ai/assistant" description="Using the assistant from the dashboard." />
  <Card title="AI safety" href="/docs/security/ai-safety" description="Permissions, confirmation, quota, and prompt injection." />
  <Card title="Configuration" href="/docs/reference/configuration" description="Every AI environment variable and flag." />
</Cards>

docs.title: Auditing and notifications
docs.description: How Flagon records every organization change in an append-only audit log inside the same transaction, and how that differs from per-person notifications.
headings: The "where": request context, not function arguments
docs.body:
Flagon writes two kinds of records when something changes, and they answer
different questions. The **audit log** answers "what happened to this
