**In practice:** you make decisions you won't resent in three years. You don't borrow against the future to make this quarter look good, not with the code, not with the trust, not with people's [energy](/handbook/time-off). You'd rather build something durable slowly than something impressive that collapses.

**What it does not mean:** slow as a personality, or using "long term" to dodge every hard call. The long game is a reason to be decisive now, not an excuse to defer forever. Patience isn't procrastination with better branding.

## Values are behavior, not posters

<Callout type="brand">
  A value you won't act on when it's inconvenient is just a slogan. These count
  when they cost something.
</Callout>

The test for any of these is what happens when it's expensive: when "make good things" means slipping a date, when "open by default" means publishing something awkward, when "the long game" means turning down easy money. That's when they count. We'd rather have four we actually use than twenty we recite. If you catch us not living them, that's a bug; say so, [here](https://github.com/flagon-io) or at [hey@flagon.io](mailto:hey@flagon.io).

docs.title: Visiting customers as an engineer
docs.description: Some things never show up on a call. Sitting next to someone while they use what you built is one of the highest-leverage things an engineer here can do.
docs.body:
We're a [remote company](/handbook/working-async), and most of the time that's exactly right. But there's a specific kind of understanding you only get in the room: watching someone use your product with their real data, their real workflow, and the three other tools they alt-tab to without thinking. People are more candid in person than in any written reply, and the friction that never quite makes it into a support ticket is obvious the moment you see it happen. Going to visit a customer is one of the best uses of an engineer's time we know of, and it's open to you, not just to a sales team.

## Who's worth visiting

The best visits are with customers who are already friendly and engaged: they give feedback without being chased, they actually want the product to get better, and they use it enough that there's something real to watch. A team that's at least partly in one office is ideal, because the point is to see people work, together, the way they normally do.

## Plan it well

A good visit is prepared for, not improvised.

1. **Know what you're going in to learn.** Go through the [support signal](/handbook/support-and-care), past calls, and what you've heard from [listening to users](/handbook/listening-to-users), and write down the pressing issues and the things you're most curious about.
2. **Find one point of contact** on their side to coordinate. Two or three days is usually the right length: enough for real time with people, not so much that you're underfoot. Tying it to a moment they're together anyway, like their own offsite, works well.
3. **Sort the logistics early.** Book travel ahead, and clear the budget with People and Ops the way [spending money](/handbook/spending-money) describes. This is normal, encouraged spending, not a favor you have to justify.
4. **Set a light agenda.** Block an hour each with a few different users. Offer something useful in return, a short training session or an open Q&A, so it's worth their time too.
5. **Do your homework.** Watch how they actually use the product before you go, so you're asking sharp questions instead of the ones five minutes of looking would have answered.

## While you're there

Let people show you, don't present at them. Ask someone to do a normal task and watch where they hesitate, where they work around something, where they expected a thing to be and it wasn't. That hesitation is the gold.

<Callout type="brand">
  If you can fix a small thing and ship it while you're still sitting there, do it. Turning "this annoys me" into "it's fixed, refresh the page" in the same afternoon is the single most convincing thing you can do in the room.
</Callout>

Be generous with your help, even on things outside the part of the product you own. You're the face of the whole company for those few days, and [owning what you build](/handbook/feature-ownership) stretches a little wider than usual while you're a guest.

## After you're home

The visit isn't done when you fly back. Write up what you learned and share it with your team, and be willing to re-order what you were planning to build in light of it, since you now know something the roadmap didn't. Then actually do the things: ship the fixes, and tell them you did, listing what changed because of their time. Following up in the weeks after is what turns a nice visit into a customer who trusts you, and it's the same [product engineering](/handbook/product-engineering) instinct as everything else: talk to users, then close the loop.

docs.title: Where we're going
docs.description: Our direction and what winning looks like, without a dated roadmap.
headings: People who are proud to work here
Direction, not a promise about products
docs.body:
People expect this page to be a roadmap: a list of features with quarters next to them. It isn't, and it won't be. We keep a [public roadmap](/roadmap) for what we're building; this page is about the direction underneath it. Dated roadmaps age badly and mostly exist to make a company look decisive on a slide. What we can tell you honestly is the kind of company we're building toward, and how we'd know we were succeeding. That's more durable than a Gantt chart, and it's the part that actually steers the decisions.

## The company we're building toward

We're building a small software company that's still here in ten years, still making things people are glad to use, still run in the open. Not the biggest, not the loudest, not the one with the flashiest funding announcement. The one that's good, and stays good, and that people trust because it's earned it over a long time.

That's a specific ambition, not a modest one. Plenty of companies get big. Very few stay good while doing it. We'd rather be the second kind. This is what [the long game](/handbook/values#the-long-game) means in practice: we optimize for still being proud of this years from now, which rules out a lot of tempting shortcuts today.

## How we'd know we're winning

Growth charts are easy to game and easy to fake, so we don't treat them as the scoreboard. Here's what we actually watch.

**Craft that holds up.** The real test isn't whether the demo dazzles. It's whether the thing still feels good to use a year in, when the novelty's gone and it's just part of your day. Work that ages well is the hardest kind to fake, so it's the kind we measure ourselves against.

**Trust you can measure by reading us.** Because we work in the open, anyone can check whether we do what we say. If the handbook and the behavior match, if you can read our reasoning and find it honest, that's a form of winning that doesn't show up in revenue. We want to be a company you can audit and come away trusting more, not less.

**Durability.** Can we survive a bad quarter without abandoning our principles? Can we say no to money that would cost us the values? A company that only holds its line when times are good doesn't really have a line. Winning is being the kind of business that stays itself under pressure.

<Callout type="brand" title="The scoreboard we care about">
  Would the people who use our work be genuinely sad if we disappeared? Would
  the people who build it be proud to say they did? If both are yes, we're
  winning, whatever the chart says.
</Callout>

## People who are proud to work here

The other half of "where we're going" is who's coming with us. We want Flagon to be a place a small crew of capable people are genuinely proud to be part of, because the work is good, the treatment is fair, and nobody has to leave their integrity at the door.

That's a real constraint on how we grow. We'd rather stay small and be somewhere people are proud of than get big and become somewhere people tolerate. If growing means turning this into a place we wouldn't recommend to a friend, then growing that way is off the table.

## Direction, not a promise about products

Notice what this page doesn't do: it doesn't name a specific product, a date, or a feature. That's deliberate. What we make will change as we learn, and pinning ourselves to a wall of dated promises is exactly the kind of showmanship we try to avoid. See [built in public](/handbook/values) for why.

What won't change is the direction: good things, made honestly, for the long term, by people who are proud to make them. Everything specific serves that. If you want to hold us to something, hold us to this.

docs.title: Which products to build
docs.description: How we decide what to build, starting from the foundation and building up, never sideways into a worse version of five other tools.
headings: Sync is the point, not a plugin
docs.body:
Deciding what to build is mostly deciding what not to. Here's the rule we hold ourselves to, so the decision isn't remade from scratch every time a good-sounding idea shows up. The day-to-day version of this, the way a team sets its priorities, is [deciding what to build](/handbook/deciding-what-to-build).

## Start at the foundation

Flagon begins as a multi-tenant platform where people define and manage their products and teams. That is the foundation, and it comes first, done properly, before anything clever gets built on top of it. Tenancy, ownership, and the core model of products and teams are the thing everything else depends on, so they get the care of a foundation, not the speed of a feature.

## Build up, not sideways

Once the foundation holds, we add the things that make it more useful: keeping definitions in sync, an API and SDKs to build against, access control, history. What we don't do is wander sideways into unrelated features because a competitor has them. A pile of features bolted onto the side just makes us a worse version of five other tools. If it doesn't make products and teams as a source of truth more true, more useful, or more trustworthy, it's a no, even when it's a good idea in the abstract.

## Sync is the point, not a plugin

The definitions have to stay true in the tools people already live in. So synchronization, in both directions, is foundational work. We don't treat it as an integration to bolt on once the "real" product is done. Being the source of truth means nothing if the truth can't reach the places that need it.

## We decide in the open

None of this happens behind a curtain. What we're weighing, what we've committed to, and what we've said no to lives on the public [roadmap](/roadmap), and the reasoning gets written down the same way we [make every other decision](/handbook/decisions). If we change our minds, you'll see why.

docs.title: Who we build for
docs.description: The teams Flagon is for, the person who feels the problem first, and who we're honestly not for.
headings: The person who feels it first
docs.body:
We build for the people responsible for how a software organization is put together: its products, its teams, who owns what, and how all of that stays true across the dozen other tools that each think they own the answer.

## The team we build for

Growing software companies where the shape of the org matters and keeps drifting. Products get renamed, teams reorganize, ownership changes, and the truth of it ends up smeared across a spreadsheet, a wiki, an identity provider, and three tools that each hold a slightly different version. Somebody spends their week reconciling that by hand, and it's still wrong by Friday.

That somebody, and the platform, engineering, and operations leaders who feel the cost of it, are who we build for.

## The person who feels it first

Usually an engineer or a platform person. They want products and teams defined once, in a system built to be the source of truth, and they want every other tool to sync with that instead of drifting from it. They don't want another place to re-enter the same org chart. They want the place the org chart actually lives, that the rest of their stack agrees with.

We go hard on making that person's life better first. Get it right for them, and the value spreads to everyone downstream who was quietly paying for the drift.

## Who we're not for

A tiny team where a shared doc is genuinely enough. If the shape of your org fits in your head, you don't need us yet, and we'd rather say so than sell you something you'll resent.

Organizations that want a locked box with no way out, either. Your definitions are yours, sync goes both directions, and export is always on the table. If lock-in is the point for you, we're the wrong choice. The fuller version of that honesty is on [who Flagon is for, and who it isn't](/not-for-everyone).

docs.title: Why Flagon exists
docs.description: The reason we started, and the one bet the whole company runs on.
docs.body:
There is already plenty of software, and plenty of companies making it. We started another one anyway. Here is why.

## Why we started

We wanted to work somewhere that operated the way we thought a company should, and it was easier to build one than to keep waiting for it to appear.

Most of us have worked at places where the stated values and the actual behavior drifted apart: the handbook said one thing, the calendar said another, and decisions arrived as law from rooms you were never in. None of that is unusual. It is just tiring, and it makes the software worse, because the people closest to the work stop bothering to have opinions. Flagon is the attempt to not do that. Not a manifesto about it, an actual company, run out loud so you can check whether we mean it.

## The one bet

Everything here rests on a single bet: that building in the open is an advantage, not a liability.

Trust is not something you buy with a marketing budget. It is a track record someone can read. So we publish the track record as we go, the [handbook](/handbook), the [roadmap](/roadmap), the reasoning, the misfires, and when we get something wrong the wrong version stays in the git history. Working this way makes the work sharper too: a decision you have to defend in public tends to lose its weak points before it ships. That is the whole thesis. The rest of this handbook is what it looks like in practice.

## What we are not doing

We are not optimizing for a quick exit. There is no acquisition we are steering toward and no plan to flip this to someone bigger. The goal is boring and hard: to still be here in a decade, still making good things, still a company worth working at. That one choice quietly settles a lot of the others, from [how we pay people](/handbook/compensation) to [how we make money](/handbook/how-we-make-money) to how fast we grow. It's [one of our values](/handbook/values#the-long-game), and the reason [staying alive](/handbook/staying-alive) matters more than looking impressive.

If watching a company try to do this in public sounds interesting rather than terrifying, you are probably our kind of person.

docs.title: Working async
docs.description: Non-linear workdays, written-first by default, and why async is what makes remote humane.
headings: Your day is yours to arrange
Write so nobody has to be online at once
What a reasonable reply looks like
Why this is the humane version
docs.body:
[How we communicate](/handbook/communication) covers the tone and the tools. This page is about the shape of the day. Async isn't a communication style we picked for flavor. It's the thing that lets a remote company actually work without quietly turning into a company that expects everyone online from 9 to 5 in one timezone, just spread across the internet.

## Your day is yours to arrange

We don't run on a shared clock. There are no fixed hours you're expected to be at your desk, no green-dot surveillance, no assumption that being visible is the same as doing the work. You know when you think well. Some people do their best work at 6am, some at 11pm, some in two blocks with a long gap where they go outside and remember they're a person. Arrange the day around that.

The deal underneath this is simple: we care about the work landing, not the hours you kept while making it. If your work is good and your teammates aren't stuck waiting on you, nobody needs to know or care what your Tuesday looked like.

<Callout type="note" title="Offline at 2, back at 8">
  A non-linear day means you can drop offline at 2pm for a doctor's
  appointment, a school pickup, or a walk, and pick the thread back up at 8.
  You don't owe anyone an explanation or a made-up excuse. Just don't leave
  someone blocked while you're gone: hand off first.
</Callout>

## Write so nobody has to be online at once

The whole thing falls apart if the work only makes sense in real time. Write for the person who reads this six hours from now, in a different timezone, with none of the context that's currently in your head.

That means: say what you need and by when. Include the links, the background, and the version of the question that doesn't require a reply just to figure out what you're asking. Make a decision request answerable in one pass instead of a back-and-forth that spans two workdays because you each caught the other's reply too late. If you find yourself writing "let's hop on a call to align," first try writing the thing you'd say on the call. Usually the call disappears.

You've written it well when someone can pick up your message cold and move without you. When that's true, timezones stop being a tax.

## What a reasonable reply looks like

Async is not an excuse to go dark, and it's not a demand that you answer instantly. Both of those break it.

A good default: reply to normal things within a work day, roughly a day. That's not a rule with a stopwatch, it's an expectation you can plan around. It means nobody should feel they have to sit on a message refreshing for an answer, and nobody should feel they have to answer at midnight to seem committed.

The exceptions are marked. If something is genuinely time-sensitive, say so explicitly and say why, and reach for something faster than a comment thread. If it isn't marked urgent, treat it as not urgent, and protect your focus accordingly. An unread message is not an emergency by default.

## Why this is the humane version

It's easy to frame async as a productivity hack, the thing that gets you long uninterrupted focus blocks. It does. But the deeper reason is fairness.

The alternative, real-time by default, quietly punishes anyone who isn't in the founder's timezone, anyone with kids or care duties, anyone whose good hours don't match the calendar's. Meetings-first remote work re-centers all of that on whoever happens to be online when the conversation happens, and everyone else inherits the decisions secondhand. Async refuses that. It says the record is the meeting, the writing is the room, and you can be a full participant from anywhere on Earth without rearranging your life around a clock you didn't choose.

That's the point. Remote-first only earns the name if you can genuinely live somewhere and be a full colleague, and async is what makes it true. If you want the norms for when real-time is the right call, [how we communicate](/handbook/communication) has them, and [how we work](/handbook/how-we-work) has the wider picture.

docs.title: Working here
docs.description: What it's actually like to work at Flagon, who thrives, and who won't.
docs.body:
This is the honest pitch, not the recruiting version. It tells you what you'd actually be signing up for, rough edges included. Read it before you decide you want in.

## Who thrives here

Self-directed people who care about craft. If you see something broken and your instinct is to fix it rather than file a ticket and wait, you'll feel at home. We hand you a problem and the room to solve it, and then we mostly get out of your way. That's freedom, and it's also a weight. Nobody is going to hover over you with a plan.

The people who do well here are opinionated but not precious. They write things down. They'd rather ship one good thing than ten fine ones, and they can tell the difference. They're comfortable being wrong in public and correcting course without making it a whole thing.

## Who won't

People who need a lot of structure. There's no dense process to hide inside, no manager assigning your day, no meeting that tells you what you're supposed to think. If that sounds unnerving rather than freeing, this will be a hard place to work, and that's a real answer. Not everyone wants the same job.

People who need an audience won't either. The status meeting, the deck built for the sake of the deck, the performance of being busy: we don't have those, and we won't invent them for anyone. See our [values](/handbook/values) for what we do instead.

## What we expect

- **Ownership.** You own outcomes, not tasks. "It wasn't my job" isn't a sentence we say much.
- **Writing.** We're remote and we build in the open, so writing is as much the job as the code is. If it isn't written down somewhere others can find it, it barely happened.
- **Working in public.** Most of what we make is readable by anyone. That takes a little courage at first and then becomes normal.

## Remote-first, and what that means

We're remote by default and async by habit. That's not a perk, it's the design: we want the best person for a thing, not the closest one, and we want a workday that bends around your life instead of the other way around. It works because we write instead of interrupt, and because "I'll get to it" is a fine answer to most messages. See [how we work](/handbook/how-we-work) for the mechanics, and [time off](/handbook/time-off) for how we think about hours.

<Callout type="note" title="Async isn't 'never talk'">
  We still hop on calls when a doc is going in circles. Async is the default,
  not a rule you get punished for breaking. Use judgment.
</Callout>

## Your first week

There's no boot camp. Week one is mostly reading and doing. You'll read the handbook, poke around the [code](https://github.com/flagon-io), and pick up something small and real (a fix, a paper cut, a rough edge) and ship it. We'd rather you touch the actual work early than sit through a week of onboarding slides. Someone will be your point of contact, questions in the [Discord](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN) are always fair game, and nobody expects you to have it all loaded in your head by Friday.

## We're small and early

Be clear-eyed about this. We're a small company early in our story, building in the open, and that's the upside and the catch in the same breath.

The upside: there's a lot still open, and you get to shape it. Your fingerprints will be all over what Flagon becomes. There's no legacy to apologize for, no committee to convince.

The catch: some things are held together with tape. Not everything is documented. Priorities shift when we learn something. If you need a company that's already got everything figured out, we're not it yet. But if you'd rather help figure it out, that's exactly the job. Come say hi at [hey@flagon.io](mailto:hey@flagon.io).

docs.title: Working in GitHub
docs.description: GitHub is where the work actually lives: the code, the handbook, the roadmap, and most of the decisions. Here's how we use it.
docs.body:
Most companies scatter their work across a chat app, a wiki, a task tracker, a docs tool, and six people's memories. We try to keep it in one place. For us that place is [GitHub](https://github.com/flagon-io): the code lives there, so does this handbook, the roadmap, and most of the decisions that shape the company. If it matters and it's writeable, it probably belongs in a repo, in the open. This is the mechanical side of [how this handbook works](/handbook/how-this-handbook-works) and [defaulting to open](/handbook/values).

## Why one place

When the work lives in one system, a new person can reconstruct how the company got here by reading, rather than by asking around and hoping someone remembers. Issues hold the discussion, pull requests hold the change and the reasoning, and the history holds the "why." A decision made in a disappearing chat message is one the company will have to make again in six months; a decision made in a pull request is one anyone can find later.

## How we use it

- **Issues are for thinking out loud.** A problem, a proposal, a rough idea: open an issue, describe it, and let people poke at it in public. Half-formed and visible beats polished and private.
- **Pull requests are how things change,** whether the thing is code or a handbook page. You make the edit, explain why in the description, and it gets reviewed and discussed before it merges. The reasoning lives next to the change.
- **Write the "why" down,** in the PR description, the commit, the issue. The diff shows what changed; you're on the hook for why. Future readers, including future you, need the reasoning more than the mechanics.
- **Public by default.** Work happens in public repos unless there's a specific reason it can't (see [what we keep private](/handbook/transparency-levels)). Closing something should have to justify itself; opening it shouldn't.

## New to working this way?

If GitHub has mostly been a code thing for you, using it to run a company can feel odd at first, and that's fine. You don't need to be a git wizard. The core loop is small: open an issue to raise something, open a pull request to change something, and say why in plain words. Ask in [Discord](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN) if you get stuck; someone will happily walk you through it.

<Callout type="brand" title="If it isn't written down, it didn't happen">
  A decision that lives only in someone's head is a decision the company doesn't
  really have yet. Writing it into an issue or a PR is how a small crew keeps
  working after the person who knew is off that day, or gone.
</Callout>

docs.title: Writing blogs as an engineer
docs.description: You just solved something hard and interesting. Writing it up is worth more than you think, both to the people who'll read it and to you. Here's how.
docs.body:
We [build in the open](/handbook/open-source), and writing about the work is part of that. When an engineer here writes up something they figured out, it does a surprising amount at once: it helps someone stuck on the same problem, it brings us users and future colleagues who like how we think, and it becomes the reference the next person on our own team reaches for. The [blog](/blog) is open to you. You don't need permission to start writing, and you don't need to be a "writer."

## What's worth writing about

The audience is people like you: engineers at growing companies, hitting the kind of problems you hit. Two questions tell you if a topic is worth a post:

- Would you send this to an engineer friend as "oh, you'll find this interesting"?
- Would it have saved you time or taught you something two years ago?

If either is a yes, write it. The most common mistake is assuming your thing is too obvious to bother with. It almost never is. The specific problem you just chased down, with the real numbers and the wrong turns you took, is exactly the post nobody else can write, because they didn't live it.

<Callout type="note" title="You underrate your own experience">
  The stuff that feels routine to you, the migration you just survived, the bug that took three days, the tradeoff you agonized over, is precisely the stuff other engineers are searching for and can't find written down honestly.
</Callout>

## How to write one

A structure that reliably works:

- **Hook:** the surprising result or the pain, up top. Earn the next paragraph.
- **Context:** just enough background for a stranger to follow, no more.
- **The journey:** what you tried, what failed, what worked, and what you'd tell your past self. The failures are the interesting part; don't tidy them out.
- **Resolution:** the specific change, the actual numbers, a chart or a screenshot if it helps.

Write it the way you'd write a good Slack message, an email to a colleague, or an internal RFC: plain and direct, in [our voice](/handbook/brand-voice) and the habits from [how we write](/handbook/how-we-write). Don't reach for a corporate register you'd never use in person. Name your sections for what's in them, not "Background" and "Conclusion."

On AI: use it to research, to outline, to sharpen a rough draft. Don't have it write the whole thing. Readers can feel a post that no human really wrote, and they discount it instantly, which defeats the entire point of putting your name on it.

## Getting it published

The mechanics are the same as any other change, because a post is just an `.mdx` file in `content/blog`:

1. Float the idea if you want early eyes, but you don't have to.
2. Open a draft pull request with the post in `content/blog`.
3. Ask for an editorial review. Expect a round or two of notes; that's the process working, not a verdict on you.
4. Merge, and it publishes.

Then, the uncomfortable but necessary part: share it. Post it where the people who'd care will see it. It feels like bragging and it isn't; a post nobody reads helped nobody, and the writing was the hard part, not the sharing. This is the last mile of [building in the open](/handbook/open-source), and it's the same standard we hold [docs](/handbook/documentation) to: if it was worth making, it's worth someone actually finding.

docs.title: Your first week
docs.description: What to expect on day one and through week one, and why the goal is momentum.
docs.body:
Welcome aboard. The goal of your first week is simple: get you comfortable, get you set up, and get you shipping something small and real. We're not going to hand you a two-week reading list and disappear. You learn this place by doing things in it, so we'll get you doing things quickly. For how we run onboarding on our end, and what we owe you, see [onboarding](/handbook/onboarding).

## Day one

Day one is mostly about getting the machinery working and meeting the people. Expect it to be low-drama on purpose.

- **Get your tools.** Accounts, access, hardware, the [GitHub org](https://github.com/flagon-io), and the [Discord](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN) where most of the day-to-day happens. If something's missing or broken, say so; sorting out access is normal first-day friction, not a you problem.
- **Meet your people.** You'll get introduced to the crew and pointed at who owns what. We're small, so this is short, and there's no org chart to memorize.
- **Start reading the handbook.** Not all of it, not today. Start with [working here](/handbook/working-here) and the values, then pull up specific pages when you have a specific question. The handbook is the source of truth; when you're unsure how something works, it's the first place to look.

Nobody expects you to be productive on day one. If you end the day with a working setup and a rough sense of who's who, that's a good day one.

## Through the week

The rest of the week is about turning "set up" into "moving." The thing we care about most is that you ship something small before the week is out.

It doesn't matter how small. A doc fix, a tiny bug, a rough edge you noticed and smoothed. The point isn't the size of the change, it's going through the whole loop once: find the thing, make the change, get it reviewed, ship it. That single trip through the pipeline teaches you more about how we work than any onboarding deck could.

<Callout type="brand" title="Ship something in week one">
  Your first-week win isn't a big feature. It's proof that you can move an idea
  all the way to shipped here. Small and real beats large and hypothetical.
</Callout>

## Ask anything

You will not understand everything in week one. Nobody does, and pretending otherwise just slows you down, so ask. There are no dumb questions in your first month, and honestly not many after that either.

If you're stuck for more than a little while, reach out instead of grinding alone. Asking early is a sign you're paying attention. We'd much rather answer the "obvious" question now than untangle a wrong assumption later.

When you spot something confusing, write it down. An unclear handbook or setup doc is a bug, and you're the person best placed to catch it, because you're seeing it fresh. Fix it or flag it. Improving the on-ramp for the next person is real, valued work.

## What we're actually after

Momentum. Not a perfect mental model of the whole system, not every corner of the codebase mapped, just the sense that you can find your footing and start contributing. Everything deeper fills in as you go.

You were hired because we think you can do the work and we want to do it with you. Week one is just where that starts. If you finish it feeling oriented, a little productive, and comfortable asking questions, you're exactly where you should be.

docs.title: Flagon documentation
docs.description: Run your organization, projects, and people in Flagon from the dashboard, the API, or an AI assistant.
docs.body:
Flagon is a self-hostable developer platform for operating your engineering system. Today you use it
to run **organizations**, the **projects** inside them, and the **people and teams** who work on
them, with access control, single sign-on, and an audit log built in. Every capability works three
ways: in the dashboard at [app.flagon.io](https://app.flagon.io), over the REST API at
`https://api.flagon.io`, and through an AI assistant (in the product or over MCP) that acts as you
and asks before it changes anything.

## Start here

<Cards>
  <Card title="Quickstart" href="/docs/get-started/quickstart" description="Create an organization and a project, invite a teammate, and make your first API call." />
  <Card title="Core concepts" href="/docs/get-started/core-concepts" description="Organizations, projects, roles, tokens, and how access adds up." />
  <Card title="Use the API" href="/docs/api/using-the-api" description="Authenticate with a token and call the same operations the dashboard uses." />
  <Card title="Connect an MCP client" href="/docs/guides/connect-an-mcp-client" description="Point an external agent at mcp.flagon.io to read the docs and operate Flagon." />
  <Card title="Self-host Flagon" href="/docs/self-hosting/overview" description="Run the API, the app, and Postgres on your own infrastructure." />
</Cards>

## Find a task

| Task | Read |
| --- | --- |
| Create an organization | [Create an organization](/docs/guides/create-an-organization) |
| Invite people and group them into teams | [Invite your team](/docs/guides/invite-your-team), [Organize with teams](/docs/guides/organize-with-teams) |
| Set the default project role for members | [Set base permissions](/docs/guides/set-base-permissions) |
| Create a project and control who can change it | [Create a project](/docs/guides/create-a-project), [Manage project access](/docs/guides/manage-project-access) |
| Delete or restore a project | [Delete and restore](/docs/guides/delete-and-restore) |
| Require two-factor or set up SSO | [Require two-factor](/docs/guides/require-two-factor), [SSO with OIDC](/docs/guides/set-up-sso-oidc), [SSO with SAML](/docs/guides/set-up-sso-saml) |
| See who changed what | [Review the audit log](/docs/guides/review-the-audit-log) |
| Script Flagon or call it from CI | [Automate with access tokens](/docs/guides/automate-with-access-tokens), [Call the API from CI](/docs/guides/call-the-api-from-ci) |
| Operate Flagon by asking | [Work with the assistant](/docs/guides/work-with-the-assistant) |
| Look up a scope, role, or error | [Scopes](/docs/reference/scopes), [Roles matrix](/docs/reference/roles-matrix), [Errors](/docs/api/errors) |
| Understand how Flagon is built | [Architecture overview](/docs/architecture/overview) |
| Fix a problem | [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting/overview) |

## Key concepts

An **organization** is the tenant: it owns projects, members, teams, tokens, and settings, and no
data crosses between organizations. A **project** is a deployable app, the core unit you work on.
**Members** hold an org role (owner, admin, or member), and each project resolves their effective
**project role** (read, triage, write, maintain, or admin) from the org's base permission, direct
grants, and team grants. **Access tokens** let scripts and agents act with a subset of that access,
limited by **scopes**. Mutations are recorded in the org's **audit log**.

See [Core concepts](/docs/get-started/core-concepts) for every term and how they fit together.

## What's coming

Deployments, logs and observability, connected context across your tools, agents, metrics, reusable
skills, and governance are planned but not built yet. The **Roadmap** group in the navigation holds a
page for each, starting with [Deployments](/docs/deploying/deployments), and the
[Introduction](/docs/get-started/introduction) says exactly what exists today.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.description: How Flagon is built and how to contribute - the repositories, local setup with make, the golden path for a new capability, tests, and keeping docs, roadmap, and changelog in the same change.
headings: The golden path for a new capability
docs.body:
Flagon is developed in the open. The product (the API, the app, and the design
system) and its documentation live in one repository, so a change and its docs
ship together. This page gets you from a fresh clone to a pull request that
passes CI, and explains the rules every change follows.

The root `AGENTS.md` in the repository is the full contributor guide (it is also
what AI coding agents read). This page summarizes it; when they differ,
`AGENTS.md` wins.

## The repositories

| Repository | What lives there |
| --- | --- |
| [flagon-io/flagon](https://github.com/flagon-io/flagon) | The API (`api/`), the app (`app/`), the design system (`packages/ui/`), the docs (`docs/`), the roadmap (`roadmap/`), and the changelog (`changelog/`). |
| [flagon-io/website](https://github.com/flagon-io/website) | The marketing site. It renders the docs, roadmap, and changelog as a client of the API, so it holds no copy of them. |

## Set up a development environment

Follow [Installation](/docs/self-hosting/installation) for the prerequisites and
the one-time steps (copy `compose.override.example.yml`, create
`app/.env.local`, `npm install`). The API needs no configuration: it binds
`127.0.0.1` by default, which runs it in development mode against the compose
Postgres. After that, the `Makefile` wraps everything; `make help` lists every
target.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `make dev` | Starts Postgres in Docker, then runs the API and the app together (Ctrl-C stops both). |
| `make api` | Runs the API on `:8080`; it migrates on boot. |
| `make app` | Builds `@flagon-io/ui`, then runs the app on `:3000`. |
| `make db` | Starts only the compose Postgres. |
| `make migrate` | Applies the API's migrations and the app's auth migrations. |
| `make seed` | Creates the demo user and organization (needs the API running). |
| `make test` | Go tests plus the design system's unit tests. |
| `make lint` | `go vet`, golangci-lint (skipped with an install hint if it is not on your `PATH`), eslint, and the design system's typecheck. |
| `make check` | Every drift check plus lint and tests: the local mirror of CI. Run it before you push. |
| `make openapi` | Writes `openapi/openapi.json` from the code. |
| `make api-types` | Regenerates the app's TypeScript API types from a fresh spec. |
| `make docs`, `make roadmap`, `make changelog` | Regenerates an embedded corpus. |

The Makefile is a thin wrapper over the commands in `AGENTS.md`, and every
recipe works under GNU make on Linux, macOS, and Windows (Git Bash).

## How Flagon is built

Three principles shape every change:

- **API-first.** Every capability is an API operation first. Operations are
  registered with huma in `api/internal/server`, and the OpenAPI spec is
  generated from them, never written by hand.
- **AI-first.** Anything you can do in the dashboard, you can do by asking the
  assistant, and the reverse.
- **One tool registry, three front doors.** The in-product assistant and the MCP
  server call the same tools, which run through the same service layer as the
  REST handlers. Adding an operation once makes it available everywhere.

Two rules follow from those and are enforced in review: the app never reaches
around the API to the domain database, and no assistant or MCP tool exists
without a real, permission-checked API operation behind it.

## The golden path for a new capability

To add a capability (say, "archive a team"), do these in order. Steps 1, 2, and
4 land in the same change; only the UI may follow later.

<Steps>

<Step title="API operation">

Register a huma operation in `api/internal/server` that calls the service layer
(`api/internal/service`), which calls the data layer (`api/internal/db`) where
row-level security and role checks apply. Give the operation a scope in
`api/internal/server/scopes.go`; enforcement fails closed, so an operation
without one is unreachable by scoped tokens. If it changes an organization's
state, add an `Action` constant in `api/internal/audit` and record the audit
entry inside the same transaction as the change.

</Step>

<Step title="Tool">

Add the tool to the registry in `api/internal/ai` (the `tools_*.go` files), with
the same scope as its operation, its `Operation` ID, and `Mutating: true` if it
writes. This is not optional: a capability with no tool is invisible to the
assistant and MCP, and counts as unfinished.

</Step>

<Step title="UI">

Build the screen in `app/`, calling the API through the gateway in
`app/src/lib/api`. Use `@flagon-io/ui` components; if the one you need does not
exist, build it in `packages/ui` rather than hand-rolling it in the app.

</Step>

<Step title="Docs">

Add or update the page under `docs/` and run `make docs` to regenerate the
embedded corpus. Commit both.

</Step>

</Steps>

## Tests

| Layer | Where | How to run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Go unit and handler tests | `api/**/*_test.go` | `make test-go` (or `cd api && go test ./...`) |
| Go database integration tests | `api/internal/db/*_integration_test.go` | Set `FLAGON_TEST_DATABASE_URL` to a Postgres the tests may use, with a role that can create roles. Without it they are skipped. CI always runs them. |
| Design system unit tests (Vitest) | `packages/ui/src/**/*.test.ts` | `npm run test:unit` |
| Component tests (Playwright) | `app/tests/` | `npm run test:e2e` in `app/` (reuses your dev server locally) |
| Product end to end (Playwright) | `app/tests/product/` | `npm run test:e2e:product` in `app/`, against the full stack with the API on the mock AI provider |

A few tests guard the architecture itself, and they fail when a change skips a
step of the golden path:

- **Scopes.** Every operation must have a scope or be explicitly exempt, and
  `api/internal/server/permissions_test.go` drives real scoped tokens against
  operations (allowed versus `403`). Copy its table for a new endpoint.
- **Tools.** `api/internal/server/guardrails_test.go` checks that every scoped
  operation has a tool, and that each tool's scope and read or write nature match
  its operation.

When you add or change a UI component, add or extend its Playwright spec; pure
logic (parsers, formatters) gets a Vitest spec too.

## Documentation, roadmap, and changelog

These are part of the work, not follow-ups, and CI checks each one:

- **Docs** live in `docs/` (see `docs/README.md`). `make docs` compiles them into
  `api/internal/docs/corpus.gen.json`, which the API embeds and serves.
- **Roadmap** items live in `roadmap/`, one file each. Move an item forward by
  changing its `stage`; `make roadmap` regenerates the corpus.
- **Changelog** entries live in `changelog/`, one dated file each. When a roadmap
  item ships, delete it from `roadmap/` and add a changelog entry in the same
  change; `make changelog` regenerates the corpus.

CI runs the `-check` mode of all three generators and fails if a committed
corpus is stale. It also regenerates the app's API types from the spec and fails
on any difference, so run `make api-types` after changing an operation's shape.

## Conventions

- **No em dashes** anywhere: code, copy, docs, or messages.
- **Don't name products Flagon's design imitates** in source or copy.
- **Organization-scoped by default.** App routes are `/<org>/...`; personal
  settings at `/settings` are the only exception.
- **Row-level security is never bypassed.** Runtime queries use the
  `NOBYPASSRLS` app role, and the assistant gets no special powers.
- **Migrations are immutable once shipped.** Fix a shipped migration with a new
  one. Do not put `BEGIN` or `COMMIT` inside a migration file; the runner wraps
  all pending migrations in one transaction.
- **Dependencies.** After changing npm dependencies, run `scripts/relock.sh`
  (requires Docker) so `package-lock.json` carries every platform's native
  binaries; otherwise `npm ci` can fail on Linux CI.

## Reporting a security issue

Please do not open a public issue for a vulnerability. Email **hey@flagon.io**
with what you found and how to reproduce it. The repository's
[SECURITY.md](https://github.com/flagon-io/flagon/blob/main/SECURITY.md) has the
full policy, and [Security overview](/docs/security/overview) describes the
security model and its current limitations.

## Sending a change

Keep changes small and focused, with the code, its tool, its tests, and its docs
together. Run `make check` before pushing; CI runs the same gates plus the
end-to-end suites, a vulnerability scan, and the API type drift check.

## Related

- [Self-hosting overview](/docs/self-hosting/overview)
- [Installation](/docs/self-hosting/installation)
- [Architecture overview](/docs/architecture/overview)
- [Tool registry](/docs/architecture/tool-registry)
- [Permissions model](/docs/architecture/permissions-model)

docs.title: Access tokens
docs.description: Personal and organization access tokens for the Flagon API and MCP server, their scopes, expiry, and how revocation works.
docs.body:
An **access token** is a bearer credential that lets a script, a CI job, or an
external agent call the Flagon [API](/docs/api/using-the-api) and the
[MCP server](/docs/ai/mcp) without a browser session. Every token acts as a
**principal** (the identity whose permissions it uses) and carries a set of
**scopes** that narrow what that principal can do through the token.

Flagon has two kinds of token, and the difference is who the token acts as:

| | Personal access token | Organization access token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acts as | You | A service principal owned by one organization |
| Reaches | Every organization you belong to | Only the organization that minted it |
| Permission ceiling | Your role in each organization | The role chosen for the token (`admin`, `member`, or `viewer`) |
| Managed at | **Settings > Personal access tokens** (`app.flagon.io/settings/tokens`) | The org's **Settings > API tokens** (`app.flagon.io/<org>/settings/tokens`) |
| Who can manage | You, for your own tokens | Organization owners and admins |
| Secret prefix | `flagon_pat_` | `flagon_oat_` |
| Survives the creator leaving | No, it is you | Yes, it belongs to the org |

## Token format

A token secret is the prefix followed by 43 random characters (32 random bytes,
URL-safe base64), for example `flagon_pat_Zq3...`. The API recognizes any
bearer credential that starts with `flagon_` as an access token.

Flagon stores only a SHA-256 hash of the secret, never the secret itself. The
token list shows a short display prefix (the kind prefix plus the first six
random characters, such as `flagon_pat_ab12cd`) so you can tell tokens apart,
along with when each was last used and when it expires.

<Callout type="warn" title="Secrets are shown once">

The full secret appears exactly once, on the page right after you generate the
token. Copy it into your secret store then. Nobody, including Flagon, can show it
to you again; if you lose it, revoke the token and generate a new one.

</Callout>

## Personal access tokens

A **personal access token** (PAT) acts as you. Anything you can do in an
organization, the token can do there too, limited further by its scopes. When
your access changes, the token's access changes with it: if you are removed from
an organization, your personal tokens stop reaching it.

Use a personal token for your own scripts, local tooling, and an MCP client on
your machine.

## Organization access tokens

An **organization access token** (OAT) belongs to the organization, not to a
person. When an owner or admin generates one, Flagon creates a dedicated
**service principal** for it: a machine identity with a membership in that one
organization at the role you pick. The token acts as that principal, so:

- it only ever reaches the organization that minted it;
- it keeps working if the person who created it leaves the organization;
- its role is the ceiling: `admin`, `member` (the default), or `viewer`
  (read-only). A token can never be an owner, so owner-only actions such as
  deleting the organization are out of its reach;
- the service principal never appears in the organization's member list, so it
  does not count as a person and cannot be managed from **People**;
- it can't take account-level actions that only make sense for a person:
  creating an organization, leaving one, listing or restoring deleted
  organizations, and syncing a profile all return `403 Forbidden`
  (`this operation requires a user; organization access tokens can't perform it`);
- it is exempt from the organization's two-factor and SSO requirements, which
  govern how people sign in (see [Security notes](#security-notes)).

Revoking the token deletes the service principal along with it. Deleting the
organization makes its organization tokens stop working at once (`401 Unauthorized`), and a restore brings them back. Creating and revoking an
organization token are recorded in the org's [audit log](/docs/platform/audit-log)
as `token.created` and `token.revoked`.

Use an organization token for CI pipelines, deploy automation, and anything that
should outlive any one person's membership.

## Scopes

A **scope** names a slice of the API, such as `read:project`. A scoped token can
call only the operations whose required scope it holds. Scopes are hierarchical:
a parent scope implies every scope beneath it, so a token holding `admin:org`
satisfies an operation that requires `write:org` or `read:org`.

| Group | Scope | Grants | Implies |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Account | `admin:user` | Full control of your account, including deletion | `user`, `read:user` |
| | `user` | Account writes (none today; your profile is edited in the dashboard) | `read:user` |
| | `read:user` | Read your profile (`GET /me`) | |
| Organizations | `admin:org` | Create, leave, delete, and restore organizations | `write:org`, `read:org` |
| | `write:org` | Manage members, invitations, security policy, SSO, and audit settings | `read:org` |
| | `read:org` | Read organizations, members, invitations, and the audit log | |
| Projects | `admin:project` | Delete and restore projects; manage collaborators, teams, and owners | `write:project`, `read:project` |
| | `write:project` | Create and update projects | `read:project` |
| | `read:project` | Read projects, collaborators, teams, and owners | |
| Teams | `admin:team` | Delete teams | `write:team`, `read:team` |
| | `write:team` | Create and edit teams and manage their membership | `read:team` |
| | `read:team` | Read teams and their members | |
| Notifications | `notifications` | Read and manage your notifications | |

The [scopes reference](/docs/reference/scopes) maps every API operation to the
scope it requires.

Two rules decide what a token can actually do:

- **Scopes are a ceiling on the role, never a grant.** A token can do something
  only if its principal's role allows it *and* the token holds the scope. A
  `write:org` token owned by a plain member still cannot remove members, because a
  member cannot.
- **Unmapped operations are closed.** An operation that has no scope assigned is
  unreachable by any scoped token. Operations are denied by default, never
  allowed by accident.

### Full access

Instead of picking scopes you can choose **Full access**. A full-access token is
not scope-limited at all; it is still bounded by its principal's role. Prefer
the narrowest set of scopes that does the job: a leaked read-only token is a much
smaller incident than a leaked full-access one.

### The permissions checklist

When you generate a token, the dashboard shows all 13 scopes above as a grouped
checklist, one group per resource. Each group has a parent scope and its finer scopes beneath
it, each row labeled with the raw scope and a one-line description. Checking a
parent checks and locks its children, because the parent already grants them.

## Expiration

Every token can expire. The presets are 7 days, 30 days (the default), 90 days,
and 1 year; you can also pick a custom date (it must be in the future) or **No
expiration**. After it expires, a token is rejected with `401 Unauthorized`.
Tokens without an expiry live until you revoke them, so reserve that for
credentials you rotate by other means.

## Creating and revoking tokens

Token management happens only in the dashboard, on purpose: the API operations
that mint and revoke tokens accept only the dashboard's own session, never a
bearer token. A leaked token therefore cannot mint more tokens or widen its own
access, and there is no assistant or MCP tool for it.

<Steps>

<Step title="Open the token page">

For a personal token, go to **Settings > Personal access tokens**. For an
organization token, open the organization's **Settings > API tokens** (owners and
admins only), then choose **Generate new token**.

</Step>

<Step title="Describe the token">

Give it a name you will recognize later (for example `CI pipeline`). For an
organization token, pick its role.

</Step>

<Step title="Pick an expiration and permissions">

Choose an expiration, then either check the scopes it needs or select **Full
access**. You must pick at least one scope or full access.

</Step>

<Step title="Copy the secret">

Choose **Generate token** and copy the secret from the confirmation page. It is
not shown again.

</Step>

</Steps>

To **revoke** a token, find it in the same list and revoke it. Revocation deletes
the token, and the next request that presents it fails with `401 Unauthorized`.
There is no grace period and no way to undo it; generate a new token instead.

For a full walkthrough, including storing the secret in CI, see
[Automate with access tokens](/docs/guides/automate-with-access-tokens).

## Using a token

Send the secret as a bearer token on every request:

```bash
curl https://api.flagon.io/me \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"
```

The same header authenticates the [MCP server](/docs/ai/mcp). The responses you
will see when something is wrong:

| Status | Message | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `401` | `invalid or expired token` | The token is unknown, revoked, expired, or belongs to a deleted organization. |
| `403` | `this token is missing the scope required for this operation` | The token is valid but lacks the scope the operation needs. |
| `403` | `you don't have permission to do that` | The scope is present, but the principal's role does not allow the action. |
| `403` | `this organization requires ...` | The organization requires two-factor authentication or single sign-on and the token's user does not meet it (personal tokens only; see below). |
| `404` | not found | The organization or resource is not visible to the principal. |
| `429` | `rate limit exceeded; retry after Ns` | The token exceeded the API's per-token rate limit. Wait for the `Retry-After` seconds. |

## Security notes

- Treat a token like a password. Keep it in a secret manager or your CI
  provider's secret store, never in source control.
- Give each automation its own token so you can revoke one without breaking the
  others, and so the token list and audit log tell you which one acted.
- Prefer organization tokens for shared automation. A personal token in CI acts
  as you and stops working if you leave.
- Check **Last used** in the token list and revoke tokens that are no longer in
  use.
- The organization [2FA](/docs/platform/two-factor) and
  [SSO](/docs/platform/sso) requirements are enforced by the API, so they apply to
  **personal** access tokens too. In an organization that requires two-factor
  authentication, a personal token whose user has not enabled it gets
  `403 Forbidden`. In one that requires SSO, a personal token works only if its
  user has signed in through one of the organization's identity providers at
  least once (organization owners are exempt from the SSO requirement, so they
  can always fix a broken setup).
- **Organization** access tokens are exempt from both requirements: their
  service principal never signs in interactively, and only owners and admins
  (who are subject to the policy themselves) can mint them. That is another
  reason to keep their scopes narrow and expirations short.

## Related

- [Automate with access tokens](/docs/guides/automate-with-access-tokens)
- [API authentication](/docs/api/authentication)
- [Scopes reference](/docs/reference/scopes)
- [Tokens and scopes (security)](/docs/security/tokens-and-scopes)
- [MCP server](/docs/ai/mcp)

docs.title: Profile and account
docs.description: Your personal Flagon account, including public profile, emails, sign-in security, sessions, personal tokens, and the organizations you belong to.
headings: Over the API and the assistant
docs.body:
You have **one Flagon account**, and it can belong to any number of
[organizations](/docs/platform/organizations). Everything personal to you lives
under **Settings** at `app.flagon.io/settings`, the one area of Flagon that sits
outside any organization. Organization settings (members, org tokens, billing)
live under each org's own **Settings** instead.

Your account and sign-in credentials are owned by the web app's auth service
(BetterAuth). The app mirrors your public profile to the API so the rest of the
platform can reference you.

## Public profile

**Settings > Public profile** is what other people see: your name, avatar, bio,
pronouns, website, company, location, up to four social links, and an optional
public email. Anyone can read it at `GET /users/{username}`, which needs no
authentication and returns only these public fields. A deleted account's profile
is hidden.

## Account

**Settings > Account** holds the settings that identify you:

- **Username**: your handle across Flagon. You can sign in with it instead of
  your email, and others use it to add you to organizations, teams, and projects.
  Usernames are unique; changing yours can break existing links to your profile.
- **Delete account**: deactivates your account and signs you out everywhere. It
  is reversible (support can restore an account deleted by mistake). You cannot
  delete your account while you own an organization: first hand ownership to
  someone else and leave, or
  [delete the organization](/docs/platform/organizations#deleting-an-organization).

## Emails

**Settings > Emails** lists the addresses on your account. Add and verify more
addresses there, and choose your **primary** email, which is used for sign-in and
for notifications. Accepting an [invitation](/docs/platform/members) verifies the
invited address, since the link proves you control that mailbox.

## Password, two-factor, and sessions

- **Settings > Password and authentication** changes your password (which signs
  out your other sessions) and sets up
  [two-factor authentication](/docs/platform/two-factor). An organization can
  require 2FA of every member.
- **Settings > Sessions** lists the devices and browsers signed in to your
  account. Revoke any session you do not recognize, or sign out every session but
  the current one.

If an organization you belong to uses [single sign-on](/docs/platform/sso), that
org's identity is linked to this same account, so one sign-in reaches every
organization you belong to.

## Personal access tokens

**Settings > Personal access tokens** (under **Developer settings**) is where you
generate and revoke **personal access tokens** (`flagon_pat_...`) for the
[API](/docs/api/using-the-api) and [MCP](/docs/ai/mcp). A personal token acts as
you, across every organization you belong to, and carries the scopes and expiry
you choose. See [Access tokens](/docs/platform/access-tokens), which also covers
organization tokens.

## Organizations, notifications, and appearance

- **Settings > Organizations** lists the organizations you belong to with your
  role in each. From there you create a new organization, leave one, and restore
  one you deleted in the last 30 days (**Recently deleted**).
- **Settings > Notifications** is your personal
  [notification](/docs/platform/notifications) feed across every organization.
- **Settings > Appearance** sets your theme: light, dark, or matching your
  system.

## Over the API and the assistant

`GET /me` returns your account and the organizations you belong to (scope
`read:user`); the assistant and MCP answer the same question with the `whoami`
tool.

```bash
curl https://api.flagon.io/me \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"
```

Profile, email, password, session, and token changes are made in **Settings**,
not through the assistant, and the API has no operations for emails, passwords,
sessions, or account deletion that a token can reach. That is deliberate: a
credential should never be able to take over the account behind it or mint more
credentials. (The API's `PUT /me/profile` exists so the app can mirror your
public profile to the API after you save it in **Settings**. Only the app can
call it; every access token gets `401 Unauthorized`, so a token can never change
your profile, your username, or your two-factor or SSO state.)

## Related

- [Access tokens](/docs/platform/access-tokens)
- [Two-factor authentication](/docs/platform/two-factor)
- [Notifications](/docs/platform/notifications)
- [Identity and auth](/docs/architecture/identity-and-auth)

docs.title: Audit log
docs.description: An immutable, organization-scoped record of who changed what, where, and when.
docs.body:
Every organization has an **audit log**: an append-only record of the changes
made to it. It answers "who did what, where, and when" for the things that
matter: projects created and deleted, access granted, members added and removed,
tokens minted, security settings changed.

The audit log belongs to the **organization** and is readable by **owners and
admins only**. It is separate from [notifications](/docs/platform/notifications),
which are personal (they belong to a user, who marks them read).

## What is recorded

Each entry captures:

- **who**: the actor (a person, or the service principal behind an organization
  access token);
- **what**: an action key such as `project.created`, the target, and a short
  human summary such as "created project Billing API";
- **where**: the actor's IP address, country, and client (user agent). The IP is
  shown only when IP disclosure is on (see below);
- **when**: the time of the change.

Entries are written **in the same database transaction** as the change they
describe, so a change and its audit entry commit together or not at all: the log
cannot drift from reality. The log is **immutable**: there is no operation to
edit or delete an entry, for anyone.

Where the "where" comes from depends on the front door:

| Front door | IP address | Country | User agent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Dashboard and in-product assistant | Your browser's address, forwarded by the app | Forwarded by the app | Your browser |
| API with an access token | The connection's address, or the proxy header the API is configured to trust (`FLAGON_CLIENT_IP_HEADER`, `Fly-Client-IP` on the hosted service) | Not recorded | Your client |
| MCP with an access token | The connection's address, as for the API | Not recorded | Your MCP client |

The API trusts forwarded client headers only from the app gateway (requests
authenticated with Flagon's internal credential), so a token holder cannot forge
the IP address or location their entries record.

Recorded actions include:

| Area | Actions |
| --- | --- |
| Organization | `organization.created`, `organization.updated`, `organization.deleted`, `organization.restored`, `organization.security_changed`, `organization.audit_config_changed` |
| Members | `member.added`, `member.role_changed`, `member.removed`, `member.left`, `invitation.sent`, `invitation.revoked`, `invitation.accepted` |
| Projects | `project.created`, `project.updated`, `project.deleted`, `project.restored` |
| Project access | `project.access_granted`, `project.access_changed`, `project.access_revoked`, `project.team_access_granted`, `project.team_access_changed`, `project.team_access_revoked`, `project.owner_added`, `project.owner_removed` |
| Teams | `team.created`, `team.updated`, `team.deleted`, `team.member_added`, `team.member_role_changed`, `team.member_removed` |
| Tokens | `token.created`, `token.revoked` (organization access tokens) |
| SSO | `sso_provider.created`, `sso_provider.updated`, `sso_provider.deleted` |

The [audit actions reference](/docs/reference/audit-actions) describes each key.

## IP disclosure

Actor IP addresses are always recorded, but they are **hidden by default**. An
owner or admin can reveal them in the log under **Settings > Audit log >
Settings**. While disclosure is off, the API returns no IP address on entries
and search does not match on IP addresses, so an undisclosed address can't be
probed by searching for it. Turning disclosure on or off is itself an audited
event (`organization.audit_config_changed`).

## Reading the log

<Tabs>

<Tab title="Dashboard">

Open the org's **Settings > Audit log**. The **Events** tab lists entries newest
first, with search and a filter by action.

</Tab>

<Tab title="API">

```bash
curl "https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/audit?q=billing&action=project.deleted" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"
```

- `q` searches across the summary, action, actor, and location (including the IP
  address only while IP disclosure is on).
- `action` filters to one action key; repeat it for several.
- `actor` filters to one actor's user id.
- `limit` sets the page size (default 30, max 100). The next page's URL comes
  back in the `Link` header with `rel="next"`; see
  [Pagination](/docs/api/pagination).

Requires `read:org` and an owner or admin role. A plain member gets
`403 Forbidden`; someone outside the organization gets `404 Not Found`.

</Tab>

<Tab title="Assistant">

Ask: "What changed in acme this week?" The assistant reads the log with
`list_audit_events` and summarizes it. This works only for owners and admins.

</Tab>

</Tabs>

For a walkthrough of common investigations, see
[Review the audit log](/docs/guides/review-the-audit-log).

## Operations

| Operation | API | Tool | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Read the log | `GET /orgs/{slug}/audit` | `list_audit_events` | `read:org` |
| Read the IP disclosure setting | `GET /orgs/{slug}/audit/config` | `get_audit_config` | `read:org` |
| Change the IP disclosure setting | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/audit/config` | `set_audit_config` | `write:org` |

Every operation also requires an owner or admin role. The log is tenant-isolated
like everything else, so one organization can never see another's history. The
[auditing architecture](/docs/architecture/auditing-and-notifications) page
explains how entries are written.

## Related

- [Review the audit log](/docs/guides/review-the-audit-log)
- [Audit actions reference](/docs/reference/audit-actions)
- [Notifications](/docs/platform/notifications)
- [Auditing and notifications](/docs/architecture/auditing-and-notifications)

docs.title: Members and invitations
docs.description: Add teammates to an organization by existing account or by email invitation, and manage their organization roles.
docs.body:
Everything in Flagon happens inside an [organization](/docs/platform/organizations),
and the people in it are its **members**. Each member has exactly one
**organization role**, which sets what they can do across the whole org. Owners
and admins manage the roster from **People** (`app.flagon.io/<org>/people`), which
has a **Members** tab and a **Pending invitations** tab.

## Organization roles

| Role | What it can do |
| --- | --- |
| **Owner** | Everything, including deleting the organization. An organization always has at least one owner. |
| **Admin** | Manage members, invitations, teams, organization tokens, and settings. Admin on every project. |
| **Member** | The default. Can create projects. Access to existing projects comes from the base permission, raised by per-project grants and teams. |

Read-only access is not a separate role for people: it is a member in an
organization whose base permission is `read`. (The API still accepts a legacy
`viewer` role, which is read-only and cannot create projects; the dashboard
only shows it for members who already hold it.) See
[Roles & permissions](/docs/platform/roles) for the full model.

Rules that always hold:

- An **admin** can manage members below them (members), but not other admins or
  owners.
- Only an **owner** can grant or remove the owner role.
- The **last owner** can never be demoted or removed (`409 Conflict`).
- You cannot change your own membership from **People**; use **Leave** under
  **Settings > Organizations** instead.

## Adding people

You add people by email or username, and Flagon does the right thing for each:

- If the person **already has a Flagon account**, they are added to the
  organization straight away and see it the next time they load the app. They get
  a notification.
- If the email **has no account yet**, Flagon creates an **invitation** and the
  API emails the person a link to register and join in one step. The API sends
  that email itself, whichever front door you used (dashboard, API, assistant,
  or MCP).

<Tabs>

<Tab title="Dashboard">

On **People**, choose **Invite people** to open the invite dialog. Add one
row per person (email or username) and pick each person's role (Member or
Admin). If an invitation email was not sent (no mail provider is configured, the
server only logs email, or delivery failed), the dialog lists that invitation's
link with a **Copy** button so you can send it yourself.

</Tab>

<Tab title="API">

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/invitations \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"login": "dev@example.com", "role": "member"}'
```

The response's `status` is `added` (an existing user joined directly) or
`invited` (a pending invitation was created). For `invited`, the response also
carries `email_sent` (whether the invitation email was handed to a mail
provider that delivers; always `false` with the log mailer) and a single-use
`token` for the invitation link, in case you also
want to deliver the link another way (`https://app.flagon.io/invite/<token>`).
The invitation exists even when `email_sent` is `false`. A `login` that is
neither an email address nor an existing username returns `422`.

To add only existing users, use `POST /orgs/{slug}/members` with `login` and an
optional `role`; it returns `404` if no user matches. Both require `write:org`.

</Tab>

<Tab title="Assistant">

Ask: "Invite dev@example.com to acme as a member." The assistant proposes
`invite_member`, which adds the person directly if they already have an account
and emails an invitation otherwise. The result says whether the email was sent
(`email_sent`); the invitation token itself is never shown to the model.

</Tab>

</Tabs>

An invitation can grant `admin` or `member` (the default), and you can never
grant a role above your own, so an admin can invite only members. `owner`
can't be granted through an invitation at all: an owner grants it by promoting
a member, or by adding an existing Flagon user directly with
`POST /orgs/{slug}/members`.

A self-hosted API sends mail through Resend when `RESEND_API_KEY` is set and
otherwise only writes the message to its log; see
[Configuration](/docs/reference/configuration).

For a walkthrough, see [Invite your team](/docs/guides/invite-your-team).

## How invitations work

A pending invitation is addressed to an email and carries the role you chose. It
shows under **Pending invitations** until it is accepted, and an owner or admin
can revoke it at any time. Invitations **expire after seven days**; an expired
link returns `410 Gone`. Only one pending invitation can exist per email
(`409 Conflict` otherwise).

When the invited person opens the link, the page already knows which organization
invited them. Without an account, they set a name, username, and password and
land in the organization. If they are already signed in with the invited email,
they just confirm. A signed-in user with a different email is refused.

The invitation link proves the person controls that mailbox, so accepting it
**doubles as email verification**: there is no separate code to enter. The email
on the new account is fixed to the invited address. Accepting is recorded in the
audit log (`invitation.accepted`) and notifies the person who invited them.

## Changing roles and removing members

Owners and admins change a member's role from the role picker on **People**, and
remove members from the same row. Removing someone ends their access to the
organization immediately, including through their personal access tokens. The
person is notified of role changes and removals, and every change is audited
(`member.added`, `member.role_changed`, `member.removed`).

## Operations

| Operation | API | Tool | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| List members | `GET /orgs/{slug}/members` | `list_members` | `read:org` |
| Add an existing user | `POST /orgs/{slug}/members` | `add_member` | `write:org` |
| Change a member's role | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/members/{userId}/role` | `set_member_role` | `write:org` |
| Remove a member | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/members/{userId}` | `remove_member` | `write:org` |
| List pending invitations | `GET /orgs/{slug}/invitations` | `list_invitations` | `read:org` |
| Invite by email | `POST /orgs/{slug}/invitations` | `invite_member` | `write:org` |
| Revoke an invitation | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/invitations/{id}` | `revoke_invitation` | `write:org` |

Beyond the scope, every write needs an owner or admin role. The member list
never includes the service principals behind
[organization access tokens](/docs/platform/access-tokens). The agent and API act
with your identity, so they can only invite people if you could, and tenant
isolation is enforced in the database.

## Related

- [Invite your team](/docs/guides/invite-your-team)
- [Roles & permissions](/docs/platform/roles)
- [Teams](/docs/platform/teams)
- [Single sign-on](/docs/platform/sso) (members can also join by signing in through your IdP)

docs.title: Notifications
docs.description: Your personal feed of what happened to you across your organizations, in the top bar and in settings.
docs.body:
**Notifications** are your personal feed of things that happened to you across
the organizations you belong to: you were added to an org, your role changed,
someone accepted your invitation, you were given access to a project. They are
**personal**: a notification belongs to you, not to an organization, and only you
can see or change it. That makes them separate from the
[audit log](/docs/platform/audit-log), the organization's shared, immutable
record of who did what.

## What you are notified about

| Type | When |
| --- | --- |
| `org.created` | You created an organization. |
| `org.member_added` | Someone added you to an organization (directly, or by inviting an email that already has an account). |
| `org.role_changed` | Your organization role changed. |
| `org.member_removed` | You were removed from an organization. |
| `org.invite_accepted` | Someone accepted an invitation you sent. |
| `org.deleted` | An organization you belong to was deleted. |
| `project.access_granted` | You were given a role on a project. |
| `project.access_changed` | Your role on a project changed. |
| `team.member_added` | You were added to a team. |

## Where they show up

- The **bell** in the top bar shows your unread count and a short feed. The feed
  is **unread first, then newest**, so an unread item is never buried under newer
  ones you have already read.
- **Settings > Notifications** (`app.flagon.io/settings/notifications`) is the
  full feed with **All** and **Unread** tabs. It spans every organization you
  belong to.

## Reading a notification

Selecting a notification opens its detail rather than jumping you somewhere:

- It **marks the notification read** (its `read_at` timestamp records when).
- From the detail you can **mark it unread** again, or **open** its linked page
  when it has one.
- **Mark all as read** clears the whole unread count at once.

A click never navigates on its own; you follow the link only when you choose to.

## Delivery

Notifications are delivered **in-product** only (the bell and the feed).
Invitation emails are a separate thing: they go to people who are not members
yet (see [Members and invitations](/docs/platform/members)).

<Callout type="warn" title="Not available yet">

Email delivery of notifications is planned. The **Email** switch under
**Settings > Notifications > Delivery** is shown but disabled, marked
**Coming soon**.

</Callout>

## Operations

Everything above is available through the API, the
[assistant](/docs/ai/assistant), and [MCP](/docs/ai/mcp):

| Operation | API | Tool | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| List your notifications | `GET /notifications` | `list_notifications` | `notifications` |
| Count unread | `GET /notifications/unread-count` | `count_unread_notifications` | `notifications` |
| Mark one read | `POST /notifications/{id}/read` | `mark_notification_read` | `notifications` |
| Mark one unread | `POST /notifications/{id}/unread` | `mark_notification_unread` | `notifications` |
| Mark all read | `POST /notifications/read-all` | `mark_all_notifications_read` | `notifications` |

`GET /notifications` returns up to `limit` items, unread first and then newest
(default 30; a value of 0 or less means 30, and anything above 100 is capped at
100). The `list_notifications` tool takes the same `limit`. As with every
change, the in-product assistant proposes marking notifications read and you
confirm it.

```bash
curl https://api.flagon.io/notifications/unread-count \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"
```

## Related

- [Audit log](/docs/platform/audit-log)
- [Profile and account](/docs/platform/account)
- [Auditing and notifications](/docs/architecture/auditing-and-notifications)

docs.title: Organizations
docs.description: Organizations own everything in Flagon (projects, members, teams, tokens, and settings), and are the unit of tenant isolation.
docs.body:
An **organization** (org) is the top-level container in Flagon and the unit of
tenancy. Your projects, members, teams, organization access tokens, security
policy, and audit log all live inside one, and permissions are always decided
per organization: being an owner of one org says nothing about your role in
