another. One Flagon account can belong to any number of organizations, and you
switch between them from the app shell.

Nearly every URL is org-scoped:

```text
app.flagon.io/<org>                    the org dashboard
app.flagon.io/<org>/projects/...       projects
app.flagon.io/<org>/people             members and invitations
app.flagon.io/<org>/teams              teams
app.flagon.io/<org>/settings/...       org settings
```

Your personal settings at `app.flagon.io/settings` are the one area outside any
organization (see [Profile and account](/docs/platform/account)).

## Tenant isolation

Organizations are isolated from each other in the database itself, with forced
Postgres row-level security: every query the API runs is scoped to the
organizations the acting user belongs to, so one org can never read or write
another's data even if application code forgets a filter. The same rule covers
every front door: the dashboard, the API, access tokens, the assistant, and MCP.
See [Tenant isolation](/docs/security/tenant-isolation) for how it works.

If you are not a member of an organization, Flagon behaves as if it does not
exist: its pages return a 404 and its API operations return `404 Not Found`,
never a hint that it is there.

## Creating an organization

The person who creates an organization becomes its first **owner**.

<Tabs>

<Tab title="Dashboard">

Choose **Create organization** from the organization switcher, or **New
organization** under **Settings > Organizations**. Both open
`app.flagon.io/new`, where you enter a name and, optionally, a slug.

</Tab>

<Tab title="API">

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.flagon.io/orgs \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "Acme", "slug": "acme"}'
```

Requires the `admin:org` scope and a personal token: an organization access
token belongs to one organization and gets `403 Forbidden` here.

</Tab>

<Tab title="Assistant">

Ask: "Create an organization called Acme." The assistant proposes
`create_organization` with the name (and a slug if you gave one), and creates it
when you confirm.

</Tab>

</Tabs>

- **Name** is the display name shown across Flagon.
- **Slug** is the org's namespace in URLs and API paths. It is optional; when
  omitted it is derived from the name (`Acme Corp.` becomes `acme-corp`). Slugs are
  unique across live organizations, so a taken slug returns `409 Conflict`. A
  [deleted](#deleting-an-organization) organization's slug is free for anyone to
  take.

For a step-by-step walkthrough, see
[Create an organization](/docs/guides/create-an-organization).

### Plan limit

The Free plan includes **one organization you own**. Creating a second owned
organization returns `402 Payment Required`. Paid plans are not live yet, so for
now this caps each account at one owned organization. Organizations you are
*invited to* do not count; you can be a member of as many as you like. Deleted
organizations do not count either, but [restoring](#restoring-an-organization)
one does, so a restore that would put you over the limit also returns
`402 Payment Required`.

## Organization settings

Owners and admins manage the organization from its **Settings**:

| Setting | Where | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Name** | Settings > General | The display name. The slug and organization ID are shown here too; the slug cannot be changed yet, since that would break existing links and API references. |
| **Member privileges** | Settings > Member privileges | The **base permission**: the default project access every member gets. See [Roles & permissions](/docs/platform/roles). |
| **API tokens** | Settings > API tokens | [Organization access tokens](/docs/platform/access-tokens): credentials owned by the org rather than a person. |
| **Authentication** | Settings > Authentication | Require [two-factor authentication](/docs/platform/two-factor), and configure and require [single sign-on](/docs/platform/sso). |
| **Audit log** | Settings > Audit log | The org's immutable [audit log](/docs/platform/audit-log), and whether actor IP addresses are disclosed in it. |
| **Billing** | Settings > Billing | The org's plan. Every organization is on the Free plan today. |
| **Deleted projects** | Settings > Deleted projects | Soft-deleted [projects](/docs/platform/projects), which can be restored. |

Renaming the organization is `PATCH /orgs/{slug}` with a new `name`, and requires
an owner or admin. Every change to an organization's settings is recorded in its
audit log.

The organization's security policy is enforced by the API itself, not only by
the dashboard: when the organization requires two-factor authentication or
single sign-on, every operation under `/orgs/{slug}` (except leaving), every
assistant message, and every MCP tool call that names the organization returns
`403 Forbidden` to a member whose sign-in does not satisfy it. See
[Two-factor authentication](/docs/platform/two-factor) and
[Single sign-on](/docs/platform/sso).

## Members, roles, and teams

People belong to an organization as **members**, each with one organization role:
**owner**, **admin**, or **member**. Owners and admins manage the roster from
**People**, adding existing Flagon users directly or inviting anyone by email. See
[Members and invitations](/docs/platform/members).

Access to projects is layered on top: the org-wide base permission, per-project
collaborator roles, **teams** that hold project access for a group, and project
ownership. [Roles & permissions](/docs/platform/roles) explains how they combine,
and [Teams](/docs/platform/teams) covers groups.

An organization must always have at least one owner: the last owner cannot be
demoted or removed.

## Leaving an organization

Any member can leave an organization from **Settings > Organizations** in their
personal settings, with `POST /orgs/{slug}/leave`, or by asking the assistant.
Leaving removes your membership immediately and is recorded in the org's audit
log as `member.left`. If you are the **only owner**, leaving is refused with
`409 Conflict`: promote another member to owner first, or delete the
organization. Leaving is exempt from the two-factor and SSO requirements, so
you can always walk away from an organization whose policy you can't meet.
Organization access tokens can't leave (`403 Forbidden`); revoke the token
instead.

## Deleting an organization

Only an **owner** can delete an organization. Anyone else gets `403 Forbidden`.

<Tabs>

<Tab title="Dashboard">

Open **Settings > General**, scroll to the **Danger zone**, and confirm by typing
the organization's slug.

</Tab>

<Tab title="API">

```bash
curl -X DELETE https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"
```

Requires the `admin:org` scope and an owner role. Organization access tokens can
never be owners, so only a personal token can do this.

</Tab>

<Tab title="Assistant">

Ask: "Delete the acme organization." The assistant confirms the exact slug with
you and proposes `delete_organization`; nothing happens until you confirm.

</Tab>

</Tabs>

Deletion is a **soft delete** that takes effect for everyone at once:

- The organization and everything in it (projects, members, teams, invitations,
  tokens, audit log) behaves as if it does not exist: its pages and API operations
  return `404 Not Found` for every member, and it drops out of everyone's
  organization list.
- Its **organization access tokens stop working** immediately (`401 Unauthorized`). Personal access tokens keep working for your other
  organizations.
- Its **slug is freed**, so a new organization can take it right away.
- Every member is notified, and the deletion is recorded in the org's audit log
  as `organization.deleted` (readable again after a restore).

Deleting an organization is also how its sole owner winds it down: the only owner
cannot leave, but can delete it.

## Restoring an organization

A deleted organization stays restorable for **30 days**. Owners see the
organizations they owned under **Settings > Organizations > Recently deleted**,
or with `GET /deleted-orgs`, which lists each with its `id` and a `purge_at` time.
Restoring one (**Restore**, or `POST /deleted-orgs/{id}/restore`) brings
everything back exactly as it was: members, projects, teams, tokens, and settings.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.flagon.io/deleted-orgs/$ORG_ID/restore \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"slug": "acme-2"}'
```

- Restore addresses the organization by **id**, since its old slug may belong to a
  new organization by now.
- If the old slug was taken while the organization was deleted, the restore is
  refused with `409 Conflict`; pass a new `slug` in the body to restore it under
  that name. The body is optional otherwise.
- Restoring counts toward the [plan limit](#plan-limit).
- Listing and restoring deleted organizations needs a personal token or a
  signed-in session; organization access tokens get `403 Forbidden`. The
  in-product assistant refuses `restore_organization`, because a conversation is
  confined to the organization it was started in.
- After `purge_at` (30 days after deletion) the organization can no longer be
  restored and restore returns `404 Not Found`.

<Callout type="note" title="Permanent purge">

Past the 30-day window the organization is out of reach for everyone. The job
that permanently erases expired organizations from the database is not built
yet.

</Callout>

## Operations

Every organization operation is available on every front door, backed by the same
permission-checked API operation:

| Operation | API | Tool | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| List your organizations | `GET /orgs` (or `GET /me`) | `list_organizations` | `read:org` |
| Create an organization | `POST /orgs` | `create_organization` | `admin:org` |
| Rename an organization | `PATCH /orgs/{slug}` | `update_organization` | `write:org` |
| Leave an organization | `POST /orgs/{slug}/leave` | `leave_organization` | `admin:org` |
| Delete an organization | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}` | `delete_organization` | `admin:org` |
| List recently deleted organizations | `GET /deleted-orgs` | `list_deleted_organizations` | `read:org` |
| Restore a deleted organization | `POST /deleted-orgs/{id}/restore` | `restore_organization` | `admin:org` |
| Read the security policy | `GET /orgs/{slug}/security` | `get_org_security` | `read:org` |
| Update the security policy | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/security` | `set_org_security` | `write:org` |
| Manage SSO providers ([details](/docs/platform/sso)) | `/orgs/{slug}/sso/providers` | `list_sso_providers`, `create_sso_provider`, ... | `read:org` / `write:org` |

Scopes are a ceiling on top of your role: a token or the assistant can never do
more than you could yourself. See the [Tool reference](/docs/ai/tools) for every
tool.

## Related

- [Create an organization](/docs/guides/create-an-organization)
- [Members and invitations](/docs/platform/members)
- [Roles & permissions](/docs/platform/roles)
- [Delete and restore](/docs/guides/delete-and-restore)
- [Multi-tenancy](/docs/architecture/multi-tenancy)

docs.title: Project access
docs.description: Per-project collaborator roles, team grants, and ownership that layer on top of organization roles.
docs.body:
Most organizations run on **organization roles** and the **base permission**
alone. But sometimes one person or team needs more reach on a **single project**
than the organization gives them. Project access adds **collaborator roles**,
**team grants**, and **ownership** for exactly that, without changing what anyone
can do on other projects.

Everything on this page is managed from a project's **Settings > Access**
(`app.flagon.io/<org>/projects/<project>/settings/access`), which has sections
for collaborators, teams, and owners.

## The roles

A project role is one of five rungs, lowest to highest. The ladder is
cumulative: each role can do everything the ones below it can.

| Role | Grants |
| --- | --- |
| **Read** | See the project, its README, and its collaborators, teams, and owners. |
| **Triage** | Read today. Reserved for work-item powers as deployment and workflow features land. |
| **Write** | Edit the project's name, description, README, and repository URL. |
| **Maintain** | Write, plus renaming the project's slug, and project-level settings (environments and configuration) as they land. |
| **Admin** | Manage the project's collaborators and team grants. |

A person with no effective role on a project cannot see it at all: it is left
out of project lists, and its pages and API operations (reads and writes alike)
return `404 Not Found`. Someone who can see a project but lacks the rung an
operation needs gets `403 Forbidden`. The API checks this in its Go layer and
Postgres row-level security enforces the same rule underneath.

`GET /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}` (and the `get_project` tool) returns your
own access in a `viewer` object: your effective `role`, whether you are an
`owner`, and the `permissions` that grants (`project:view`, `project:write`,
`project:manage`, `project:admin`, `project:own`). The dashboard uses it to hide
controls you can't use; the server still checks every operation.

**Ownership** sits above the ladder as a separate tier. See
[Project ownership](#project-ownership).

## How access combines

A person can pick up access to a project three ways, and their **effective role**
is the **highest** of them:

- the **organization floor**: what their org role and the base permission grant
  on every project;
- their **explicit collaborator grant** on this project, if any;
- the role of any **team** they belong to that has been granted access to this
  project.

| Org role | Floor project role |
| --- | --- |
| Owner | Admin (plus owner powers) |
| Admin | Admin (plus owner powers) |
| Member | The base permission (default `read`; `none` means no floor) |
| Viewer (legacy) | Read |

Because the effective role is a maximum, a grant can only **raise** someone on a
specific project, never lower them below their organization floor. Granting
`read` to a member whose floor is already `write` changes nothing; granting
`admin` lets that member manage the project's collaborators without making them
an org admin anywhere else. To keep a project private to a group, set the base
permission to `none` and grant access explicitly.

## Collaborators

A **collaborator** is an organization member with an explicit role on one
project. Anyone who can see the project can see its collaborators; people with an
effective `admin` role (or owner powers) can add, change, and remove them.

<Tabs>

<Tab title="Dashboard">

Open the project, go to **Settings > Access**, and add a collaborator by
username or email with a role. Change or remove them from the same list.

</Tab>

<Tab title="API">

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/projects/billing-api/members \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"login": "dev@example.com", "role": "write"}'
```

</Tab>

<Tab title="Assistant">

Ask: "Give dev@example.com write access to billing-api." The assistant proposes
`add_project_member` and runs it when you confirm.

</Tab>

</Tabs>

- A collaborator must already be a **member of the organization**: a project
  grant elevates an existing member, it never adds outsiders (`409 Conflict`,
  `that user must be an organization member first`).
- You can't change your own grant (`409 Conflict`); another project admin has
  to.
- **Removing** a collaborator drops them back to their organization-level access.
- The person is notified when they are granted access or their role changes.

## Team access

Share a project with a **team** instead of listing people one by one. Grant the
team a role from the ladder and every member of the team inherits it on this
project. A project can be shared with many teams and a team can hold access to
many projects; each grant is independent. Team grants are managed in the same
**Settings > Access** page. See [Teams](/docs/platform/teams).

## Project ownership

**Ownership** is a distinct relation that sits **above** the admin rung. An owner
can do everything an admin can, and in addition:

- **delete and restore** the project;
- **manage the project's owners**, which is also how you transfer a project: add
  the new owner, then remove the old one.

A project can have **multiple owners**, and an owner can be an **individual user
or a team** (making a team an owner makes every member of it an owner). A person
has owner powers when any of these is true:

- they are an org owner or admin (always, on every project);
- they are listed as a direct owner;
- they belong to a team listed as an owner.

Creating a project does **not** make you its owner. A member who creates a
project is instead granted an explicit **admin** collaborator role on it, so
they can manage its access from day one. Because org owners and admins
always hold owner authority, an organization can never be locked out of its own
project even if the explicit owner list is empty. See
[Transfer project ownership](/docs/guides/transfer-project-ownership).

## Operations

| Operation | API | Tool | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| List collaborators | `GET /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/members` | `list_project_members` | `read:project` |
| Add a collaborator | `POST /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/members` | `add_project_member` | `admin:project` |
| Change a collaborator's role | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/members/{userId}/role` | `set_project_member_role` | `admin:project` |
| Remove a collaborator | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/members/{userId}` | `remove_project_member` | `admin:project` |
| List team grants | `GET /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/teams` | `list_project_teams` | `read:project` |
| Grant a team a role | `POST /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/teams` | `add_project_team` | `admin:project` |
| Change a team's role | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/teams/{team}/role` | `set_project_team_role` | `admin:project` |
| Remove a team's access | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/teams/{team}` | `remove_project_team` | `admin:project` |
| List owners | `GET /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/owners` | `list_project_owners` | `read:project` |
| Add an owner (user or team) | `POST /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/owners` | `add_project_owner` | `admin:project` |
| Remove an owner | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/owners/{type}/{principalId}` | `remove_project_owner` | `admin:project` |

Collaborator and team management needs an effective project `admin` role; adding
and removing owners needs owner powers, not merely `admin`. Every change is
audited (`project.access_granted`, `project.access_changed`,
`project.access_revoked`, `project.team_access_granted`,
`project.team_access_changed`, `project.team_access_revoked`,
`project.owner_added`, `project.owner_removed`).

## Related

- [Manage project access](/docs/guides/manage-project-access)
- [Transfer project ownership](/docs/guides/transfer-project-ownership)
- [Roles & permissions](/docs/platform/roles)
- [Teams](/docs/platform/teams)
- [Projects](/docs/platform/projects)

docs.title: Projects
docs.description: A project is the core unit in Flagon, a deployable app that belongs to an organization, with a README, access controls, and soft delete.
docs.body:
A **project** is the core unit in Flagon: one deployable app or service. There is
no separate "app" layer above it. Every project belongs to exactly one
[organization](/docs/platform/organizations), and its URL lives under that org:
`app.flagon.io/<org>/projects/<project>`.

Today a project holds its identity (name, slug, description), a Markdown README,
a repository URL, and its access controls. Deployments and environments attach
to projects as they land (see [Environments](/docs/platform/environments)).

## Project fields

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | Display name, for example `Checkout Service`. |
| `slug` | The URL segment, unique among the org's live projects. Derived from the name when omitted. Changing it renames the project and changes its URL. |
| `description` | A one-line summary shown under the project name. |
| `readme` | Markdown rendered on the project's **Overview** tab. |
| `repository_url` | The source repository. Shown as a **Repository** link on the project page. |

## Creating a project

A project created by the assistant is identical to one created by hand, because
every path calls the same permission-checked API operation.

<Tabs>

<Tab title="Dashboard">

On **Projects**, choose **New project**. Enter a project name (the slug is
derived from it unless you change it) and optionally a description and
repository URL. Add the README from the project's **Overview** tab once the
project exists.

</Tab>

<Tab title="API">

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/projects \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "Billing API", "description": "Invoices and payments"}'
```

Returns `201 Created` with the project. A taken slug returns `409 Conflict`.
Requires `write:project` and an organization role of member or higher (the
legacy read-only `viewer` role can't create projects).

</Tab>

<Tab title="Assistant">

Ask: "Create a project called billing-api." The assistant proposes
`create_project` and creates it when you confirm.

</Tab>

</Tabs>

Creating a project does not make you its owner; org owners and admins hold owner
authority on every project, and anyone else can be added as an owner afterward.
A member who creates a project is automatically granted an explicit `admin` role
on it (audited as `project.access_granted`), so they can manage it even when the
organization's base permission is `read` or `none`.
See [Create a project](/docs/guides/create-a-project) for a walkthrough.

## The project page

A project reads like a repository. The **Overview** tab renders the README, and
people with write access can edit it (with Edit and Preview) in place.
**Settings** has two sections: **General** (name, slug, description, repository
URL, and the Danger zone with delete) and **Access** (collaborators, teams, and
owners).

## Editing a project

Change a project's name, slug, description, or repository URL from
**Settings > General**, and its README from the Overview tab, by asking the
assistant (`update_project`), or with `PATCH /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}`.
Edits are partial: only the fields you send change. Editing the name,
description, README, or repository URL requires an effective project role of
`write` or higher. Renaming the slug changes the project's URL and breaks
outside references to it, so it requires `maintain` or higher. A project you
can't see returns `404`; one you can see but not edit returns `403` (see
[Project access](/docs/platform/project-access)).

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/projects/billing-api \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"repository_url": "https://example.com/acme/billing-api"}'
```

`GET /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}` includes a `viewer` object with your own
effective `role`, whether you are an `owner`, and your `permissions` on the
project; the dashboard uses it to show only the controls you can use.

To fetch a project with its organization inlined, use
`GET /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}?expand[]=organization` (see
[Expanding responses](/docs/api/expanding-responses)).

## Deleting and restoring

Deleting a project is a **soft delete**: the project disappears from every list
and URL, but it can be restored for **30 days**, the same window as a deleted
organization. Deleting **frees the slug immediately**, so you can create a new
project with the same name right away.

Delete and restore are **owner-tier** actions: a project owner (a user or a
team) or an org owner or admin. A project `admin` who is not an owner can manage
access but cannot delete the project.

<Tabs>

<Tab title="Dashboard">

Delete from **Settings > General > Danger zone**, confirming by typing the
project's slug. Deleted projects are listed under the org's
**Settings > Deleted projects** (org owners and admins), each with the days left
to restore it and a **Restore** button. If the old slug has been taken, a dialog
asks for a new one.

</Tab>

<Tab title="API">

```bash
curl -X DELETE https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/projects/billing-api \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"

curl -X POST https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/projects/billing-api/restore \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"
```

Both require `admin:project`. The restore body is optional; send
`{"slug": "new-slug"}` only to restore under a new slug.
`GET /orgs/{slug}/deleted-projects` lists projects deleted in the last 30 days,
each with `deleted_at` and `purge_at` (org owners and admins only; anyone else
gets `403`).

</Tab>

<Tab title="Assistant">

Ask: "Which projects were deleted recently? Restore billing-api." The assistant
reads the archive with `list_deleted_projects` and proposes `restore_project`,
with a `new_slug` if the old one has been taken.

</Tab>

</Tabs>

Restore brings back the most recently deleted project with that slug that is
still inside the 30-day window. If a live project has taken the slug since,
restore returns `409 Conflict` (`that project slug is now taken; restore it under a new slug`) unless you pass a new `slug`. After `purge_at` the project
can no longer be restored and restore returns `404 Not Found` (`no restorable project with that slug`). The job that permanently erases expired projects from
the database is not built yet. See
[Delete and restore](/docs/guides/delete-and-restore).

## Operations

| Operation | API | Tool | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| List projects | `GET /orgs/{slug}/projects` | `list_projects` | `read:project` |
| Read a project | `GET /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}` | `get_project` | `read:project` |
| Create a project | `POST /orgs/{slug}/projects` | `create_project` | `write:project` |
| Edit a project | `PATCH /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}` | `update_project` | `write:project` |
| Delete a project | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}` | `delete_project` | `admin:project` |
| List deleted projects | `GET /orgs/{slug}/deleted-projects` | `list_deleted_projects` | `read:project` |
| Restore a project | `POST /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/restore` | `restore_project` | `admin:project` |

The list operations support search (`q`) and cursor pagination; see
[Pagination](/docs/api/pagination). Project changes are audited as
`project.created`, `project.updated`, `project.deleted`, and `project.restored`.

## Related

- [Project access](/docs/platform/project-access)
- [Create a project](/docs/guides/create-a-project)
- [Delete and restore](/docs/guides/delete-and-restore)
- [Roles & permissions](/docs/platform/roles)

docs.title: Roles & permissions
docs.description: How organization roles, the base permission, project roles, teams, and project ownership combine into what someone can do.
docs.body:
Flagon uses a **fixed set of roles**, layered so that broad organization access
and fine-grained per-project access compose predictably. There are four pieces
(organization roles, the base permission, project roles, and team roles) plus a
separate **ownership** relation on projects. Custom roles are not offered: the
vocabulary on this page is the whole model.

On top of roles, every request made with an [access token](/docs/platform/access-tokens)
is also limited by the token's **scopes**. Roles decide what a person can do;
scopes can only narrow that for one credential.

## Organization roles

Every member has exactly one organization role:

| Role | What it can do |
| --- | --- |
| **Owner** | Everything, including deleting and restoring the organization. There must always be at least one owner. |
| **Admin** | Manage members, invitations, teams, organization tokens, the security policy, SSO, and the audit log. |
| **Member** | The default. Project access comes from the **base permission**, raised by explicit grants and team grants. |

Org owners and admins are admins on every project and hold owner authority on
every project, so the organization can never be locked out of its own work.

`viewer` is a legacy read-only organization role. The API still accepts it, and
it is one of the roles an [organization access token](/docs/platform/access-tokens)
can act with, but the dashboard no longer offers it for people: read-only
membership is a member plus a `read` base permission.

## Base permission

The **base permission** is the default project role every member gets on every
project in the organization. Owners and admins set it under
**Settings > Member privileges**.

| Level | Effect on every project |
| --- | --- |
| `none` | No access. Members see only the projects they are granted directly or through a team. |
| `read` | Read. This is the default. |
| `write` | Write. |
| `admin` | Admin. |

The dashboard offers these four (`none` is labeled **No access**). The API and
the `set_org_security` tool also accept the finer `triage` and `maintain` rungs;
anything else returns `422` (`invalid base permission`). A member can be **raised** above
the base on a specific project by an explicit grant, but never dropped below it.
Changes to the base permission are audited as
`organization.security_changed`. See
[Set base permissions](/docs/guides/set-base-permissions).

## Project roles

Projects use a five-rung collaborator ladder. Each rung includes everything
below it.

| Role | Grants |
| --- | --- |
| **Read** | See the project, its README, and its collaborators, teams, and owners. A project you cannot read returns `404 Not Found`, including for write operations, so its existence is not disclosed. |
| **Triage** | Read today. Reserved for work-item powers as deployment and workflow features land. |
| **Write** | Edit the project's name, description, README, and repository URL. |
| **Maintain** | Write, plus renaming the project's slug (it changes the project's URL and breaks outside references) and project-level settings as they land. |
| **Admin** | Manage the project's collaborators and team grants. |

An operation on a project you can read but whose rung you lack returns
`403 Forbidden`. The rules are enforced twice: in the API's Go layer and again
by Postgres row-level security (reading a project row needs read, updating one
needs write), so a missing check in code still can't leak or change a project.

Grants go to an individual collaborator or to a **team**. See
[Project access](/docs/platform/project-access).

## Team roles

A **team** is a named group of members that holds shared project access. Its
internal roles govern the team itself, separate from any project access it
carries:

| Role | What it can do |
| --- | --- |
| **Maintainer** | Manage the team's membership and edit the team. The creator of a team is its first maintainer. |
| **Member** | Belong to the team and inherit its project grants. |

Only org owners and admins create and delete teams. See [Teams](/docs/platform/teams).

## Project ownership

**Ownership** sits **above** the admin rung; it is not a rung on the ladder. An
owner can do everything an admin can, plus **delete and restore** the project and
**manage its owners** (which is how ownership is transferred). A project can have
several owners, and an owner can be an individual user or a team.

Creating a project does not make you its owner. When a member (not an org owner
or admin) creates a project, Flagon grants them an explicit **admin** role on it,
recorded in the audit log as `project.access_granted`, so they can manage what
they created even when the base permission is `read` or `none`. Org owners and
admins are implicit owners of every project; anyone else needs to be added as an
owner.

## How they combine

A person's effective **role** on a project is the highest of:

```text
max( organization floor, explicit project grant, team grants )
```

where the organization floor is `admin` for org owners and admins, the base
permission for members (no floor at all when it is `none`), and `read` for the
legacy `viewer` role. Team grants count only while the person is still on the
team. **Owner powers** apply on top of that role whenever the
person owns the project directly, owns it through a team, or is an org owner or
admin.

For example, in an organization whose base permission is `read`:

| Person | Floor | Grants | Effective |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Org admin | `admin` + owner | none | Admin, with owner powers |
| Member | `read` | none | Read |
| Member | `read` | direct `write` | Write |
| Member on team Platform | `read` | Platform has `admin` | Admin |
| Member on team Release | `read` | Release is a project owner | Read, with owner powers |

## Scopes on top of roles

A token or the assistant never exceeds the person (or service principal) it acts
as. For a token, the effective permission is the intersection of the role above
and the token's scopes: holding `admin:project` does not let a read-only member
delete a project, and an owner using a `read:project` token cannot edit one. The
in-product assistant uses your session, so it is bounded by your role alone. The
[permissions model](/docs/architecture/permissions-model) explains the full
evaluation order.

## Related

- [Project access](/docs/platform/project-access)
- [Members and invitations](/docs/platform/members)
- [Teams](/docs/platform/teams)
- [Access tokens](/docs/platform/access-tokens)
- [Roles matrix](/docs/reference/roles-matrix)

docs.title: SCIM provisioning
docs.description: The planned design for provisioning and deprovisioning members from your identity provider with SCIM 2.0.
docs.body:
<Callout type="warn" title="Not available yet">

SCIM is designed but not built. None of the endpoints on this page exist, and
there is no SCIM setting in the dashboard. Today, members are provisioned when
they first sign in through your [SSO](/docs/platform/sso) provider, and removed by
an owner or admin from **People**.

</Callout>

**SCIM** (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) lets an identity provider
such as Okta or Microsoft Entra ID **push** users into a Flagon organization and
remove them automatically, so membership follows your directory. It is one step
beyond [SSO](/docs/platform/sso), which provisions a member only the first time
they sign in and never removes anyone.

## How it will work

An organization owner or admin will mint a **SCIM provisioning token** (a scoped
[organization access token](/docs/platform/access-tokens)) and give the IdP two
values:

- **SCIM base URL**: `https://api.flagon.io/scim/v2`
- **Bearer token**: the provisioning token

The IdP then calls Flagon's SCIM API to create, update, deactivate, and remove
users, which map onto organization memberships. All writes are designed to go
through the same membership, RBAC, and [audit](/docs/platform/audit-log) paths as
everything else, so a SCIM-provisioned member is indistinguishable from one added
by hand.

## Planned endpoints (SCIM 2.0)

| Method and path | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /scim/v2/ServiceProviderConfig` | Advertise supported capabilities. |
| `GET /scim/v2/Users?filter=userName eq "..."` | Look up a user by email. |
| `POST /scim/v2/Users` | Provision a member. An existing Flagon account is added to the org; otherwise a pending invitation is created and completed at sign-up. |
| `GET /scim/v2/Users/{id}` | Read one provisioned user. |
| `PATCH /scim/v2/Users/{id}` | `active: false` removes the membership; `active: true` restores it. |
| `DELETE /scim/v2/Users/{id}` | Deprovision (remove the membership). |
| `GET`, `POST`, `PATCH /scim/v2/Groups` | Optional later step: map IdP groups to org roles or teams. |

Responses will use standard SCIM envelopes (`schemas`, `meta`, and a
`ListResponse` with `totalResults`, `startIndex`, and `itemsPerPage`) and the SCIM
error format. When SCIM ships, this page moves to `published` and the dashboard
gains a SCIM section under **Settings > Authentication**.

## Related

- [Single sign-on](/docs/platform/sso)
- [Members and invitations](/docs/platform/members)
- [Access tokens](/docs/platform/access-tokens)

docs.title: Single sign-on (SSO)
docs.description: Connect your identity provider with OIDC or SAML so members sign in to Flagon through it, and optionally require it.
headings: Manage providers from the API, assistant, or MCP
docs.body:
**Single sign-on** (SSO) lets members sign in to Flagon through your company's
identity provider (IdP), such as Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, or Google Workspace.
SSO is configured **per organization**, so each org connects its own IdP, and both
**OIDC** (OpenID Connect) and **SAML 2.0** are supported.

When someone signs in through an organization's IdP, Flagon **provisions their
membership** automatically: they become a member of the organization the provider
belongs to. You manage who has access in your IdP, and it flows into Flagon.

Managing SSO providers requires an organization **owner or admin**.

## Set up a provider

Go to your org's **Settings > Authentication**, find **SSO providers**, and
choose **New provider**. Every provider has:

- **Provider ID**: a short lowercase slug (letters, digits, and hyphens, 2 to 63
  characters, starting with a letter or digit), for example `acme-okta`. It is
  part of the callback URLs, so it cannot be changed later, and it is unique
  across Flagon.
- **Email domain**: your users' email domain, for example `acme.com`. The
  **Sign in with SSO** flow uses it to route a user to the right provider, and
  subdomains such as `eng.acme.com` match too. A domain can belong to only one
  provider (`409 Conflict` otherwise).

For step-by-step setup with a real IdP, see
[Set up SSO with OIDC](/docs/guides/set-up-sso-oidc) and
[Set up SSO with SAML](/docs/guides/set-up-sso-saml).

### OIDC

1. In your IdP, create an OIDC application and set its **redirect (callback)
   URI** to:

   ```text https://app.flagon.io/api/auth/sso/callback/<providerId> ```

2. In Flagon, choose **OIDC** and enter the provider ID, email domain, the
   **Issuer URL** (for example `https://acme.okta.com`; Flagon discovers the rest
   from `<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration`), and the application's
   **Client ID** and **Client secret**.
3. Save. Members can now sign in with SSO.

### SAML 2.0

1. In Flagon, choose **SAML**, set the provider ID and email domain, and paste
   your IdP's **SSO URL (entry point)** and **signing certificate (PEM)**. The
   **SP entity ID** is an identifier for this connection, for example
   `https://app.flagon.io/saml/acme`.
2. Save, then copy the two URLs Flagon shows for the provider into your IdP:
   - **ACS (Assertion Consumer Service) URL**:
     `https://app.flagon.io/api/auth/sso/saml2/sp/acs/<providerId>`
   - **SP metadata URL** (many IdPs can import this directly):
     `https://app.flagon.io/api/auth/sso/saml2/sp/metadata?providerId=<providerId>`
3. In the IdP, set the audience (SP entity ID) to the value you entered in
   Flagon, make sure the assertion includes the user's **email**, and assign the
   users or groups who should have access.

## Signing in

On the login page, members choose **Sign in with SSO** and enter their work
email. Flagon matches the email's domain to a provider and redirects to the IdP.
On return, the member is signed in and their organization membership is ensured.
A person with no Flagon account gets one created and is added to the organization
automatically. The join is recorded in the org's
[audit log](/docs/platform/audit-log).

### One account, many organizations

You have a single Flagon account, and each organization connects its own IdP.
When you go through an org's SSO while already signed in, Flagon **links that
org's SSO identity to your current account**, whatever email the IdP asserts. So
one account can belong to org A (through Okta), org B (through Microsoft Entra
ID), and an org with no SSO at all, and a single sign-in reaches all of them.

## Requiring SSO

Once a provider is configured, an owner or admin can turn on **Require single
sign-on** under **Settings > Authentication** (or set `require_sso` with
`set_org_security`). With it on, members and admins who have not signed in
through the org's provider are sent to a "single sign-on required" page when they
open the organization, and must continue with SSO first.

The API enforces the same requirement, so it holds on every front door, not just
in the dashboard:

| Caller | Allowed when SSO is required |
| --- | --- |
| Dashboard session (including the assistant) | The current session was established through one of the organization's providers. |
| Personal access token (API or MCP) | The token's user has signed in through one of the organization's providers at least once. |
| Organization access token | Always: its service principal never signs in interactively. |
| Organization owner | Always (see break-glass below). |

Anyone else gets `403 Forbidden` (`this organization requires single sign-on; sign in through the organization's identity provider to continue`) on every
operation under `/orgs/{slug}` except leaving the organization, on assistant
messages and confirmed actions, and on MCP tool calls that name the
organization.

- **Lockout safety**: the API refuses to turn the requirement on
  (`403 Forbidden`, `sign in through one of the organization's SSO providers before requiring single sign-on`) unless you have signed in through one of the
  org's providers yourself, whether you use the dashboard, the API, or the
  assistant.
- **Owner break-glass**: owners are exempt from the requirement, so an owner can
  always reach settings to fix or disable SSO even if the IdP is misconfigured.

You can require SSO, [two-factor authentication](/docs/platform/two-factor), or
both. Changes to the requirement are audited as `organization.security_changed`.

## Manage providers from the API, assistant, or MCP

SSO providers are an ordinary Flagon setting owned by the API. Everything the
settings page does is also an API operation and a tool:

| Operation | API | Tool | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| List providers | `GET /orgs/{slug}/sso/providers` | `list_sso_providers` | `read:org` |
| Read a provider | `GET /orgs/{slug}/sso/providers/{provider}` | `get_sso_provider` | `read:org` |
| Add a provider | `POST /orgs/{slug}/sso/providers` | `create_sso_provider` | `write:org` |
| Update a provider | `PATCH /orgs/{slug}/sso/providers/{provider}` | `update_sso_provider` | `write:org` |
| Remove a provider | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/sso/providers/{provider}` | `delete_sso_provider` | `write:org` |

Only organization **owners and admins** can read or change SSO configuration,
whatever the token's scopes. Changes are audited as `sso_provider.created`,
`sso_provider.updated`, and `sso_provider.deleted`.

An update is partial: fields you leave out, including secrets, are unchanged. The
provider ID and protocol cannot be changed; remove the provider and add a new one
instead. Besides the fields on the settings page, the API and tools accept OIDC
`scopes`, `pkce`, and `discovery_endpoint`, and SAML `audience`,
`want_assertions_signed`, `authn_requests_signed`, and a service-provider
`private_key`.

## How secrets are handled

- The OIDC **client secret** and a SAML **private key** are **write-only**. You
  send them when you add a provider or rotate them with an update; no read ever
  returns them. The settings page, the API, and every tool show only whether a
  secret is set (`client_secret_set`, `private_key_set`).
- Secrets are stored apart from the rest of the provider's configuration and are
  **encrypted at rest** with AES-256-GCM under the API's `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY`
  (a base64-encoded 32-byte key, required in production). A database dump,
  backup, or replica alone never yields them. Rows written before encryption
  existed are encrypted automatically when the API boots.
- The only path that reads them decrypted is an internal operation reachable
  solely by the sign-in service with Flagon's internal credential, never by an
  access token. The sign-in service's own provider cache (in the app's auth
  database) holds the secret in plaintext, because the OIDC and SAML flows need
  it.
- Removing a provider clears its secrets.

## How it fits together

- The **API is the source of truth** for SSO configuration: it stores each
  provider, validates it, enforces tenant isolation (row-level security, owners
  and admins only), and audits every change.
- The IdP protocol work (OIDC and SAML, assertion validation, signing) runs in the
  app's sign-in service, built on BetterAuth's SSO plugin. It keeps a **cache** of
  provider configuration, which it refreshes from the API at the start of every
  SSO sign-in, callback, and SAML request. A change made anywhere applies on the
  next sign-in, and a removed provider (or a deleted organization) stops working.
  If the API cannot be reached, SSO sign-in fails closed rather than using a stale
  provider.
- Providers registered before the API owned SSO are **adopted** into the API the
  first time they are used (or when an owner opens the Authentication settings).
  Operators can adopt them all at once with `npm run sso:backfill` in `app/`; it
  is idempotent, and a provider removed through the API is never brought back.
- A verified SSO login calls the API across the internal trust boundary to ensure
  the member exists, so SSO users flow through the same membership, RBAC, and
  audit paths as everyone else. See
  [Identity and auth](/docs/architecture/identity-and-auth).

## Related

- [Set up SSO with OIDC](/docs/guides/set-up-sso-oidc)
- [Set up SSO with SAML](/docs/guides/set-up-sso-saml)
- [Two-factor authentication](/docs/platform/two-factor)
- [SCIM provisioning](/docs/platform/scim)
- [Sign-in and SSO troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting/sign-in-and-sso)

docs.title: Teams
docs.description: Named groups of organization members that hold shared access to projects.
docs.body:
A **team** is a named group of members inside an organization. Instead of
granting project access one person at a time, you build a team once and grant
*the team* a role on the projects it needs. Every member of the team inherits
that access, and when someone joins or leaves the team, their project reach
follows automatically.

Teams live under **Teams** (`app.flagon.io/<org>/teams`). Only organization
owners and admins create and delete teams; the person who creates a team becomes
its first maintainer.

## Team roles

A team has two internal roles that govern the team itself. They are separate
from any access the team holds on a project.

| Role | What it can do |
| --- | --- |
| **Maintainer** | Manage the team's membership (add and remove members, choose who is a maintainer) and edit the team's name, slug, and description. |
| **Member** | Belong to the team and inherit the project access granted to it. |

Organization owners and admins can always manage any team, whether or not they
are on it. Deleting a team is reserved for them: a maintainer runs a team but
does not disband it.

## How teams get project access

A team carries no project access on its own. You grant it a **project role**,
one rung of the collaborator ladder (`read`, `triage`, `write`, `maintain`, or
`admin`), on a specific project, and every team member gains that role there. A
team can also be made a project **owner**, which makes every member an owner of
that project. See [Project access](/docs/platform/project-access) for what each
rung and ownership can do.

- **A team can hold access to many projects.** Grant the same team `write` on
  one project and `admin` on another; each grant is independent.
- **A project can be shared with many teams.** A project lists the teams it is
  shared with alongside its individual collaborators.

Because a person's effective role on a project is the **highest** of all their
grants, being on a team can only ever raise someone's access on a project, never
lower it.

## Creating and managing a team

<Tabs>

<Tab title="Dashboard">

On **Teams**, choose **New team**, give it a name (the slug is derived from it
unless you set one) and an optional description. Open the team to add members,
change who is a maintainer, and see the projects it can reach. Grant a team
access to a project from that project's **Settings > Access**.

</Tab>

<Tab title="API">

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/teams \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "Platform", "description": "Runs the shared infrastructure"}'

curl -X POST https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/teams/platform/members \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"login": "dev@example.com", "role": "member"}'
```

</Tab>

<Tab title="Assistant">

Ask: "Create a Platform team and add dev@example.com to it." The assistant
proposes `create_team` and then `add_team_member`; each runs when you confirm.

</Tab>

</Tabs>

People you add to a team must already be members of the organization: a team
elevates existing members, it never brings in outsiders. For a walkthrough, see
[Organize with teams](/docs/guides/organize-with-teams).

Deleting a team removes it from the organization, and its project grants and
ownerships stop having effect immediately. The team is soft-deleted in the
database, but there is no restore operation, so treat deletion as final.

Team changes are audited: `team.created`, `team.updated`, `team.deleted`,
`team.member_added`, `team.member_role_changed`, and `team.member_removed`.

## Operations

| Operation | API | Tool | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| List teams | `GET /orgs/{slug}/teams` | `list_teams` | `read:team` |
| Read a team | `GET /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}` | `get_team` | `read:team` |
| Create a team | `POST /orgs/{slug}/teams` | `create_team` | `write:team` |
| Edit a team | `PATCH /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}` | `update_team` | `write:team` |
| Delete a team | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}` | `delete_team` | `admin:team` |
| List team members | `GET /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/members` | `list_team_members` | `read:team` |
| Add a team member | `POST /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/members` | `add_team_member` | `write:team` |
| Change a team role | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/members/{userId}/role` | `set_team_member_role` | `write:team` |
| Remove a team member | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/members/{userId}` | `remove_team_member` | `write:team` |
| List a team's projects | `GET /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/projects` | `list_team_projects` | `read:team` |

Granting a team a role on a project, or making it an owner, is a project
operation and requires `admin:project` (see
[Project access](/docs/platform/project-access)). Scopes are a ceiling on top of
your role, and tenant isolation is enforced in the database.

## Related

- [Organize with teams](/docs/guides/organize-with-teams)
- [Project access](/docs/platform/project-access)
- [Roles & permissions](/docs/platform/roles)
- [Members and invitations](/docs/platform/members)

docs.title: Two-factor authentication
docs.description: Add an authenticator-app second step to your sign-in, and require it for everyone in an organization.
docs.body:
**Two-factor authentication** (2FA) adds a second step at sign-in, so a leaked
password alone cannot open your account. Flagon's second factor is a time-based
one-time password (TOTP) from an authenticator app, with backup codes for when
you lose your device. You turn it on for your own account; an organization can
additionally require it of every member.

## Turn on 2FA for your account

Go to **Settings > Password and authentication** (`app.flagon.io/settings/security`)
and enable **Authenticator app (TOTP)**:

1. Confirm your password.
2. Scan the QR code with an authenticator app (1Password, Google Authenticator,
   Authy, and similar).
3. Save your **backup codes** somewhere safe. Each lets you sign in once if you
   lose your device.

From then on, signing in asks for a 6-digit code (or a backup code) after your
password. 2FA belongs to your account, so it applies in every organization you
belong to.

## Require 2FA for an organization

An organization owner or admin can require every member to have 2FA enabled.

<Tabs>

<Tab title="Dashboard">

Open the org's **Settings > Authentication** and turn on **Require two-factor
authentication**.

</Tab>

<Tab title="API">

`PUT /orgs/{slug}/security` replaces the whole policy, so send all three fields:

```bash
curl -X PUT https://api.flagon.io/orgs/acme/security \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"enforce_two_factor": true, "require_sso": false, "base_permission": "read"}'
```

Read the current policy first with `GET /orgs/{slug}/security` so you do not
change the other fields by accident. Requires `write:org` and an owner or admin
role.

</Tab>

<Tab title="Assistant">

Ask: "Require two-factor authentication in acme." The assistant proposes
`set_org_security` with only `enforce_two_factor` changed; the tool leaves the
other fields as they are.

</Tab>

</Tabs>

What happens next:

- Members without 2FA, owners included, are sent to a "two-factor
  authentication required" page when they open the organization, and must set it
  up before they can continue.
- The API enforces the same rule. A member without 2FA gets `403 Forbidden`
  (`this organization requires two-factor authentication; enable it on your account to continue`) on every operation under `/orgs/{slug}` except leaving
  the organization, on assistant messages and confirmed actions, and on MCP tool
  calls that name the organization. This covers dashboard sessions and
  **personal access tokens** alike.
- **Organization access tokens** are exempt: their service principal never signs
  in, so 2FA does not apply to it.
- **Lockout safety**: the API refuses to turn the requirement on unless your own
  2FA is already enabled (`403 Forbidden`, `enable two-factor authentication on your own account before requiring it for the organization`), whether you use
  the dashboard, the API, or the assistant. Turning it off is always allowed.
- The change is recorded in the org's [audit log](/docs/platform/audit-log) as
  `organization.security_changed`.

<Callout type="tip" title="Before you turn it on">

Because the API enforces the requirement, scripts and MCP clients that use a
member's personal access token stop working in this organization until that
member enables 2FA. Move shared automation to an
[organization access token](/docs/platform/access-tokens) first.

</Callout>

This pairs with [single sign-on](/docs/platform/sso): you can require SSO, 2FA,
or both. See [Require two-factor authentication](/docs/guides/require-two-factor)
for a rollout walkthrough.

## Related

- [Require two-factor authentication](/docs/guides/require-two-factor)
- [Single sign-on](/docs/platform/sso)
- [Profile and account](/docs/platform/account)
- [Authentication (security)](/docs/security/authentication)

docs.title: Usage and AI limits
docs.description: How assistant usage is metered per organization, the rolling daily limit, and what happens when you reach it.
docs.body:
Flagon meters usage **per organization**, so limits and plans apply to the org,
not to an individual. Today that metering covers the
[assistant](/docs/ai/assistant): every assistant turn and every confirmed action
is recorded against the organization it ran in, and a rolling daily limit caps
how many there can be. Plan-based limits and billing will build on the same
records.

## What is metered

Each time the assistant does work, Flagon writes a usage record for the
organization the conversation belongs to:

- **Each assistant turn** (one message you send, including every read tool it
  runs and every model call along the way) records one entry with the model used
  and the input and output tokens it consumed.
- **Each confirmed action** (a change the assistant proposed and you approved)
  records one entry for the tool that ran.

Both kinds count toward the daily limit. If a turn's usage cannot be recorded,
the turn fails with `503 Service Unavailable` rather than running unmetered.

Calling the REST API directly, or calling tools over [MCP](/docs/ai/mcp), runs no
model on Flagon's side and is **not** metered as AI usage. Usage records are
tenant-isolated like everything else: no other organization can read them.

## The daily limit

Each organization can make a fixed number of AI calls in any **rolling 24
hours**. The default is **100 per organization**, which is what the hosted
service uses. The limit is checked when you send the assistant a message and
again before a confirmed action runs: once the organization has reached it,
either request fails with `429 Too Many Requests` and the message
`AI usage limit reached for this organization`, and neither the model nor the
action runs.
Because the window is rolling, capacity returns gradually as older calls age past
24 hours; there is no midnight reset.

Everything else keeps working when the limit is reached. The dashboard, the API,
and MCP are not affected, and anything the assistant can do you can still do
yourself.

## Plans

Every organization is on the **Free** plan today, shown under the org's
**Settings > Billing**. The Free plan includes the AI daily limit above and one
organization you own; creating a second owned organization returns
`402 Payment Required` (see [Organizations](/docs/platform/organizations#plan-limit)).

<Callout type="warn" title="Not available yet">

Paid plans, billing, and the org's **Usage** page (it shows a "Coming soon"
preview) are not built yet. See the [roadmap](https://flagon.io/roadmap).

</Callout>

## Self-hosting

On your own instance the limit and the model are configuration on the API server:

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FLAGON_AI_DAILY_LIMIT` | `100` | Maximum AI calls per organization per rolling 24 hours. `0` means unlimited: fine for a private instance, never for a shared one. |
| `FLAGON_AI_PROVIDER` | `auto` | `anthropic`, `openai` (any OpenAI-compatible endpoint), `mock` (offline, no key), or `auto`. Pinning `anthropic` or `openai` without its credentials, or an unknown value, stops the API at startup. |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | none | Enables the Anthropic provider. |
| `FLAGON_AI_BASE_URL` | none | Base URL of an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, such as a local Ollama or vLLM server. `OPENAI_BASE_URL` also works. |
| `FLAGON_AI_API_KEY` | none | Key for the OpenAI-compatible endpoint (leave empty for keyless local servers). `OPENAI_API_KEY` also works. |
| `FLAGON_AI_MODEL` | provider default | The model the assistant runs. |

Pointing the assistant at a model you host yourself gives you a flat cost; the
daily limit still applies unless you raise or disable it. See
[The assistant](/docs/ai/assistant#providers-and-models) for how the provider is
chosen and [Configuration](/docs/reference/configuration) for every setting.

## Related

- [The assistant](/docs/ai/assistant)
- [Organizations](/docs/platform/organizations)
- [Configuration reference](/docs/reference/configuration)
- [Self-hosting](/docs/self-hosting/overview)

docs.title: Audit actions
docs.description: Every action key the organization audit log records, what triggers it, and the target type and id it points at.
docs.body:
Every change to an organization's state writes one entry to its **audit log**,
in the same database transaction as the change, so an entry exists exactly when
the change committed. Each entry has a stable, dotted **action key**
(`resource.verb`), a **target** (a type and an id), a human-readable
**summary**, the actor, and where the request came from. This page lists every
action key, generated from the `Action` constants in `api/internal/audit` and
the call sites that record them.

Use the keys to filter the log: `GET /orgs/<org>/audit?action=project.deleted`
(repeat `action` for several), or the **Action** filter in the dashboard. Only
organization owners and admins can read the log; a plain member gets `403` and a
non-member gets `404`. See
[Audit log](/docs/platform/audit-log).

## Projects

Project entries target the project by **slug** (`target_type` is `project`),
including the access and ownership entries.

| Action | Recorded when | Target | Example summary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `project.created` | A project is created. | `project`, slug | `created project Billing API` |
| `project.updated` | A project's name, slug, description, README, or repository URL changes. The target is the slug after the update. | `project`, slug | `updated project Billing API` |
| `project.deleted` | A project is soft-deleted. | `project`, slug | `deleted project Billing API` |
| `project.restored` | A deleted project is restored. The target is the slug it was restored under. | `project`, slug | `restored project Billing API`, `restored project Billing API as billing-api-v2` |
| `project.access_granted` | A user is granted a role on a project. Also recorded when a member who is not an organization owner or admin creates a project and is granted `admin` on it automatically. | `project`, slug | `granted ana write on billing-api`, `granted the creator admin on billing-api` |
| `project.access_changed` | A collaborator's project role changes. | `project`, slug | `changed a collaborator's role to maintain on billing-api` |
| `project.access_revoked` | A collaborator's grant is removed. | `project`, slug | `revoked a collaborator's access to billing-api` |
| `project.team_access_granted` | A team is granted a role on a project. | `project`, slug | `granted team platform write on billing-api` |
| `project.team_access_changed` | A team's project role changes. | `project`, slug | `changed team platform's role to admin on billing-api` |
| `project.team_access_revoked` | A team's project grant is removed. | `project`, slug | `revoked team platform's access to billing-api` |
| `project.owner_added` | A user or team becomes a project owner. | `project`, slug | `made ana an owner of billing-api`, `made team platform an owner of billing-api` |
| `project.owner_removed` | A project owner is removed. | `project`, slug | `removed an owner from billing-api` |

## Teams

Team entries target the team by **slug** (`target_type` is `team`).

| Action | Recorded when | Target | Example summary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `team.created` | A team is created. | `team`, slug | `created team Platform` |
| `team.updated` | A team's name, slug, or description changes. | `team`, slug | `updated team Platform` |
| `team.deleted` | A team is deleted. | `team`, slug | `deleted team platform` |
| `team.member_added` | A user is added to a team. | `team`, slug | `added ana to team platform as member` |
| `team.member_role_changed` | A team member's role changes. | `team`, slug | `changed a member's role to maintainer on team platform` |
| `team.member_removed` | A user is removed from a team. | `team`, slug | `removed a member from team platform` |

## Members and invitations

| Action | Recorded when | Target | Example summary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `member.added` | An existing user is added to the organization (directly, or by inviting their email or username), or a user joins for the first time through the organization's SSO. | `member`, user id | `added ana@example.com as member`, `joined via single sign-on` |
| `member.role_changed` | A member's organization role changes. | `member`, user id | `changed a member's role to admin` |
| `member.removed` | An owner or admin removes a member. | `member`, user id | `removed a member` |
| `member.left` | A member leaves the organization. | `member`, user id | `left the organization` |
| `invitation.sent` | An email invitation is sent to someone who does not have an account yet. | `invitation`, invitation id | `invited ana@example.com as member` |
| `invitation.revoked` | A pending invitation is revoked. | `invitation`, invitation id | `revoked an invitation` |
| `invitation.accepted` | An invitee accepts and joins. The actor is the new member. | `member`, user id | `ana@example.com accepted an invitation and joined the organization` |

## Organization

Organization entries target the organization by **id** (`target_type` is
`organization`).

| Action | Recorded when | Target | Example summary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `organization.created` | The organization is created. | `organization`, id | `created organization Acme` |
| `organization.updated` | The organization is renamed. | `organization`, id | `renamed the organization to Acme Inc` |
| `organization.audit_config_changed` | Actor IP disclosure in the audit log is turned on or off. | `organization`, id | `enabled actor IP disclosure in the audit log` |
| `organization.security_changed` | The security policy changes. One entry per setting that changed: the two-factor requirement, the SSO requirement, or the base permission. | `organization`, id | `enabled the two-factor authentication requirement`, `disabled the single sign-on requirement`, `set the base member permission to write` |
| `organization.deleted` | The organization is soft-deleted. | `organization`, id | `deleted the organization Acme` |
| `organization.restored` | A deleted organization is restored. | `organization`, id | `restored the organization Acme` |

## Access tokens

Only **organization** access tokens are audited, because the log belongs to an
organization. Personal access tokens are not recorded here.

| Action | Recorded when | Target | Example summary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `token.created` | An organization access token is created. | `token`, token id | `created organization token deploy-bot` |
| `token.revoked` | An organization access token is revoked. | `token`, token id | `revoked organization token deploy-bot` |

## Single sign-on

SSO entries target the provider by its **provider id** (`target_type` is
`sso_provider`).

| Action | Recorded when | Target | Example summary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sso_provider.created` | An OIDC or SAML provider is added. Also recorded, with no actor, when a provider registered before the API owned SSO configuration is imported. | `sso_provider`, provider id | `added OIDC single sign-on provider acme-okta`, `imported SAML single sign-on provider acme-entra from the sign-in service` |
| `sso_provider.updated` | A provider's configuration changes. | `sso_provider`, provider id | `updated single sign-on provider acme-okta`, `updated single sign-on provider acme-okta (credentials changed)` |
| `sso_provider.deleted` | A provider is removed. | `sso_provider`, provider id | `removed single sign-on provider acme-okta` |

## The shape of an event

`GET /orgs/<org>/audit` returns `{"events": [...]}`, newest first, 30 per page by
default (`limit` up to 100). When there are more, the response carries a `Link`
header with `rel="next"`; follow it (it holds an opaque `cursor`). Filter with
`q` (search), `action` (repeatable), and `actor` (a user id). Each event:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | The entry's id. |
| `action` | One of the keys above. |
| `target_type`, `target_id` | What the change was made to, as listed per action. |
| `summary` | The human-readable predicate shown in the dashboard. |
| `actor_id`, `actor_name`, `actor_email`, `actor_username`, `actor_avatar_url` | Who did it. For an organization access token, the actor is the token's service user and the name is the token's name. |
| `actor_ip` | The client IP, or `null` unless the organization has turned on IP disclosure (owners and admins, under the audit log settings). |
| `actor_country`, `actor_user_agent` | Where the request came from. Always shown when known. |

The IP and user agent come from the request itself. For requests the dashboard
forwards, the API trusts the client details the dashboard passes along; for
access token and MCP callers it uses the connection's peer address, or the
header named by `FLAGON_CLIENT_IP_HEADER` when the API sits behind a proxy (see
[Configuration](/docs/reference/configuration)). Assistant actions record the IP
and user agent of the person who confirmed them.
| `created_at` | When the change committed. |

The log is append-only: there is no operation to edit or delete an entry.

## Related

- [Audit log](/docs/platform/audit-log)
- [Review the audit log](/docs/guides/review-the-audit-log)
- [Pagination and search](/docs/api/pagination)
- [Auditing and notifications](/docs/architecture/auditing-and-notifications)

docs.title: Configuration
docs.description: Every flag and environment variable of the API server (flagon-server) and every environment variable the web app and its scripts read, with defaults and what production requires.
docs.body:
Flagon runs as two services, and each is configured entirely through its
environment: the **API server** (`flagon-server`, Go, in `api/`) and the **web
app** (Next.js, in `app/`). This page lists every setting each one reads,
generated from `api/cmd/flagon-server/main.go` and every `process.env` read in
`app/`. For how to put them together on a real deployment, see
[Self-hosting](/docs/self-hosting/configuration).

<Callout type="warn" title="Set these in production">
The API: `DATABASE_URL`, `FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL`, `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN`, and
`FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY`. In production mode the server refuses to start without
them (and refuses the public development token). Set `RESEND_API_KEY` too, or
invitation emails are only logged. The app: `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`,
`BETTER_AUTH_URL`, `DATABASE_URL`, `FLAGON_API_URL`, `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN`
(the same value as the API's), and `RESEND_API_KEY`. Each is marked **Required
in production** below.
</Callout>

## API server: `flagon-server`

`flagon-server` has two commands:

- `flagon-server serve` applies pending migrations, then serves the HTTP API.
- `flagon-server migrate` provisions the runtime database role and applies
  migrations, then exits.

Every setting is a command-line flag backed by an environment variable. On
startup the server also loads `.env.local` and then `.env` from its working
directory if they exist. A variable that is already set is never overridden, so
the precedence is: real environment, then `.env.local`, then `.env`, then the
flag default. A flag given on the command line wins over all of them.

### Development and production mode

The server runs in one of two modes, and production mode refuses the insecure
conveniences that make a fresh checkout work with zero setup.

| Flag | Environment variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--environment` (`serve` only) | `FLAGON_ENV` | empty | `development` (or `dev`) or `production` (or `prod`). When unset, the server is in **production** mode when it runs on Fly.io (`FLY_APP_NAME` is set) or binds any non-loopback interface (such as `FLAGON_HOST=0.0.0.0`, which the container image sets), and in **development** mode when bound to loopback (`127.0.0.1`, `::1`, or `localhost`), which is the default off Fly. `migrate` reads `FLAGON_ENV` and `FLAGON_HOST` from the environment to decide the same way. |

In development mode:

- `DATABASE_URL` and `FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL` fall back to the local Docker
  Compose Postgres (the migrator and the app role). Runtime queries still use
  the app role; the server never runs them as the migrator, in any mode.
- `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN` falls back to the public value `dev-internal-token`,
  with a warning.
- `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY` falls back to a fixed, publicly known key, with a
  warning.
- Links in emails default to `http://localhost:3000`.

In production mode, a missing `DATABASE_URL`, `FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL`,
`FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN`, or `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY`, or an internal token equal to
`dev-internal-token`, stops the server at startup with an error that names the
variable. The Docker Compose file sets `FLAGON_ENV=development` for its API
service, because the container binds all interfaces.

A bare `flagon-server serve` with no configuration binds `127.0.0.1` and runs
in development mode, so a fresh checkout works with zero setup. If you run the
binary directly on a server behind a reverse proxy on the same machine, it is
still bound to loopback, so set `FLAGON_ENV=production` explicitly.

### Database (both commands)

These are global flags, shared by `serve` and `migrate`. The API uses two
Postgres roles on purpose: a schema owner that only migrates, and a runtime role
without `BYPASSRLS` that every request uses, so row-level security always
applies. See [Multi-tenancy](/docs/architecture/multi-tenancy).

| Flag | Environment variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--database-url` | `DATABASE_URL` | Development only: `postgres://flagon:flagon@localhost:5432/flagon_api?sslmode=disable` | The migrator (schema owner) connection. Used only to run migrations and provision the runtime role. **Required in production.** |
| `--app-database-url` | `FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL` | Development only: `postgres://flagon_app:flagon_app@localhost:5432/flagon_api?sslmode=disable` | The runtime connection, as the `NOBYPASSRLS` app role, used for every request. **Required in production** for `serve`: the server never runs runtime queries as the migrator there. |

### Server (`serve`)

| Flag | Environment variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--internal-token` | `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN` | Development only: `dev-internal-token` | The shared secret the web app authenticates to the API with. Must match the app's `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN`. **Required in production**: use a long random value; the public development value is refused. |
| `--secrets-key` | `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY` | Development only: a fixed public key | Base64-encoded 32-byte AES-256 key that encrypts stored credentials (SSO client secrets and SAML keys) at rest. Generate one with `openssl rand -base64 32`. On every boot the server encrypts any stored credential still in plaintext or under a retired key. **Required in production.** |
| `--secrets-keys-retired` | `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEYS_RETIRED` | empty | Comma-separated base64 keys that used to be `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY`, kept only to decrypt during a rotation. On boot every stored credential sealed under one of them is re-sealed under the current key. Remove them once the boot log reports nothing left to re-seal. See [Secrets](/docs/security/secrets#rotating-the-encryption-key). |
| `--host` | `FLAGON_HOST` | `127.0.0.1` off Fly; all interfaces on Fly | The interface to bind, for both the API and metrics listeners. The default binds loopback only, which also selects development mode when `FLAGON_ENV` is unset. Containers set `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces; the API image does this for you), which selects production mode. |
| `--port` | `PORT` | `8080` | The public HTTP API port. |
| `--metrics-port` | `METRICS_PORT` | `9091` | The private Prometheus port (`/metrics`). Never expose it publicly. |
| `--mcp-host` | `FLAGON_MCP_HOST` | empty | A hostname dedicated to the MCP server (the hosted service uses `mcp.flagon.io`). On that host the MCP endpoint is served at `/` and every other path returns `404`. Empty means MCP is served only at `/mcp`. |
| `--app-url` | `FLAGON_APP_URL` | `https://app.flagon.io` in production, `http://localhost:3000` in development | Public base URL of the web app, used for links in emails the API sends (invitation accept links). Set it when you self-host. |

### Request limits (`serve`)

| Flag | Environment variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--max-body-bytes` | `FLAGON_MAX_BODY_BYTES` | `4194304` (4 MiB) | Maximum request body, in bytes, on every route including the MCP endpoint. A larger body gets `413`. API operations also keep their own 1 MiB limit. |
| `--rate-limit` | `FLAGON_RATE_LIMIT` | `50` | Sustained requests per second per principal: each signed-in user, each access token, or each client IP for unauthenticated callers. `0` disables rate limiting. The limiter is in memory and per instance, so N API machines allow up to N times this. Over the limit, requests get `429` with `Retry-After`. |
| `--rate-burst` | `FLAGON_RATE_BURST` | `300` | How many requests a principal may make at once before the sustained rate applies. |
| `--client-ip-header` | `FLAGON_CLIENT_IP_HEADER` | empty | A proxy header that carries the real client IP, such as `Fly-Client-IP` (the hosted service sets this). Used to rate limit unauthenticated callers and as the IP the audit log records for access token and MCP callers. Empty means only the TCP peer address is trusted. Set it only when every request reaches the API through a proxy that overwrites the header, or callers can spoof their IP. |

`GET /healthz` and `GET /readyz` are never rate limited. See
[Limits](/docs/reference/limits).

### Email (`serve`)

The API sends invitation emails itself, for every front door (dashboard, REST,
assistant, and MCP).

| Flag | Environment variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--mail-provider` | `FLAGON_MAIL_PROVIDER` | empty (same as `auto`) | `auto`, `resend`, or `log`. `auto` uses Resend when `RESEND_API_KEY` is set, otherwise the log mailer, which writes each email to the server log and delivers nothing (the server warns about this in production). With the log mailer an invitation reports `email_sent: false`, so the inviter is shown the link to share. `resend` without a key, or an unknown value, stops the server at startup. |
| `--resend-api-key` | `RESEND_API_KEY` | empty | Resend API key for transactional email. Set it in production, or invitation emails are not delivered. |
| `--mail-from` | `FLAGON_MAIL_FROM`, then `RESEND_FROM` | `Flagon <onboarding@resend.dev>` | The sender address, such as `Flagon <hello@example.com>`. |

### AI assistant (`serve`)

The assistant always runs: with no model configured it falls back to an offline
mock, so you can use Flagon with no AI keys at all. See
[AI runtime](/docs/architecture/ai-runtime).

| Flag | Environment variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--ai-provider` | `FLAGON_AI_PROVIDER` | empty (same as `auto`) | `auto`, `anthropic`, `openai`, or `mock`. `auto` uses Anthropic when `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is set, else an OpenAI-compatible endpoint when `FLAGON_AI_API_KEY` or `FLAGON_AI_BASE_URL` is set, else the mock. Pinning `anthropic` without `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, pinning `openai` with neither an API key nor a base URL, or an unknown value stops the server at startup. |
| `--anthropic-api-key` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | empty | Anthropic API key. |
| `--anthropic-workspace-id` | `ANTHROPIC_WORKSPACE_ID` | empty | Optional Anthropic workspace the usage is attributed to. |
| `--ai-base-url` | `FLAGON_AI_BASE_URL`, then `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | empty (`https://api.openai.com/v1` when the OpenAI-compatible provider is used) | Base URL of any OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions endpoint: OpenAI, OpenRouter, Together, Groq, vLLM, or Ollama at `http://localhost:11434/v1`. |
| `--ai-api-key` | `FLAGON_AI_API_KEY`, then `OPENAI_API_KEY` | empty | Key for the OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Leave empty for keyless local servers such as Ollama. |
| `--ai-model` | `FLAGON_AI_MODEL` | empty (provider default) | The model id. Defaults: `claude-haiku-4-5` for Anthropic, `gpt-4o-mini` for OpenAI-compatible, `mock` for the mock. |
