| `--ai-system-prompt-file` | `FLAGON_AI_SYSTEM_PROMPT_FILE` | empty (built-in prompt) | Path to a file that replaces the built-in system prompt. If it cannot be read, the server logs a warning and keeps the built-in prompt. |
| `--ai-daily-limit` | `FLAGON_AI_DAILY_LIMIT` | `100` | Maximum assistant calls per organization per rolling 24 hours. `0` means unlimited; do not use `0` in production. See [Limits](/docs/reference/limits). |

When two environment variables are listed, the first one that is set wins. If a
configured provider rejects its key at request time (a `401` or `403` from the
provider), or the Anthropic provider has no key, the assistant answers `503` with
`the AI agent is not configured`.

### Not configurable

The documentation, roadmap, and changelog corpora are compiled into the binary,
so there is nothing to configure for them. Server timeouts (a 10-second limit
for request headers, a 5-second budget per database query) are constants in the
code; see [Limits](/docs/reference/limits).

## Web app

The app reads its environment at runtime (server side) and, for a few values,
at build time. In development, `app/.env.local` is loaded automatically;
`app/.env.example` is the template.

### Auth

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` | none | The secret the sign-in service signs sessions with. Generate one with `openssl rand -base64 32`. **Required in production.** |
| `BETTER_AUTH_URL` | `http://localhost:3000` where a fallback exists | The app's public origin, such as `https://app.flagon.io`. Used as the sign-in service's base URL, for SSO callback URLs, and for the copyable invitation link the dashboard shows when an invitation email was not delivered. **Required in production.** |
| `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`, `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` | none | Enable Google sign-in when both are set. |
| `GITHUB_CLIENT_ID`, `GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET` | none | Enable GitHub sign-in when both are set. |

The social sign-in buttons are always shown, and are disabled until their
provider is configured. The app derives `NEXT_PUBLIC_GOOGLE_AUTH_ENABLED` and
`NEXT_PUBLIC_GITHUB_AUTH_ENABLED` from the variables above at build time; do not
set those yourself.

### Database

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DATABASE_URL` | none | The app's own Postgres database, which holds accounts, sessions, and sign-in data (separate from the API's domain database; locally it is `flagon_app` on the same Postgres). SSL certificate verification is on unless the URL has `sslmode=disable`. **Required in production.** Auth pages load without it, but every sign-in fails. |

### API gateway

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FLAGON_API_URL` | `http://localhost:8080` | Base URL of the API server. **Required in production.** |
| `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN` | Development only: `dev-internal-token` | The shared secret the app sends to the API. Must equal the API's `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN`. Outside production it falls back to the same public development value the API uses; in production an unset token makes every call to the API fail with an error. **Required in production.** |

### Email

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RESEND_API_KEY` | none | Key for sending the app's own transactional email (sign-in codes, email verification, password reset) through Resend. Invitation emails are sent by the API, which reads its own `RESEND_API_KEY` (see above). Without it, development logs each email to the console, and production refuses to send, so the flow that needed the email fails loudly. **Required in production.** |
| `RESEND_FROM` | `Flagon <onboarding@resend.dev>` | The sender address for the app's emails. |

### Build and runtime

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NODE_ENV` | set by Next.js | `production` switches on secure cross-site session cookies, requires `RESEND_API_KEY` and `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN`, and turns off development helpers (the demo login prefill, the dev email endpoint, and returning the invitation link even when the email was sent). |
| `NEXT_BUILD_STANDALONE` | unset | Set to `1` to build Next.js's standalone output, used by the self-host Docker image. |
| `CI` | unset | Set by CI; makes the Playwright end-to-end tests run against a production build with retries. |

### Scripts

These are read only by the scripts in `app/scripts/`, never by the running app.
The scripts also read `DATABASE_URL`, `FLAGON_API_URL`, and
`FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN` as above.

| Variable | Used by | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SEED_EMAIL` | `npm run db:seed` | `demo@flagon.dev` | Demo user email. Also the login the development sign-in page pre-fills. |
| `SEED_USERNAME` | `npm run db:seed` | `demo` | Demo user username. |
| `SEED_PASSWORD` | `npm run db:seed` | `password12345` | Demo user password. Also pre-filled in development. |
| `SEED_NAME` | `npm run db:seed` | `Demo User` | Demo user display name. |
| `SEED_ORG_NAME` | `npm run db:seed` | `Demo Org` | Name of the baseline organization the seed creates through the API. |
| `SEED_ORG_SLUG` | `npm run db:seed` | `demo` | Its slug. |
| `SEED_SKIP_ORG` | `npm run db:seed` | unset | Set to skip creating the organization. |
| `SEED_ALLOW_PROD` | `npm run db:seed` | unset | The seed refuses to run when `NODE_ENV=production` unless this is set. |
| `RESTORE_LOGIN` | `npm run restore-user` | none | The email or username of a soft-deleted account to restore, when not passed as an argument. |

### End-to-end tests

Read only by the Playwright product suite in `app/tests/product/`, which also
reads `SEED_EMAIL`, `SEED_USERNAME`, `SEED_PASSWORD`, and `SEED_ORG_SLUG` to sign
in as the demo user.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `E2E_OWNER_EMAIL` | `owner@flagon.dev` | Email of a second seeded user who owns no organization, for tests that create and delete a whole organization (seed it with `SEED_SKIP_ORG=1`). |
| `E2E_OWNER_USERNAME` | `e2e-owner` | Its username. |
| `E2E_OWNER_PASSWORD` | `password12345` | Its password. |
| `E2E_AI_PROVIDER` | unset | Set to `mock` when the API runs with `FLAGON_AI_PROVIDER=mock`. The assistant test is skipped otherwise, because a real model is not deterministic. |

- [Secrets](/docs/security/secrets)
- [Deployment topology](/docs/architecture/deployment-topology)

docs.title: Glossary
docs.description: Concise definitions of the terms used across Flagon's product, API, and documentation.
docs.body:
Short definitions of the terms Flagon uses, in alphabetical order. Each links to
the page with the details.

## A

**Access token.** A secret starting with `flagon_` that authenticates API and
MCP requests as a principal. Either a personal access token or an organization
access token. Created and revoked only in the dashboard. See
[Authentication and scopes](/docs/api/authentication).

**Action key.** The stable, dotted name of an audit log entry, such as
`project.deleted`. See [Audit actions](/docs/reference/audit-actions).

**Admin (organization role).** Manages an organization's members, teams,
security, SSO, tokens, and audit log, and is implicitly an owner of every
project. Cannot delete the organization. See
[Roles matrix](/docs/reference/roles-matrix).

**Admin (project role).** The highest rung of the project role ladder: can
manage the project's collaborators and team grants.

**Assistant.** The AI agent built into the dashboard. It operates Flagon on your
behalf with your permissions, runs reads freely, and proposes every change for
you to confirm. See [Assistant](/docs/ai/assistant).

**Audit log.** An organization's append-only record of every change to its
state: who did what, to what, when, and from where. Readable by owners and
admins. See [Audit log](/docs/platform/audit-log).

## B

**Base permission.** The organization-wide floor of project access every member
gets on every project: `none`, `read` (the default), `triage`, `write`,
`maintain`, or `admin`. Explicit grants can raise it for a person, never lower
it.

## C

**Changelog.** The public list of shipped changes, one Markdown file per entry
in the `changelog/` folder, served by the API at `GET /changelog`.

**Collaborator.** An organization member with a direct role grant on one
project.

**Corpus.** The compiled, embedded form of a content tree (docs, roadmap, or
changelog) that the API serves. Regenerated with `make docs`, `make roadmap`, and
`make changelog`. See [Content corpora](/docs/architecture/content-corpora).

**Cursor.** The opaque value in a list response's `Link` header that fetches the
next page. See [Pagination and search](/docs/api/pagination).

## D

**Dashboard.** The Flagon web app at `app.flagon.io`. It holds your session and
calls the API on your behalf.

**Deleted archive.** Where soft-deleted resources wait to be restored for 30
days: an organization's deleted projects (listed for owners and admins), and the
organizations you owned that were deleted in the last 30 days.

## E

**Effective role.** A person's actual role on a project: the highest of their
organization-derived role, their direct grant, and every grant from a team they
belong to.

**Expand.** The `expand[]` query parameter that inlines a related object in a
response instead of only its id. See
[Expanding responses](/docs/api/expanding-responses).

## F

**Full access.** A token created with no scope restrictions. It is still bounded
by its principal's role.

## G

**Gateway.** The web app's role in front of the API: it verifies your session,
then forwards the request to the API with the internal token and your identity.
It never writes domain data itself.

**Grant.** A role given to a user or a team on one project.

## H

**Human in the loop.** The rule that the assistant never changes anything on
its own: it returns a proposal and the change runs only after you confirm it.

## I

**Internal token.** The shared secret (`FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN`) the web app uses
to call the API. Some operations, such as token management and the assistant,
accept only this credential, never an access token.

**Invitation.** An emailed link that lets someone without a Flagon account join
an organization. Valid for 7 days.

## M

**Maintain.** The fourth project role, between `write` and `admin`. Today it
adds renaming a project's slug; more project settings will attach to it.

**Maintainer (team role).** Can edit a team and manage its members. A team's
creator is its first maintainer.

**MCP.** The Model Context Protocol. Flagon's MCP server lets external agents
such as Claude Desktop and Cursor use the same tools as the assistant, at
`mcp.flagon.io` or `/mcp`. See [MCP server](/docs/ai/mcp).

**Member (organization role).** Works in an organization; their project access
starts at the base permission.

**Member (team role).** Belongs to a team and inherits its project grants and
ownerships.

**Metering.** Counting assistant calls per organization so the daily limit can
be enforced. See [Limits](/docs/reference/limits).

**Mock provider.** The offline AI provider the API uses when no model is
configured. It keeps the assistant working with no keys.

## N

**Notification.** A personal message to one user, such as being added to a
project. Separate from the audit log. See
[Notifications](/docs/platform/notifications).

## O

**Operation.** One API endpoint, identified by its `operationId` (for example
`create-project`). Every operation an access token can reach has a scope and
(all but one) a matching tool.

**Organization.** The tenant everything else lives in: members, teams,
projects, tokens, security settings, and the audit log. Dashboard URLs start with
its slug (`app.flagon.io/<org>`). See
[Organizations](/docs/platform/organizations).

**Organization access token.** A token that acts as a service principal inside
one organization, with a role chosen at creation. Prefix `flagon_oat_`. Exempt
from the organization's 2FA and SSO requirements, and refused (`403`) on
account-level operations such as creating or leaving an organization.

**Owner (organization role).** Full control of an organization, including
deleting it. An organization always has at least one.

**Owner (project tier).** A user or team above the project role ladder that can
delete and restore the project and manage its owners. Every organization owner
and admin is implicitly one.

## P

**Personal access token.** A token that acts as you in every organization you
belong to. Prefix `flagon_pat_`.

**Planned.** A docs page status for a feature that is not built yet. The page
appears in navigation with a "not written yet" state.

**Principal.** Whoever a request acts as: a person, or an organization access
token's service principal.

**Project.** The core unit of work in an organization: a deployable app or
service with a name, slug, description, README, and repository URL. See
[Projects](/docs/platform/projects).

**Project role.** A rung on the ladder, lowest first: `read`, `triage`, `write`,
`maintain`, `admin`.

**Proposal.** A change the assistant has prepared but not run, shown for you to
confirm or dismiss.

**Public tool.** A tool the unauthenticated MCP server exposes. Today only the
documentation tools, `search_docs` and `get_doc`.

## Q

**QUERY method.** An HTTP method for safe, read-only requests with a body. Every
paginated list accepts it as an alternative to `GET`.

## R

**Rate limit.** A per-principal cap on API requests per second (default 50,
bursts of 300). Over it, requests get `429` with a `Retry-After` header. See
[Limits](/docs/reference/limits).

**Read.** The lowest project role: see the project and who has access.

**Request id.** The `X-Request-Id` header on every API response. Quote it when
reporting a failure; server logs record it. See [Errors](/docs/api/errors).

**Roadmap.** The public board of planned work, one Markdown file per item in the
`roadmap/` folder, each at a stage of `concept`, `alpha`, or `beta`. Served at
`GET /roadmap`.

**Row-level security (RLS).** Postgres policies that restrict every query to the
rows the acting user may see. The API's runtime database role cannot bypass
them. See [Tenant isolation](/docs/security/tenant-isolation).

## S

**Scope.** A named permission on an access token, such as `read:project`.
Parents imply children. See [Scopes](/docs/reference/scopes).

**Service principal.** The non-human user an organization access token acts as.
It is a member of one organization with the token's role, and appears in the
audit log under the token's name.

**Slug.** The URL-safe identifier of an organization, project, or team, such as
`billing-api`. Derived from the name when you do not give one.

**Soft delete.** Deleting by marking a resource deleted rather than erasing it,
so it can be restored. Organizations and projects are soft-deleted.

**SSO provider.** An organization's OIDC or SAML identity provider
configuration, such as Okta or Microsoft Entra ID. See
[Single sign-on](/docs/platform/sso).

**SSO requirement.** An organization setting that requires members to sign in
through one of the organization's SSO providers. The API enforces it on every
organization operation; owners are exempt so they can always fix a broken
provider. See [Roles matrix](/docs/reference/roles-matrix).

## T

**Team.** A named group of organization members that can be granted a project
role or made a project owner as a unit. See [Teams](/docs/platform/teams).

**Tool.** One entry in the shared tool registry. The same tool is available to
the assistant and over MCP, with the same scope as its API operation. See
[Tools](/docs/ai/tools).

**Tool registry.** The single list of tools in `api/internal/ai` behind the
assistant and the MCP server.

**Triage.** The second project role, between `read` and `write`, reserved for
future powers.

**Two-factor requirement.** An organization setting that requires every member
to have two-factor authentication enabled before they can open the organization
or use it through the API, a personal access token, the assistant, or MCP. See
[Two-factor authentication](/docs/platform/two-factor).

## V

**Viewer.** A legacy organization role, still accepted by the API and by
organization access tokens, with read access to every project and no write
access.

**Visibility.** A docs page setting: `public` pages are served to everyone;
`internal` pages are readable only through the in-product assistant and the
authenticated MCP server. No page is internal today.

## W

**Write.** The third project role: edit a project's metadata.

## Related

- [Core concepts](/docs/get-started/core-concepts)
- [Roles matrix](/docs/reference/roles-matrix)
- [Scopes](/docs/reference/scopes)
- [Using the API](/docs/api/using-the-api)

docs.title: Limits
docs.description: Every quota, page size, retention window, expiry, size cap, and timeout Flagon enforces, with the value and where it is set.
docs.body:
This page collects every limit the API and app enforce, with the exact value and
whether you can change it. Values marked **Configurable** come from a setting in
the [configuration reference](/docs/reference/configuration); everything else
is a constant in the code.

## Plans and quotas

| Limit | Value | What happens at the limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Organizations you **own** on the free plan | 1 | Creating another organization, or restoring a deleted one you owned, fails with `402 Payment Required`. Being a member of other organizations is unlimited. |
| Assistant calls per organization | 100 per rolling 24 hours. **Configurable** with `FLAGON_AI_DAILY_LIMIT` (`0` means unlimited). | The next message to the assistant, or the next confirmation of a proposed change, fails with `429 Too Many Requests` (`AI usage limit reached for this organization`, no `Retry-After` header) until older calls age out of the 24-hour window. |
| API requests per principal | 50 per second sustained, bursts of up to 300. **Configurable** with `FLAGON_RATE_LIMIT` (`0` disables) and `FLAGON_RATE_BURST`. | The request fails with `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the seconds to wait. See the rate limits section below. |

How assistant calls are counted: each message you send to the assistant counts
as one call, however many tool steps it takes, and each proposed change you
confirm counts as one more. The count is shared by everyone in the organization.
The limit is checked before a message runs and again before a confirmed change
runs, so once the organization is at its limit, confirming a proposal made
earlier also fails with `429`. MCP tool calls are not metered. See
[Usage and AI limits](/docs/platform/usage).

## Rate limits

Every API request draws from a token bucket that belongs to its **principal**:

- a signed-in dashboard user (each user has their own bucket);
- an access token (each token has its own bucket, whether or not it turns out
  to be valid);
- the client IP, for requests with no credential.

The bucket refills at `FLAGON_RATE_LIMIT` requests per second (default `50`) and
holds up to `FLAGON_RATE_BURST` requests (default `300`). An empty bucket
answers `429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header in whole seconds;
wait that long, then retry. `GET /healthz` and `GET /readyz` are never limited.

The limiter lives in memory on each API instance, so with several instances a
principal's effective ceiling is up to that many times the configured rate. It
is an abuse guard, not a quota: assistant usage has its own per-organization
meter, above.

## Lists and pages

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Paginated lists (`limit`) | Default 30, maximum 100. Larger values are clamped to 100. |
| Audit log (`limit`) | Default 30, maximum 100. `0` or a negative value means 30; larger values are clamped to 100. |
| Notifications (`limit`) | Default 30, maximum 100. `0` or a negative value means 30; larger values are clamped to 100. |
| Docs search (`GET /docs/search`, `search_docs` tool) | Default 5 results. |
| Assistant and MCP list tools | Up to 100 items per tool call. `list_projects` takes a search and a cursor to page further; the other list tools return the first 100. `list_notifications` and `list_audit_events` take a `limit` instead (default 30, maximum 100). |

## Retention and expiry

| Item | Window |
| --- | --- |
| A deleted organization | Restorable by an owner for 30 days after deletion. After that it no longer appears in **Settings > Organizations** and cannot be restored. |
| A deleted project | Restorable by a project owner (or an organization owner or admin) for 30 days after deletion, the same window as organizations. The deleted-projects list shows each project's `purge_at`; after it, the project no longer appears and restoring it answers `404`. |
| An invitation | Valid for 7 days. Accepting after that fails with `410 Gone`. |
| Personal and organization access tokens | You choose at creation: 7, 30 (default), or 90 days, a custom future date, or no expiration. |
| The audit log | Append-only. Entries are not deleted. |

## Requests

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Request body size | 1 MiB for API operations. A global cap on every route, including the MCP endpoint, of 4 MiB by default (**Configurable** with `FLAGON_MAX_BODY_BYTES`). Larger bodies are rejected with `413`. |
| Reading a request body | 5 seconds. |
| Sending request headers | 10 seconds (the server's `ReadHeaderTimeout`), on both the API and metrics listeners. Response time is not capped, because an assistant turn can legitimately run long. |
| Each database query | 5 seconds. |
| `/readyz` database check | 3 seconds. |
| `/internal/rls-check` self-test | 5 seconds. |
| Migrations at startup | 2 minutes. |

## Assistant

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Model steps per message | 6. Each step is one model call; read tools run between steps, and proposed changes wait for your confirmation. |
| Output tokens per model call | 1,024. |
| Timeout per model call | 60 seconds for Anthropic, 120 seconds for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. |

## Names and identifiers

| Item | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Organization, project, and team slugs | Lowercase letters and digits, with single hyphens between runs. Anything else in the input collapses to one hyphen. A slug is derived from the name when you omit it, and a name must contain at least one letter or digit. |
| Slug uniqueness | Organization slugs are unique among live organizations; project and team slugs are unique within their organization. Deleting a project or team frees its slug immediately. |
| SSO provider id | 2 to 63 characters: lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens, starting with a letter or digit. |

## Related

- [Configuration](/docs/reference/configuration)
- [Usage and AI limits](/docs/platform/usage)
- [Pagination and search](/docs/api/pagination)
- [Errors](/docs/api/errors)

docs.title: Roles matrix
docs.description: Who can do what in Flagon, by organization role, base permission, team role, and project role, derived from the permission checks in the API.
docs.body:
Flagon decides what a person may do from **roles** at three levels: their role
in the organization, their role on a team, and their effective role on each
project. This page is the complete matrix, derived from the checks the API
enforces in `api/internal/db` (`rbac.go`, `project_rbac.go`, `project_owners.go`,
`teams.go`, `invitations.go`, `org_security.go`) and in Postgres row-level
security. The dashboard, the assistant, MCP, and access tokens all go through
the same checks, and an access token's [scopes](/docs/reference/scopes) can only
narrow them further.

## Organization roles

| Role | Who holds it |
| --- | --- |
| `owner` | Full control, including deleting the organization. The creator is the first owner. An organization always has at least one owner. |
| `admin` | Manages the organization: members, invitations, teams, security, SSO, tokens, and the audit log. Implicitly an owner of every project. |
| `member` | Works in the organization. Their project access starts from the organization's **base permission**. |

The API still accepts a legacy `viewer` role for compatibility (existing viewer
memberships were converted to `member`, and the dashboard no longer offers it).
A viewer gets read access to every project and cannot create or edit projects.
Organization access tokens can still be created with the `viewer` role.

### Organization actions

| Action | Owner | Admin | Member |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| See the organization, its members, pending invitations, and teams | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Rename the organization | Yes | Yes | No |
| Add an existing user, or invite by email | Yes | Yes, as `admin` or below | No |
| Change a member's role | Yes, any role | Only for members below admin, and not to `owner` | No |
| Remove a member | Yes | Only members below admin | No |
| Leave the organization | Yes, unless the only owner | Yes | Yes |
| Read and change the security policy (2FA requirement, SSO requirement, base permission) | Yes | Yes | No |
| Configure SSO providers | Yes | Yes | No |
| Read the audit log and change its configuration | Yes | Yes | No (`403`) |
| Create, list, and revoke organization access tokens | Yes | Yes | No |
| See the organization's deleted-projects archive | Yes | Yes | No (`403`) |
| Restore a deleted project (within 30 days) | Yes | Yes | Only as an owner of that project |
| Delete the organization | Yes | No | No |
| Restore a deleted organization (within 30 days) | Yes, if you were an owner | No | No |

Rules that apply to every member change:

- **You cannot grant above your own role.** Only an owner can grant or revoke
  `owner`. Invitations can grant `admin`, `member`, or `viewer`, never `owner`.
- **Admins manage only roles strictly below their own.** An admin cannot change
  or remove another admin or an owner.
- **The last owner is protected.** Demoting or removing the only owner fails with
  `409`, and the only owner cannot leave.
- **You cannot change your own membership** through the member endpoints; use
  **Leave** instead (`409`).
- **You cannot lock yourself out.** Turning on the 2FA requirement fails with
  `403` unless your own account has two-factor authentication, and turning on
  the SSO requirement fails with `403` unless you have signed in through one of
  the organization's SSO providers at least once.

### Organization security policy

When an organization requires two-factor authentication or single sign-on, the
API enforces it on every `/orgs/<org>/...` operation (leaving the organization
is exempt), on every assistant and MCP tool that names the organization, and on
the assistant endpoints. A member who does not meet the policy gets `403` with a
message saying what to fix.

| Caller | 2FA requirement | SSO requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Signed-in session | Needs 2FA on the account. | The current session must have been established through one of the organization's SSO providers. |
| Personal access token | Needs 2FA on the token owner's account. | The token owner must have signed in through one of the organization's SSO providers at least once. |
| Organization access token | Exempt. | Exempt. |
| Organization `owner` | Applies. | Exempt, so an owner can always reach the settings to fix a broken provider. |

### Organization access tokens

An organization access token acts as a **service principal**: a non-human
member of one organization with the role chosen when the token was created
(`admin`, `member`, or `viewer`). Its access to projects follows that role like
any member's. A few account-level operations need a human and answer `403` for
a service principal: creating an organization, leaving one, listing your
recently deleted organizations, restoring an organization, and syncing a
profile.

## Base permission

The **base permission** is the organization-wide floor of project access that
every `member` gets on every project, before any explicit grant. Owners and
admins sit above it. Set it under the organization's **Settings > Member
privileges**, or with `PUT /orgs/<org>/security` (owners and admins).

| Base permission | Members' access to every project |
| --- | --- |
| `none` | None. A member sees only projects they are granted directly or through a team. |
| `read` (default) | Read. |
| `triage` | Triage. |
| `write` | Write. |
| `maintain` | Maintain. |
| `admin` | Admin. |

The dashboard offers `none`, `read`, `write`, and `admin`; the API also accepts
`triage` and `maintain`. A grant can only raise a member above the base
permission, never lower them below it.

## Project roles

Each project has a ladder of five roles, lowest first. A higher role holds every
capability of the roles below it.

| Role | Rank |
| --- | --- |
| `read` | 1 |
| `triage` | 2 |
| `write` | 3 |
| `maintain` | 4 |
| `admin` | 5 |

Above the ladder is a separate **owner** tier. A project owner is a user or a
team added under the project's owners, and every organization owner and admin is
implicitly an owner of every project, so the organization can never be locked
out of its own project.

### Effective project role

A person's effective role on a project is the **highest** of:

1. **The organization-derived role**: `admin` for organization owners and
   admins; the base permission for members (nothing when it is `none`).
2. **A direct grant** on the project (a collaborator entry).
3. **Every team grant** for a team they belong to.

Ownership (direct, through a team, or implicit for organization owners and
admins) is checked separately and grants everything.

### Project actions

| Action | Minimum |
| --- | --- |
| See the project, its collaborators, teams, and owners | `read`. A project you cannot read answers `404`, as if it did not exist. |
| Edit project metadata (name, description, README, repository URL) | `write` |
| Rename the project's slug (changes its URL) | `maintain` |
| Add, change, or remove collaborators; grant, change, or revoke team access | `admin` |
| Delete and restore the project | Owner tier |
| Add and remove project owners (users or teams) | Owner tier |

A project you can see but lack the role for answers `403`. The dashboard reads
your access from the `viewer` object on `GET /orgs/<org>/projects/<project>`
(`role`, `owner`, and `permissions`) and hides controls you cannot use.

`triage` has no distinct powers yet beyond `read`; it is on the ladder so that
powers can be attached to it later without reshuffling grants.

Creating a project is an organization-level action: any organization member
with the `owner`, `admin`, or `member` role can create one (a legacy `viewer`
cannot). The creator is recorded as `created_by`. A creator who is not an
organization owner or admin is automatically granted `admin` on the new project
(audited as `project.access_granted`), so they can manage it even when the base
permission is `read` or `none`. Creating a project does not make you an owner of
it.

Collaborators must already be organization members: a direct grant raises an
existing member on one project, and you cannot change your own grant.

### Tokens and project actions

The scope an access token needs lines up with these tiers, but the role check
still applies: `write:project` covers creating and updating projects,
`admin:project` covers collaborator, team, and owner management and delete and
restore. An `admin:project` token held by someone who is not a project owner
still cannot delete that project.

## Team roles

| Role | Can |
| --- | --- |
| `maintainer` | Edit the team's name, slug, and description; add, change, and remove team members. The person who creates a team becomes its first maintainer. |
| `member` | Belong to the team and inherit its project grants and ownerships. |

| Team action | Org owner or admin | Team maintainer | Anyone else in the org |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| See teams, their members, and their projects | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Create a team | Yes | No | No |
| Edit a team, manage its members | Yes | Yes | No |
| Delete a team | Yes | No | No |
| Grant a team access to a project | Project `admin` or owner tier, as above | | |

Deleting a team removes its project grants and ownerships from effect.

## Personal actions

Every signed-in user can, for themselves: read their account (`GET /me`),
create, list, and revoke personal access tokens, read and manage their
notifications, and create organizations (the free plan includes one owned
organization; see [Limits](/docs/reference/limits)).

## Related

- [Roles](/docs/platform/roles)
- [Project access](/docs/platform/project-access)
- [Scopes](/docs/reference/scopes)
- [Permissions model](/docs/architecture/permissions-model)
- [Set base permissions](/docs/guides/set-base-permissions)

docs.title: Scopes
docs.description: Every access token scope, what it implies, and the exact API operations and assistant tools each one gates.
headings: Operations no access token can reach
docs.body:
A **scope** is a named permission an access token carries. When you create a
token you either grant full access or choose scopes; a scoped token can call
only the operations whose required scope it holds. This page lists every scope
and every operation it gates, generated from the scope table in
`api/internal/server/scopes.go` (`operationScopes`) and the tool registry in
`api/internal/ai`.

Scopes are a ceiling on top of the principal's role, never a grant beyond it: a
token can do at most what the person (or, for an organization token, the
service principal's role) could do. See [Roles matrix](/docs/reference/roles-matrix).

## How scopes combine

- **Parents imply children.** Holding a parent scope satisfies any operation that
  requires one of its children.
- **Full access** (a token created with no scopes) is not scope-limited at all;
  it is bounded only by the role behind it.
- **Fail-closed.** An operation with no entry in the scope table cannot be called
  by any scoped token. CI enforces that every registered operation is either
  scoped or explicitly listed as unreachable (the last section below).
- **One vocabulary.** Every assistant and MCP tool declares the same scope as
  the operation it fronts, so an MCP client authenticated with a scoped token can
  see and run only the matching tools. The documentation tools (`search_docs`,
  `get_doc`) are public and need no scope.
- **Some operations need a person.** An organization access token is refused
  with `403` on `create-org`, `leave-org`, `list-deleted-orgs`, and
  `restore-org`, whatever scopes it holds, because those act on a human's
  account.

## All scopes

| Scope | Grants | Implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `read:user` | Read your own account. | |
| `user` | Account writes. No operation needs it today: your profile is edited in the dashboard. | `read:user` |
| `admin:user` | Full account control. Reserved for destructive account operations; none is token-reachable today. | `user`, `read:user` |
| `read:org` | Read organizations, members, pending invitations, the security policy, SSO providers, the audit log and its configuration, and your recently deleted organizations. | |
| `write:org` | Rename an organization; manage members and invitations; change the security policy, SSO providers, and audit configuration. | `read:org` |
| `admin:org` | Create, leave, delete, and restore organizations. | `write:org`, `read:org` |
| `read:project` | Read projects, the deleted-projects archive, and each project's collaborators, teams, and owners. | |
| `write:project` | Create and update projects. | `read:project` |
| `admin:project` | Delete and restore projects; manage a project's collaborators, team grants, and owners. | `write:project`, `read:project` |
| `read:team` | Read teams, their members, and the projects they can access. | |
| `write:team` | Create and edit teams and manage their membership. | `read:team` |
| `admin:team` | Delete teams. | `write:team`, `read:team` |
| `notifications` | Read your notifications and mark them read or unread. | |

The `QUERY` rows below are the body-based twins of paginated lists (see
[Pagination and search](/docs/api/pagination)). They are not in the OpenAPI spec
but require the same scope as their `GET` form, and the `GET` form's tool covers
them.

## Account

### `read:user`

| Operation | Method and path | Tool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `get-me` | `GET /me` | `whoami` |

### `user`

No operation requires `user` today; it implies `read:user`. Your profile is
edited in the dashboard, and the dashboard mirrors it into the API through
`PUT /me/profile` (`sync-profile`), which only the app can call: no access token
reaches it, whatever its scopes.

### `admin:user`

No operation requires `admin:user` today. It exists so destructive account
operations (such as deleting your account) have a scope when they become API
operations. Account deletion currently happens only in the dashboard.

## Organization

### `read:org`

| Operation | Method and path | Tool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `list-deleted-orgs` | `GET /deleted-orgs` | `list_deleted_organizations` |
| `list-orgs` | `GET /orgs` | `list_organizations` |
| `list-audit-log` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/audit` | `list_audit_events` |
| `get-audit-config` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/audit/config` | `get_audit_config` |
| `list-invitations` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/invitations` | `list_invitations` |
| `query-invitations` | `QUERY /orgs/{slug}/invitations` | `list_invitations` |
| `list-members` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/members` | `list_members` |
| `query-members` | `QUERY /orgs/{slug}/members` | `list_members` |
| `get-org-security` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/security` | `get_org_security` |
| `list-sso-providers` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/sso/providers` | `list_sso_providers` |
| `get-sso-provider` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/sso/providers/{provider}` | `get_sso_provider` |

### `write:org`

| Operation | Method and path | Tool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `update-org` | `PATCH /orgs/{slug}` | `update_organization` |
| `set-audit-config` | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/audit/config` | `set_audit_config` |
| `invite-member` | `POST /orgs/{slug}/invitations` | `invite_member` |
| `revoke-invitation` | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/invitations/{id}` | `revoke_invitation` |
| `add-member` | `POST /orgs/{slug}/members` | `add_member` |
| `remove-member` | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/members/{userId}` | `remove_member` |
| `set-member-role` | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/members/{userId}/role` | `set_member_role` |
| `set-org-security` | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/security` | `set_org_security` |
| `create-sso-provider` | `POST /orgs/{slug}/sso/providers` | `create_sso_provider` |
| `update-sso-provider` | `PATCH /orgs/{slug}/sso/providers/{provider}` | `update_sso_provider` |
| `delete-sso-provider` | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/sso/providers/{provider}` | `delete_sso_provider` |

### `admin:org`

| Operation | Method and path | Tool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `restore-org` | `POST /deleted-orgs/{id}/restore` | `restore_organization` |
| `create-org` | `POST /orgs` | `create_organization` |
| `delete-org` | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}` | `delete_organization` |
| `leave-org` | `POST /orgs/{slug}/leave` | `leave_organization` |

Leaving an organization needs `admin:org`, not `write:org`. The assistant
in the dashboard refuses `restore_organization`, because a deleted
organization is outside every conversation's organization; restore it from
**Settings > Organizations**, the API, or MCP.

## Projects

### `read:project`

| Operation | Method and path | Tool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `list-deleted-projects` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/deleted-projects` | `list_deleted_projects` |
| `query-deleted-projects` | `QUERY /orgs/{slug}/deleted-projects` | `list_deleted_projects` |
| `list-projects` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/projects` | `list_projects` |
| `query-projects` | `QUERY /orgs/{slug}/projects` | `list_projects` |
| `get-project` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}` | `get_project` |
| `list-project-members` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/members` | `list_project_members` |
| `query-project-members` | `QUERY /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/members` | `list_project_members` |
| `list-project-owners` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/owners` | `list_project_owners` |
| `query-project-owners` | `QUERY /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/owners` | `list_project_owners` |
| `list-project-teams` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/teams` | `list_project_teams` |
| `query-project-teams` | `QUERY /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/teams` | `list_project_teams` |

### `write:project`

| Operation | Method and path | Tool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `create-project` | `POST /orgs/{slug}/projects` | `create_project` |
| `update-project` | `PATCH /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}` | `update_project` |

### `admin:project`

| Operation | Method and path | Tool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `delete-project` | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}` | `delete_project` |
| `add-project-member` | `POST /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/members` | `add_project_member` |
| `remove-project-member` | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/members/{userId}` | `remove_project_member` |
| `set-project-member-role` | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/members/{userId}/role` | `set_project_member_role` |
| `add-project-owner` | `POST /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/owners` | `add_project_owner` |
| `remove-project-owner` | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/owners/{type}/{principalId}` | `remove_project_owner` |
| `restore-project` | `POST /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/restore` | `restore_project` |
| `add-project-team` | `POST /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/teams` | `add_project_team` |
| `remove-project-team` | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/teams/{team}` | `remove_project_team` |
| `set-project-team-role` | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/projects/{project}/teams/{team}/role` | `set_project_team_role` |

## Teams

### `read:team`

| Operation | Method and path | Tool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `list-teams` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/teams` | `list_teams` |
| `query-teams` | `QUERY /orgs/{slug}/teams` | `list_teams` |
| `get-team` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}` | `get_team` |
| `list-team-members` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/members` | `list_team_members` |
| `query-team-members` | `QUERY /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/members` | `list_team_members` |
| `list-team-projects` | `GET /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/projects` | `list_team_projects` |
| `query-team-projects` | `QUERY /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/projects` | `list_team_projects` |

### `write:team`

| Operation | Method and path | Tool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `create-team` | `POST /orgs/{slug}/teams` | `create_team` |
| `update-team` | `PATCH /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}` | `update_team` |
| `add-team-member` | `POST /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/members` | `add_team_member` |
| `remove-team-member` | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/members/{userId}` | `remove_team_member` |
| `set-team-member-role` | `PUT /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}/members/{userId}/role` | `set_team_member_role` |

### `admin:team`

| Operation | Method and path | Tool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `delete-team` | `DELETE /orgs/{slug}/teams/{team}` | `delete_team` |

## Notifications

### `notifications`

| Operation | Method and path | Tool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `list-notifications` | `GET /notifications` | `list_notifications` |
| `read-all-notifications` | `POST /notifications/read-all` | `mark_all_notifications_read` |
| `notifications-unread-count` | `GET /notifications/unread-count` | `count_unread_notifications` |
| `read-notification` | `POST /notifications/{id}/read` | `mark_notification_read` |
| `unread-notification` | `POST /notifications/{id}/unread` | `mark_notification_unread` |

## Operations no access token can reach

These operations have no scope on purpose, so every access token, even a
full-access one, is refused. They are either public or callable only by the
dashboard with its internal credential.

| Operation | Method and path | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `get-user` | `GET /users/{username}` | Public: a user's public profile. Needs no token at all. |
| `get-invitation` | `GET /invitations/{token}` | Public: the invitation landing page, where the invitation token is the credential. |
| `accept-invitation` | `POST /invitations/{token}/accept` | Dashboard only: the dashboard accepts the invitation on the invitee's behalf. |
| `create-pat`, `list-pats`, `revoke-pat` | `/me/tokens` | Dashboard only: tokens never manage tokens, so a token cannot mint or widen its own access. |
| `create-oat`, `list-oats`, `revoke-oat` | `/orgs/{slug}/tokens` | Dashboard only, for the same reason. |
| `ai-send-message` | `POST /ai/messages` | Dashboard only: the assistant itself. External agents use the [MCP server](/docs/ai/mcp). |
| `ai-execute-action` | `POST /ai/actions/execute` | Dashboard only: the assistant's confirm step for a proposed change. |
| `set-account-deleted` | `PUT /me/deleted` | Dashboard only: mirrors the account's deleted state. |
| `provision-sso-member` | `POST /internal/sso/provision-member` | Dashboard only: runs after the sign-in service verifies an SSO assertion. |
| `get-sso-provider-configs` | `GET /internal/sso/providers` | Dashboard only: full SSO configuration, secrets included, for the sign-in service. |
| `import-sso-provider` | `POST /internal/sso/providers/import` | Dashboard only: one-time adoption of providers registered before the API owned them. |

The content routes (`/docs`, `/roadmap`, `/changelog`), the health probes, and
the MCP endpoint are outside the OpenAPI spec and outside this table; see
[OpenAPI and clients](/docs/api/openapi).

## Related

- [Authentication and scopes](/docs/api/authentication)
- [Roles matrix](/docs/reference/roles-matrix)
- [Assistant tools](/docs/ai/tools)
- [Access tokens](/docs/platform/access-tokens)

docs.title: AI safety
docs.description: The controls that keep Flagon's assistant and MCP server inside your permissions - acting as you, scope and role ceilings, the organization security policy, one organization per conversation, confirmation for changes, quotas, and how to think about prompt injection.
headings: It acts as you, never as itself
MCP has no confirmation step of its own
docs.body:
Flagon's assistant and its MCP server can read and change real data: members,
projects, access, SSO configuration. A language model decides which tool to call,
and language models can be wrong or be manipulated by the text they read. So
Flagon does not rely on the model behaving well. The safety comes from what the
model is allowed to reach, and from keeping a person in the loop for changes.

This page lists those controls, what each one guarantees, and where the
guarantees stop. The runtime itself is described on
[AI runtime](/docs/architecture/ai-runtime).

```text
           Dashboard assistant                   MCP client + token
                    │                                     │
                    ▼                                     ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
 │ member? 2FA/SSO policy? quota left? │  │ token valid? scope? policy?  │
 └──────────────────┬──────────────────┘  └───────────────┬──────────────┘
                    ▼                                     │
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐                  │
 │ model picks tools                   │                  │
 │   read   -> runs now                │                  │
 │   change -> proposal, you confirm   │                  │
 └──────────────────┬──────────────────┘                  │
                    └──────────────────┬──────────────────┘
                                       ▼
 ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ same service layer as the REST API, acting as you:                    │
 │ role checks, row-level security, audit log                            │
 └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## It acts as you, never as itself

The assistant has no account, no role, and no database access of its own. Every
tool call carries the requesting person's identity (`ToolContext` in
`api/internal/ai/registry.go`) and calls the same `api/internal/service` method as
the matching REST operation. That method runs the same role checks inside a
database transaction bound to you, under the same row-level security. If you
cannot see an organization, neither can the assistant acting for you; if you
cannot delete a project, the tool call fails with the same "you don't have
permission to do that".

This is the most important guarantee on this page because it does not depend on
the model at all. However the model is prompted, the worst it can do is something
you were already allowed to do.

The organization's security policy applies here too. When an organization requires
two-factor authentication or SSO and you do not meet it, the assistant's endpoints
and any assistant or MCP tool call that names that organization fail with the same
`403` as the REST API. See [Authentication](/docs/security/authentication).

## The ceiling on each surface

| Surface | Acts as | Ceiling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dashboard assistant | The signed-in user | The user's roles. No token scopes apply. |
| MCP with a token | The token's principal | The principal's roles, narrowed by the token's scopes. |
| MCP without a token | Nobody | The public documentation tools only. |

Over MCP, `tools/list` returns only the tools a token's scopes allow, and
`tools/call` rejects a tool outside them. A tool's scope is the same one its REST
operation requires, and a test in CI (`api/internal/server/guardrails_test.go`)
fails the build if any tool's scope or read/write nature drifts from its
operation. See [Tool registry](/docs/architecture/tool-registry).

## One organization per conversation

A dashboard conversation belongs to the organization you started it in, and its
tool calls are confined to that organization. Usage is metered against it, so the
assistant must not act anywhere else. A tool call that names a different
organization is refused with `403` and a message such as
`this conversation is scoped to the "acme" organization and can't act in "other"; switch to that organization in Flagon to work there`. `restore_organization`, which addresses an
organization by id rather than by slug, is refused from the assistant outright;
restore deleted organizations from the dashboard.

MCP has no conversation organization. An MCP call reaches whatever the token's
principal can reach within the token's scopes: every organization you belong to
for a personal token, or its one organization for an organization token.

## Changes wait for a person

In the dashboard, read tools run immediately, and tools that change data do not.
The agent turns each one into a **proposal**: the tool, the exact input, and a
one-line summary produced by code from that input (for example
`Remove "u_42" from "acme"`), not written by the model. Nothing changes
until you confirm, which calls `POST /ai/actions/execute`. That endpoint runs only
tools marked as mutating, and before running one it checks again that you are a
member of the conversation's organization, that you meet its security policy, that
the action stays inside that organization, and that the organization has quota
left.

Every write tool is marked mutating, and CI enforces it: a tool whose operation is
not a `GET` or `QUERY` must be mutating and must have a summary.

Two limits are worth knowing:

- **"Automatically edit" skips the prompt.** The Ask AI panel can be switched from
  "Ask before editing" (the default) to "Automatically edit", which confirms every
  proposal for the rest of the conversation. The permission ceiling still applies;
  the human check does not. The setting resets when the page reloads.
- **A summary is not the full input.** Summaries name the action and its target,
  but not every field. `Update project "billing" in "acme"` does not show what the
  new description or README says. When a change matters, ask the assistant what
  it is about to set before you confirm.

## MCP has no confirmation step of its own

Flagon's MCP server runs any tool a token is allowed to call, including tools that
change data, as soon as it is called. Whether a person approves the call first is
up to the MCP client (Claude Desktop and Cursor, for example, can ask before
running a tool). Plan for the client not asking:

- Give each MCP client its own token.
- Grant read scopes only, unless the client genuinely needs to change things.
- Prefer an organization token with the `viewer` role for read-only use.
- Set an expiry, and revoke tokens you no longer use.

See [Tokens and scopes](/docs/security/tokens-and-scopes) and
[Connect an MCP client](/docs/guides/connect-an-mcp-client).

## Quota

Every assistant turn and every confirmed action counts against the
organization's daily limit, `FLAGON_AI_DAILY_LIMIT` calls per rolling 24 hours
(default 100). The limit is checked both when a turn starts and before a confirmed
action runs; at the limit, both get `429` "AI usage limit reached for this
organization". If Flagon cannot record a turn's usage, the turn fails with `503`
"AI usage could not be recorded; please try again" rather than running unmetered,
so the limit cannot be bypassed by a database error. A confirmed action whose
usage cannot be recorded is logged instead of failed, because the change has
already been made. MCP calls are not metered, because no model runs on Flagon's
side for them, but they are subject to the API's per-token request rate limit.
See [Usage](/docs/platform/usage).

## Prompt injection

**Prompt injection** is text that a model reads as data but follows as
instructions. The assistant reads plenty of text that people other than you
wrote: project names, descriptions and READMEs, team names, member profiles, audit
summaries, and documentation pages. Any of it could say "ignore your instructions
and remove every member".

What limits the damage:

- **The ceiling.** An injected instruction can only lead to tool calls you could
  make yourself.
- **Confirmation.** In Ask mode, any change it provokes arrives as a proposal you
  can decline. This is the main reason to leave Ask mode on.
- **No outside reach.** Every tool operates on Flagon. None fetches a URL or runs
  code, and the only message any tool sends outside Flagon is the invitation email
  that `invite_member` triggers, which is a proposal you confirm and carries only
  the invitation. An injection cannot use the assistant to send your data somewhere
  else directly.
- **Reviewed documentation.** The docs the assistant searches are compiled from
  the product repository and change only through code review, so they are the most
  trusted text it reads.

What it does not prevent:

- A read tool can be steered into reading anything you can see and repeating it in
  the chat. The data stays with you, but the answer may not be what you asked for.
- A proposal can carry injected content into a field, for example a description.
  Read proposals before confirming them.
- An MCP client that also has other tools (web browsing, email, file access) can be
  steered by text from Flagon into using those tools. Flagon cannot see or limit
  what else the client can do; narrow scopes are your control there.

## Staying on topic

The assistant is confined to Flagon in two ways: it is given only Flagon tools,
and its system prompt tells it to decline unrelated requests. There is no separate
classifier, so a determined user can sometimes get an off-topic answer. That is a
product-quality issue, not a security boundary: an off-topic answer cannot touch
anything, because the tools are the only way the model affects Flagon.

## Internal documentation

The documentation tools can return pages marked `visibility: internal` only to
authenticated callers: the in-product assistant, which always acts for a signed-in
user, and MCP clients that present a valid access token. Anonymous MCP callers and
the public `/docs` routes never see them. No page is internal today; the handbook
is public. See
[Content corpora](/docs/architecture/content-corpora).

## What the model provider sees

Each assistant turn sends the system prompt, the tool definitions, your
conversation, and the results of the read tools it ran to the configured model
provider. That can include names, emails, and project details from your
organization, and anything you type, including a secret you paste into a request
such as configuring an SSO provider. If that is not acceptable, point Flagon at a
model you host yourself (an OpenAI-compatible server such as Ollama or vLLM), or
enter sensitive values on the settings page instead of in the chat. See
[Secrets](/docs/security/secrets).

Error details never reach the model: a tool failure it cannot classify is logged on
the server and reported to the model as a generic message.

## Related

<Cards>
  <Card title="AI runtime" href="/docs/architecture/ai-runtime" description="Providers, the agent loop, proposals, and metering." />
  <Card title="Tool registry" href="/docs/architecture/tool-registry" description="How scopes and tools stay in lockstep with the API." />
  <Card title="Work with the assistant" href="/docs/guides/work-with-the-assistant" description="Using the assistant day to day." />
  <Card title="MCP" href="/docs/ai/mcp" description="Connecting external AI clients to Flagon." />
</Cards>

docs.title: Authentication
docs.description: How Flagon proves who you are - dashboard sessions, two-factor authentication, organization SSO, access tokens, and the internal token that carries your identity from the app to the API.
docs.body:
Authentication is the question every request answers first: who is this? Flagon
splits the answer across its two services on purpose. The **app** (the Next.js
dashboard) signs people in and holds their session. The **API** never sees a
password or a session cookie; it accepts either an access token or a request from
the app that vouches for an already verified user. This page covers each way in
and the boundary between the two services.

For what happens after identity is known, see
[Permissions model](/docs/architecture/permissions-model).

```text
           Browser                  Script, CI, MCP client
               │ session cookie                │ Bearer flagon_pat_...
               ▼                               │     or flagon_oat_...
 ┌─────────────────────────────┐               │
 │ app (Next.js, BetterAuth)   │               │
 │ password, 2FA, SSO session  │               │
 └─────────────┬───────────────┘               │
               │ Bearer <internal token>       │
               │ X-Flagon-User-Id              │
               ▼                               ▼
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ API: combinedAuth                                          │
 │   flagon_ prefix  -> resolve the token, check its scope    │
 │   anything else   -> internal token + X-Flagon-User-Id     │
 └─────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                               ▼
             acts as the user or the service principal
```

## The ways in

| Caller | Sends | Checked by | Acts as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Dashboard (browser) | Session cookie to the app | BetterAuth in the app | The signed-in user, with no scope limit |
| App to API | Internal token plus identity headers | `combinedAuth` or `internalAuth` in the API | The user the app names |
| Scripts, CI, MCP clients | `Authorization: Bearer flagon_...` | `combinedAuth` in the API | The token's principal, limited by its scopes |
| Anyone | Nothing | Public routes only | Nobody |

## Dashboard sign-in

The app runs [BetterAuth](https://www.better-auth.com) (`app/src/lib/auth.ts`)
against its own database, separate from the API's. It supports:

- **Email and password**, with email verification required before first use. The
  verification email carries a one-time code and a link that contains it.
- **Usernames** alongside email addresses.
- **Password reset** by emailed link, valid for one hour.
- **Google and GitHub sign-in**, each enabled only when its client id and secret
  are configured.
- **Organization SSO** over OIDC or SAML, described below.

A successful sign-in creates a BetterAuth session held in a cookie. In production
the cookie is `SameSite=None; Secure` so a SAML assertion posted back from an
identity provider still carries it; cross-site request forgery is covered by
BetterAuth's origin checks rather than by `SameSite`. In local development it is
`SameSite=Lax`.

Every sign-in path creates a session, and a hook on session creation blocks it for
a soft-deleted account.

### Rate limits on sign-in

Authentication endpoints are rate limited, with counters stored in the app's
database so the limit holds across every server instance:

| Endpoint | Limit per 60 seconds |
| --- | --- |
| Sign up with email | 5 |
| Send a verification code | 3 |
| Verify an email code | 10 |
| Request a password reset | 3 |
| Reset a password | 10 |
| Everything else under the auth routes | 20 |

## Two-factor authentication

Users can enroll a TOTP authenticator app (issuer "Flagon") with backup codes.
Once enrolled, sign-in asks for a code as a second step. See
[Two-factor authentication](/docs/platform/two-factor).

An organization owner or admin can **require** two-factor authentication for the
organization (`enforce_two_factor` on `PUT /orgs/{slug}/security`). When it is on,
the organization layout in the dashboard sends any member without two-factor
enabled to a `/2fa-required` page instead of the organization.

The **API** enforces the requirement too (`CheckOrgAccess` in
`api/internal/service/access.go`), so it holds for every way in, not only the
dashboard. It runs on every `/orgs/{slug}/...` operation except leaving the
organization, on every assistant and MCP tool call that names the organization,
and on the assistant's own endpoints. The app mirrors each user's two-factor state
to the API so it can decide. A member without two-factor authentication gets
`403` with the detail "this organization requires two-factor authentication;
enable it on your account to continue", whether they use the dashboard or a
personal access token.

Two details:

- **Organization access tokens are exempt.** Their principal is a service account
  that never signs in interactively, and it is created by an owner or admin who is
  subject to the policy when they create it.
- **You cannot lock yourself out.** Turning the requirement on without two-factor
  on your own account is refused with `403` "enable two-factor authentication on
  your own account before requiring it for the organization".

## Organization SSO

Each organization can configure its own identity providers, OIDC or SAML, so
organization A can use Okta while organization B uses Microsoft Entra ID. The
configuration belongs to the **API**: it is created and edited through
`/orgs/{slug}/sso/providers` (owners and admins, scope `write:org`), the matching
assistant and MCP tools, or the settings page, and every change is audited.

The protocol flow (redirects, assertion validation, cryptography) runs in the app
through BetterAuth's SSO plugin. The plugin's own provider-management endpoints are
switched off. Instead, before any SSO request runs, the app re-syncs the provider
it is about to use from the API (`app/src/lib/sso-hook.ts`), so a change or a
deletion in the API takes effect on the next sign-in. If the API cannot answer, SSO
fails closed with "Single sign-on is temporarily unavailable".

After BetterAuth verifies an assertion, the app calls the API's internal
`POST /internal/sso/provision-member` to make the user a member of the provider's
organization (as `member` by default). This runs on every SSO sign-in, and a first
join is recorded in the audit log as "joined via single sign-on".

Account linking follows two rules. If you are already signed in when you go
through an organization's SSO, the SSO identity is linked to your current account,
whatever email the identity provider asserts. If nobody is signed in, nothing is
linked automatically by matching email addresses.

An owner or admin can also **require** SSO (`require_sso`). Members and admins who
have not signed in through the organization's provider are sent to an
`/sso-required` page. Owners are exempt, so an owner can always reach settings to
fix a broken provider. Like the 2FA requirement, the API enforces it on every way
in:

- **Dashboard sessions.** The app records which SSO provider, if any, the current
  session was established through and sends it to the API as
  `X-Flagon-Auth-Sso-Provider`. The API trusts that header only alongside the
  internal token. If the session did not come through one of the organization's
  live providers, the answer is `403` "this organization requires single sign-on;
  sign in through the organization's identity provider to continue".
- **Personal access tokens.** A token carries no session, so the rule is that its
  owner must have signed in through one of the organization's providers at least
  once (a linked SSO identity, mirrored from the app). Otherwise the answer is
  `403` "this organization requires single sign-on; sign in through the
  organization's identity provider at least once before using a personal access
  token with it".
- **Organization access tokens** are exempt, as for two-factor authentication.

Turning the requirement on without having signed in through one of the
organization's providers yourself is refused with `403` "sign in through one of the
organization's SSO providers before requiring single sign-on". See
[SSO](/docs/platform/sso).

<Callout type="info" title="Email domains are not verified">
A provider may name an email domain so that "sign in with SSO" routes addresses at
that domain to it. Flagon ensures each domain belongs to at most one live provider,
but it does not verify that the organization controls the domain.
</Callout>

## The app-to-API boundary

When the dashboard needs data, a server-side route in the app calls the API
through one function, `send` in `app/src/lib/api/client.ts`. It adds:

- `Authorization: Bearer <FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN>`
- `X-Flagon-User-Id` and `X-Flagon-User-Email`, from the verified session
- `X-Flagon-Client-Ip`, `X-Flagon-Client-Country`, and `X-Flagon-Client-Ua`, from
  the browser's request, for the audit log

The API trusts the identity headers **only** alongside a valid internal token,
compared in constant time. The browser never holds the internal token and never
talks to the API directly for domain data.

The API has two gates (`api/internal/server/identity.go`):

- **`combinedAuth`** guards ordinary operations. A bearer value starting with
  `flagon_` is treated as an access token, resolved, and checked against the
  operation's scope. Anything else must equal the internal token, and then
  `X-Flagon-User-Id` must be present.
- **`internalAuth`** accepts only the internal token. It guards what only the app
  may do: managing access tokens, the assistant's endpoints, SSO provisioning and
  the SSO configuration read, invitation acceptance, and the profile and account
  soft-delete mirrors. The profile mirror (`PUT /me/profile`) carries the
  username and the two-factor and SSO state, all owned by the app's auth layer,
  so no access token can write it.

Both fail closed: a wrong token is `401` "invalid internal token", and a missing
user id is `401` "missing user identity". A production API refuses to start
without an internal token at all; if one is somehow missing at request time, the
endpoints answer `503` "identity API is not configured".

Before either gate runs, every request passes the API's request limits: bodies
over `FLAGON_MAX_BODY_BYTES` (4 MiB by default) get `413`, and each
principal (a signed-in user, an access token, or an anonymous client IP) has a
token-bucket rate limit, 50 requests per second sustained with bursts of 300 by
default, beyond which the API answers `429` with a `Retry-After` header. See
[Configuration](/docs/reference/configuration).

<Callout type="danger" title="The internal token can act as any user">
Whoever holds the internal token can call the API as any user id they choose. Keep
it secret, identical on the app and the API, and unique per deployment. The
development value `dev-internal-token` is used only in development mode, by both
the API and the app. In production the API refuses to start without
`FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN` or with that public value, and the app throws on its first
API call if the variable is unset. See [Secrets](/docs/security/secrets).
</Callout>

## Access tokens

Scripts, CI jobs, and MCP clients authenticate with personal or organization
access tokens sent as `Authorization: Bearer flagon_pat_...` or
`flagon_oat_...`. On the REST API an invalid, expired, or revoked token is `401`
"invalid or expired token". If the API cannot check the token at all (for
example, its database is unavailable), it answers `503` instead, with the cause
logged against the request id, so a good token is never reported as invalid. MCP answers with a JSON-RPC error instead of
downgrading the caller to anonymous. Formats, storage, and scopes are on
[Tokens and scopes](/docs/security/tokens-and-scopes).

## What needs no authentication

Some routes are public by design:

- `GET /users/{username}`: a public profile, through a function that returns only
  public fields.
- `GET /invitations/{token}`: the invitation landing page; the unguessable token is
  the credential.
- `GET /docs`, `/docs/nav`, `/docs/search`, `/docs/page`, `/roadmap`, `/changelog`:
  public content.
- `POST /mcp` without a token: the public documentation tools only.
- `GET /openapi.json` and `/openapi.yaml`, `GET /healthz`, `GET /readyz`, and
  `GET /internal/rls-check`.

## Related

<Cards>
  <Card title="Tokens and scopes" href="/docs/security/tokens-and-scopes" description="Token formats, hashing, expiry, revocation, and least privilege." />
  <Card title="Identity and auth" href="/docs/architecture/identity-and-auth" description="The architecture view of accounts, sessions, and identity mirroring." />
  <Card title="Set up SSO with OIDC" href="/docs/guides/set-up-sso-oidc" description="Connect an OIDC identity provider step by step." />
  <Card title="Require two-factor" href="/docs/guides/require-two-factor" description="Turn on the organization 2FA requirement." />
</Cards>

docs.title: Security overview
docs.description: Flagon's security model on one page - the trust boundaries, what each layer enforces, the defaults that fail closed, current limitations, and how to report a vulnerability.
docs.body:
Flagon holds the map of your engineering system: who is in your organization,
which projects exist, who can change them, and how people sign in. This page is
the security model in one place. Each section links to a page that goes deeper.

The short version: the **API is the only writer** of your organization's data, it
decides every request as a specific person, and the database underneath it
refuses to show one organization's rows to another even if the API asks. The
assistant and the MCP server go through the same checks as everything else, with
no extra powers.

```text
   Browser                    Scripts, CI, MCP clients
      │ session cookie            │ Authorization: Bearer flagon_...
      ▼                           │
 ┌──────────────────────────┐     │
 │ app (Next.js)            │     │
 │ sign-in, 2FA, SSO        │     │
 │ auth rate limits         │     │
 └────────────┬─────────────┘     │
              │ internal token + verified user id
              ▼                   ▼
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ API (Go)                                             │
 │ body size cap, per-principal rate limit              │
 │ token scopes -> org 2FA/SSO policy -> org role       │
 │   -> project role                                    │
 │ every org change audited in the same transaction     │
 └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                            │ NOBYPASSRLS role, user bound per transaction
                            ▼
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Postgres: row-level security on every tenant table   │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## The trust boundaries

**The app** (`app/`, the dashboard at `app.flagon.io`) owns sign-in. It runs
BetterAuth with email and password, email verification, optional Google and
GitHub sign-in, TOTP two-factor authentication, and per-organization SSO (OIDC and
SAML). It keeps the session and forwards each request to the API as the verified
user. See [Authentication](/docs/security/authentication).

**The API** (`api/`, `api.flagon.io`) owns the domain: organizations, members,
teams, projects, tokens, SSO configuration, the audit log, notifications, and AI
usage. It trusts exactly two credentials: the app's internal token (with the user
id the app vouches for) and Flagon access tokens. Every operation checks a token's
scopes, then the organization's security policy (its two-factor and SSO
requirements), then the caller's organization and project roles. See
[Permissions model](/docs/architecture/permissions-model).

**The database** enforces tenant isolation on its own. The API's runtime database
role cannot bypass row-level security, and every transaction is bound to the
acting user, so a query that forgets to filter by organization still cannot see
another organization's rows. See [Tenant isolation](/docs/security/tenant-isolation).

## What fails closed

These defaults deny access when something is missing or misconfigured, rather
than allow it:

- **Unmapped operations.** A scoped token can reach only operations that have a
  scope in `operationScopes`. An operation with no scope is denied to every scoped
  token, and a CI test fails if a new operation has neither a scope nor a written
  exemption.
- **Unbound transactions.** Row-level security reads the user from a
  transaction-local setting. If it is not set, the policies match no rows.
- **Tokens never manage tokens.** Creating, listing, and revoking access tokens
  accept only the app's internal token, so a leaked token cannot mint a stronger
  one.
- **Unknown MCP tools.** An anonymous MCP caller sees only public tools; asking for
  any other tool reports it as unknown.
- **AI usage recording.** If the assistant cannot record a turn's usage, the turn
  fails rather than going unmetered.
- **Audit recording.** If an audit entry cannot be written, the change it
  describes rolls back.
- **Production configuration.** In production the API refuses to start without
  `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN` (or with the public development value
  `dev-internal-token`), `DATABASE_URL`, `FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL`, or
  `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY`. The development fallbacks (the compose database URLs,
  the public internal token, and the public encryption key) exist only when the
  server runs in development mode, and runtime queries never run as the migrator
  role in any mode. See [Production](/docs/self-hosting/production).
- **Internal token missing at request time.** If the API somehow has no internal
  token configured, the endpoints that need it answer `503` instead of running.
- **Organization security policy.** When an organization requires two-factor
  authentication or SSO, the API checks it on every `/orgs/{slug}/...` operation,
  every assistant and MCP tool call that names the organization, and the
  assistant's own endpoints. A member who does not meet the policy gets `403`,
  whether they come through the dashboard or with a personal access token.
- **Internal documentation.** Pages marked `internal` (none today) are served
  only through the assistant and the authenticated MCP, never on the public
  `/docs` routes or to anonymous MCP callers.
- **Error details.** A `5xx` response never carries raw internal error text (SQL,
  hostnames, provider responses). The detail is logged on the server with the
  request id, and every response carries an `X-Request-Id` header to quote.

## Credentials at a glance

| Credential | Held by | Stored as | Details |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Session cookie | Browser | BetterAuth session in the app's database | [Authentication](/docs/security/authentication) |
| Personal or organization access token | Scripts, CI, MCP clients | SHA-256 hash in the API database | [Tokens and scopes](/docs/security/tokens-and-scopes) |
| Internal token | The app | Environment variable on both services | [Secrets](/docs/security/secrets) |
| SSO client secret or SAML key | The API, cached by the app | Encrypted with AES-256-GCM in the API database; plaintext in the app's SSO cache; never returned to users | [Secrets](/docs/security/secrets) |
| Invitation link | The invitee's email | SHA-256 hash, expires after 7 days | [Tokens and scopes](/docs/security/tokens-and-scopes) |

## The AI surfaces

The assistant and the MCP server call the same service layer as the REST API and
act as the requesting user, so they can never exceed that user's role, and over
MCP never exceed the token's scopes. The organization's 2FA and SSO requirements
apply to both. In the dashboard, anything that changes data is proposed and waits
for you to confirm it, unless you switch the conversation to "Automatically edit",
and a conversation can act only inside the organization it was started in.
Assistant usage, including confirmed actions, is capped per organization per day.
See [AI safety](/docs/security/ai-safety).

## Current limitations

Flagon is early, and some controls are narrower than they will be. We would rather
you know:

- **SSO email domains are not verified.** A provider can name an email domain for
  "sign in with SSO" routing. Flagon allows each domain on at most one live
  provider, but it does not check that the organization controls the domain.
- **The app's SSO cache holds secrets in plaintext.** The API encrypts SSO client
  secrets and SAML signing keys at rest, but the app's BetterAuth SSO plugin keeps
  its own copy of the provider configuration, secrets included, in plaintext in
  the app database, because the sign-in flow needs them. See
  [Secrets](/docs/security/secrets).
- **Rate limiting is per instance.** The API's request rate limiter keeps its
  counters in memory on each machine, so with several API machines a caller's
  effective ceiling is that many times the configured rate. The assistant's daily
  quota is stored in the database and holds across machines.
- **"Automatically edit" skips confirmation.** A user can switch an assistant
  conversation to apply changes without asking. The permission ceiling still
  applies; the human check does not. MCP has no confirmation step of its own
  either; that is up to the MCP client.
- **Some principals are exempt from the organization policy by design.**
  Organization owners are exempt from the SSO requirement (so an owner can always
  reach settings to fix a broken provider), and organization access tokens are
  exempt from both the 2FA and SSO requirements because no person signs in with
  them. A personal access token passes an SSO requirement once its owner has
  signed in through one of the organization's providers at least once.
- **SCIM provisioning is designed but not built.** See [SCIM](/docs/platform/scim).

## Reporting a vulnerability

If you find a security issue in Flagon, email **hey@flagon.io** with what you
found and how to reproduce it. Please do not open a public issue for it. We will
acknowledge your report, work on the fix, and credit you if you would like. The
repository's [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/flagon-io/flagon/blob/main/SECURITY.md)
