  <Card title="Multi-tenancy" href="/docs/architecture/multi-tenancy" description="The architecture view of organizations, roles, and RLS." />
  <Card title="Permissions model" href="/docs/architecture/permissions-model" description="The role checks that run on top of isolation." />
  <Card title="Database" href="/docs/self-hosting/database" description="Setting up the two roles when you run Flagon yourself." />
  <Card title="Security overview" href="/docs/security/overview" description="The whole model on one page." />
</Cards>

docs.title: Tokens and scopes
docs.description: How Flagon access tokens are generated, stored as hashes, scoped, expired, and revoked, and how to hand them out with the least privilege.
headings: What a token is made of
Tokens and the organization security policy
docs.body:
An **access token** is a long random string that lets a script, a CI job, or an
MCP client call Flagon without a browser. Flagon has two kinds: a **personal
access token** (PAT) acts as you, and an **organization access token** (OAT) acts
as a service principal that belongs to one organization. Both are sent as a
bearer credential, both carry **scopes** that limit which operations they can
reach, and neither can ever do more than the identity behind it.

This page covers what a token is made of, how Flagon stores it, and how to issue
tokens with the least privilege. For how scopes combine with roles on each
request, see [Permissions model](/docs/architecture/permissions-model). To create
one, see [Access tokens](/docs/platform/access-tokens).

```text
  created in the dashboard (settings -> Tokens)
        │
        ▼
  flagon_pat_ + 43 random characters   shown once, then never again
        │
        ├──► SHA-256 hex digest    stored in access_tokens.token_hash
        └──► flagon_pat_ab12cd     stored as the display prefix

  on each request:  Bearer secret -> SHA-256 -> lookup -> live?
                    -> principal + scopes -> scope gate -> role checks
```

## Two kinds of token

| | Personal (PAT) | Organization (OAT) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prefix | `flagon_pat_` | `flagon_oat_` |
| Acts as | You | A service principal created for the token |
| Reaches | Every organization you belong to, with your role in each | Only its own organization |
| Role | Yours, as it changes | Fixed at creation: `admin`, `member` (default), or `viewer` |
| Managed by | You, under your personal settings | Owners and admins, under the organization's settings |
| Audited | No (it belongs to no organization) | Creation and revocation, as `token.created` and `token.revoked` |

An OAT's service principal is a real user row (`svc_...` with an address at
`svc.flagon.local`) marked as a service account. It holds a membership in the
organization at the token's role, is left out of the people list, and is not tied
to the person who created the token, so removing that person does not break your
automation. A `viewer` OAT can read but not create or edit.

Some operations only make sense for a person, so an OAT is refused them whatever
its scopes: creating an organization, leaving one, listing and restoring deleted
organizations, and mirroring a personal profile. They answer `403` "this operation
requires a user; organization access tokens can't perform it".

Because an OAT's reach and role are fixed, it is the better choice for shared
automation. A PAT follows you: if you are promoted, it gains power; if you leave an
organization, it loses access there.

## What a token is made of

`generateToken` in `api/internal/db/tokens.go` reads 32 bytes from the operating
system's cryptographic random source, encodes them as unpadded base64url (43
characters), and prepends the prefix, giving `flagon_pat_` or `flagon_oat_`
followed by 43 characters: 256 bits of randomness. The prefix makes tokens easy to
recognize in logs and secret scanners, and it is how the API tells a token apart
from the app's internal token.

## How tokens are stored

Flagon never stores the secret. It stores:

- `token_hash`: the SHA-256 digest of the full secret, hex-encoded, with a unique
  index;
- `token_prefix`: the prefix plus the first six random characters (for example
  `flagon_pat_ab12cd`), so you can tell tokens apart in a list.

The plaintext secret is returned exactly once, in the response that creates it.
It cannot be retrieved afterwards by anyone, including Flagon. A single, unsalted
SHA-256 is appropriate here because the input is 256 bits of randomness, not a
human-chosen password: there is nothing to guess.

To authenticate a request, the API hashes the presented bearer value and calls
`flagon.resolve_access_token`, which matches the hash, requires the token to be
live, updates `last_used_at`, and returns the principal and scopes. A token is
live when it has not expired and, for an OAT, its organization has not been
deleted. Anything else is `401` "invalid or expired token".

## Scopes

A token either has **full access** (no scope list; limited only by its
principal's role) or a list of scopes. Creating a token requires at least one
known scope or full access; an unknown scope is rejected with `422`.

| Scope | Covers | Implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `read:user` | Read your profile | |
| `user` | Account writes (none today; your profile is edited in the dashboard) | `read:user` |
| `admin:user` | Reserved for destructive account operations | `user`, `read:user` |
| `read:org` | Read orgs, members, invitations, security policy, SSO providers, audit log | |
| `write:org` | Manage members, invitations, org settings, security policy, SSO providers | `read:org` |
| `admin:org` | Create, leave, delete, and restore orgs | `write:org`, `read:org` |
| `read:project` | Read projects, collaborators, team grants, owners | |
| `write:project` | Create and update projects | `read:project` |
| `admin:project` | Delete and restore projects, manage collaborators, team grants, owners | `write:project`, `read:project` |
| `read:team` | Read teams and their members | |
| `write:team` | Create and edit teams, manage team membership | `read:team` |
| `admin:team` | Delete teams | `write:team`, `read:team` |
| `notifications` | Read and manage your notifications | |

Every operation's required scope is listed in
[Scopes](/docs/reference/scopes). A scope is a ceiling, never a grant: an
`admin:org` token held by a plain member still cannot manage members.

Some operations are unreachable by any token, whatever its scopes: creating,
listing, and revoking tokens, and the assistant's own endpoints. A token can
therefore never mint a stronger token or widen its own access.

## Expiry

When you create a token you choose an expiry. The dashboard offers 7, 30 (the
default), 90, or 365 days, a custom date, or no expiration. The API accepts
`expires_in_days` or an absolute `expires_at` timestamp, which wins if both are
given and must be in the future. A token with no expiry lives until it is revoked.

The API does not impose a maximum lifetime. Prefer an expiry for anything that
leaves your laptop.

## Revocation

Revoking a token deletes it; revoking an OAT also deletes its service principal
and membership. Because every request re-resolves the token by hash, revocation
takes effect on the very next request. There is no way to edit a token's scopes or
role after creation: create a new token and revoke the old one.

Tokens also stop working when:

- they expire;
- their organization is deleted (OATs);
- the person behind a PAT loses membership in an organization (for that
  organization only, through row-level security).

The dashboard lists each token's prefix, scopes, expiry, and last use, so you can
spot tokens nobody is using.

## Least privilege, in practice

- **Use an OAT for automation.** It is bound to one organization, has a fixed role,
  and does not depend on any one person's account.
- **Choose the lowest role.** A reporting job needs a `viewer` OAT, not `admin`.
- **Choose the narrowest scopes.** A job that lists projects needs `read:project`.
  Parent scopes include their children, so pick the lowest level that works.
- **One token per consumer.** Separate tokens for CI, each MCP client, and each
  script let you revoke one without breaking the rest.
- **Set an expiry and rotate.** Put a reminder next to the expiry date.
- **Keep secrets in a secret store.** Your CI provider's secret settings, not a
  repository or a chat message. If a token leaks, revoke it first.

## Tokens and the organization security policy

The API enforces an organization's two-factor and SSO requirements on token
requests too, over REST and MCP alike:

- **A PAT** follows its owner. If the organization requires two-factor
  authentication and the owner has not enabled it, requests for that organization
  get `403`. If the organization requires SSO, the owner must have signed in
  through one of its providers at least once; until then requests get `403`
  explaining that. Owners of the organization are exempt from the SSO requirement.
- **An OAT** is exempt from both requirements, because its service principal never
  signs in. Its reach is controlled by the owners and admins who create it, and
  they are subject to the policy when they do.

See [Authentication](/docs/security/authentication) for the exact messages.

## Rate limits

Each token has its own request budget on the API: 50 requests per second
sustained, with bursts of up to 300, by default. Past it, requests get `429` with
a `Retry-After` header saying how many seconds to wait. The budget is counted per
API machine, and self-hosters can change it with `FLAGON_RATE_LIMIT` and
`FLAGON_RATE_BURST`. See [Limits](/docs/reference/limits).

## Invitation links

Invitation links use the same machinery with the prefix `flagon_inv`. Only the
SHA-256 hash is stored, the link is valid for 7 days, and it can be accepted only
by a signed-in user whose email matches the invitation.

## Related

<Cards>
  <Card title="Access tokens" href="/docs/platform/access-tokens" description="Creating and managing tokens in the dashboard." />
  <Card title="Scopes reference" href="/docs/reference/scopes" description="Every operation and the scope it requires." />
  <Card title="Call the API from CI" href="/docs/guides/call-the-api-from-ci" description="A worked example of a scoped organization token in a pipeline." />
  <Card title="Connect an MCP client" href="/docs/guides/connect-an-mcp-client" description="Give an AI client a token with only the scopes it needs." />
</Cards>

docs.title: Configuration
docs.description: The settings every self-hosted Flagon instance needs, how the API and the app read them, and where the full list lives.
docs.body:
Flagon is configured entirely through environment variables. The API also
accepts each setting as a command-line flag. This page lists the essentials you
need to get an instance running and keep it safe; every setting, with its flag
name and default, is in the [configuration reference](/docs/reference/configuration).

## How the API reads configuration

The API server (`flagon-server`, built with urfave/cli) resolves every setting in
this order, first match wins:

1. A command-line flag, such as `--port 9000`.
2. A real environment variable, such as `PORT=9000`.
3. `.env.local`, then `.env`, in the directory you run the binary from (both are
   gitignored; `api/` when you run it from source).
4. The built-in default.

List everything the running binary accepts with:

```bash
cd api
go run ./cmd/flagon-server serve --help
```

The database URLs are global flags shared by `serve` and `migrate`; everything
else belongs to `serve`.

## Development and production mode

The API runs in one of two modes, and the mode decides whether it may fall back to
public development values:

| `FLAGON_ENV` | Mode |
| --- | --- |
| `development` (or `dev`) | Development. |
| `production` (or `prod`) | Production. |
| unset | Production when running on Fly.io (`FLY_APP_NAME` is set) or when the server binds anything other than a loopback address (such as `FLAGON_HOST=0.0.0.0`). Development when it binds loopback (`127.0.0.1`, `::1`, or `localhost`). |

Off Fly, the default `FLAGON_HOST` is `127.0.0.1`, so a bare `flagon-server serve`
on your own machine binds loopback only and runs in development mode with zero
setup. A container must bind every interface to be reachable, so the API image
sets `FLAGON_HOST=0.0.0.0`, and a container with no `FLAGON_ENV` is in production
mode. That is deliberate: a server reachable from a network fails closed.

If you run the binary directly on a host (for example under systemd) behind a
reverse proxy on the same machine, it binds loopback and would otherwise count as
development, so set `FLAGON_ENV=production` explicitly. Setting it on every
production deployment is the safest habit.

In **development**, unset settings fall back to the local compose Postgres, the
public internal token `dev-internal-token`, and a public encryption key, each with
a warning in the log. In **production** the API refuses to start instead:

| Missing or wrong | Startup error |
| --- | --- |
| `DATABASE_URL` | `DATABASE_URL is required in production (set FLAGON_ENV=development for local development)` |
| `FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL` | `FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL is required in production: runtime queries must use the NOBYPASSRLS app role, never the migrator (set FLAGON_ENV=development for local development)` |
| `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN` | `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN is required in production: set a long random secret shared with the app (set FLAGON_ENV=development for local development)` |
| `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN=dev-internal-token` | `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN is set to the public development value; set a real secret in production` |
| `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY` | `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY is required in production: set a base64-encoded 32-byte key (openssl rand -base64 32)` |

The `migrate` command needs only `DATABASE_URL`. Production mode also changes two
defaults: `FLAGON_APP_URL` becomes `https://app.flagon.io` instead of
`http://localhost:3000`, and the log mail sender is reported as a warning because
invitation emails are not delivered.

## How the app reads configuration

The app reads plain environment variables. In development, `next dev` and the
app's scripts (`db:migrate`, `db:seed`) also load `app/.env.local`;
`app/.env.example` lists the variables with comments. A few values are read at
**build** time (see [Installation](/docs/self-hosting/installation#run-the-app-for-production-with-node)),
so set them before `npm run build`.

## The essentials

### API

| Variable | Default | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FLAGON_ENV` | empty (decided by the bind address) | `development` or `production`. See the mode table above. |
| `DATABASE_URL` | development: `postgres://flagon:flagon@localhost:5432/flagon_api?sslmode=disable`; production: required | The **migrator** role: owns the schema, runs migrations, and provisions the app role. Used only at boot. |
| `FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL` | development: `postgres://flagon_app:flagon_app@localhost:5432/flagon_api?sslmode=disable`; production: required | The **app** role used for every request. Row-level security is enforced against it. Change the password in production. |
| `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN` | development: `dev-internal-token`; production: required | The shared secret the app authenticates to the API with. Must match the app's value. |
| `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY` | development: a public key; production: required | A base64-encoded 32-byte key that encrypts stored SSO client secrets and SAML keys. Generate with `openssl rand -base64 32` and back it up: a key cannot open values sealed with another one. To rotate, see `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEYS_RETIRED`. |
| `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEYS_RETIRED` | empty | Comma-separated former `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY` values, used only to decrypt. On boot the API re-seals everything still under one of them with the current key. See [Rotating the encryption key](/docs/security/secrets#rotating-the-encryption-key). |
| `PORT` | `8080` | The public HTTP port. |
| `FLAGON_HOST` | `127.0.0.1` off Fly (all interfaces on Fly) | The interface to bind. The default is loopback only, which selects development mode when `FLAGON_ENV` is unset. The API container image sets `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces), which selects production mode. |
| `METRICS_PORT` | `9091` | The private port that serves Prometheus metrics at `/metrics`. |
| `FLAGON_MCP_HOST` | empty | A dedicated host name for the MCP endpoint, such as `mcp.example.com`. See [Production](/docs/self-hosting/production#a-dedicated-mcp-host). |
| `FLAGON_CLIENT_IP_HEADER` | empty | A proxy header that carries the real client IP, such as `Fly-Client-IP`. Empty trusts only the TCP peer address. Set it only when every request reaches the API through a proxy that overwrites the header, or callers can spoof their IP in the audit log and the rate limiter. |
| `FLAGON_MAX_BODY_BYTES` | `4194304` (4 MiB) | Largest accepted request body, on every route including MCP. Larger bodies get `413`. |
| `FLAGON_RATE_LIMIT` | `50` | Sustained requests per second per principal (a user, an access token, or an anonymous client IP). `0` disables. Counted in memory on each API machine. |
| `FLAGON_RATE_BURST` | `300` | Requests a principal may make at once before the sustained rate applies. |

### Email

The API sends invitation emails itself, whichever front door created the
invitation.

| Variable | Default | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FLAGON_MAIL_PROVIDER` | `auto` | `resend`, `log`, or `auto`, which uses Resend when `RESEND_API_KEY` is set and otherwise writes emails to the server log. Pinning `resend` without a key fails at startup. |
| `RESEND_API_KEY` | empty | The API's Resend key. Without it, nobody receives invitation emails. |
| `FLAGON_MAIL_FROM` | `Flagon <onboarding@resend.dev>` | The sender address. `RESEND_FROM` is also accepted. |
| `FLAGON_APP_URL` | `https://app.flagon.io` in production, `http://localhost:3000` otherwise | The app's public URL, used for the accept link in invitation emails. Self-hosters must set it. |

### AI

| Variable | Default | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FLAGON_AI_PROVIDER` | `auto` | `anthropic`, `openai` (any OpenAI-compatible endpoint), `mock`, or `auto`, which picks Anthropic if a key is set, then an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, then the offline mock. Pinning a provider without its credentials, or naming an unknown one, fails at startup. |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | empty | Enables the Anthropic provider. |
| `FLAGON_AI_BASE_URL` | empty | Base URL of an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, for example `http://localhost:11434/v1` for Ollama. `OPENAI_BASE_URL` is also accepted. |
| `FLAGON_AI_API_KEY` | empty | Key for that endpoint; leave empty for keyless local servers. `OPENAI_API_KEY` is also accepted. |
| `FLAGON_AI_MODEL` | provider default | The model the assistant runs. |
| `FLAGON_AI_DAILY_LIMIT` | `100` | Maximum AI calls per organization per rolling 24 hours. `0` means unlimited. |

### App

| Variable | Required | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` | yes | The auth layer's signing and encryption key. It also encrypts stored two-factor secrets, so keep it stable: changing it breaks existing sessions and enrolled authenticators. Generate with `openssl rand -base64 32`. |
| `BETTER_AUTH_URL` | yes | The app's public URL, such as `https://flagon.example.com`. Used for callbacks and email links. |
| `DATABASE_URL` | yes | The app's own database (`flagon_app`). Not the API's. |
| `FLAGON_API_URL` | yes | Where the app reaches the API, server-side. Defaults to `http://localhost:8080`. |
| `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN` | yes | Must equal the API's `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN`. In development an unset value falls back to `dev-internal-token`, matching the API's development default. In production (`NODE_ENV=production`) there is no default: the app throws "FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN is required in production" on its first API call. |
| `RESEND_API_KEY` | in production | Sends the app's email (verification codes and password resets) through Resend. In production the app refuses to drop an email when this is missing. Invitation emails come from the API and need the API's own `RESEND_API_KEY`. |
| `RESEND_FROM` | no | The sender address. Defaults to `Flagon <onboarding@resend.dev>`. |

Google and GitHub sign-in are optional: set `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` and
`GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET`, or `GITHUB_CLIENT_ID` and `GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET`, before
building the app. Without them the buttons stay visible but disabled.

<Callout type="danger" title="Never force development mode on a reachable server">

The development fallbacks are well-known values. Anyone who can reach an API
running with `dev-internal-token` can act as any user through the internal path.
Production mode refuses those values, so do not set `FLAGON_ENV=development` on a
server others can reach. Set a long random `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN`, a real
`FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY`, and a real app-role password instead.

</Callout>

## Related

- [Configuration reference](/docs/reference/configuration)
- [Installation](/docs/self-hosting/installation)
- [Production](/docs/self-hosting/production)
- [Usage and AI limits](/docs/platform/usage)

docs.title: Database
docs.description: The two Postgres databases, the migrator and NOBYPASSRLS app roles, how the API provisions them on boot, and notes for managed Postgres and pgbouncer.
headings: How the API provisions the app role
docs.body:
Flagon stores everything in Postgres. The API owns one database and the app owns
another, and the API talks to its database through two different roles. This
split is the foundation of tenant isolation, so it is worth understanding before
you point Flagon at a managed database.

## Two databases

| Database | Connection setting | Owner | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `flagon_api` | the API's `DATABASE_URL` and `FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL` | the API | All domain data: organizations, members, invitations, teams, projects and their access, access tokens, the audit log, notifications, SSO provider configuration, and AI usage records. |
| `flagon_app` | the app's `DATABASE_URL` | the app | BetterAuth's tables (`users`, `sessions`, `accounts`, `verifications`, `two_factors`, `rateLimit`), a cache of SSO providers (`sso_providers`), and `user_emails`. |

The two are never queried together. The app reaches domain data only through the
API. You can put both databases in one Postgres server (the local compose file
does) or in two separate servers (Flagon's hosted instance does); the data
boundary is the same.

<Callout type="note" title="Same variable name, different databases">

Both processes read a variable called `DATABASE_URL`. On the API it is the
migrator connection to `flagon_api`; on the app it is the connection to
`flagon_app`. If you run both on one machine, set each in its own environment.

</Callout>

## Two roles for the API

The API never runs requests with the role that owns its schema:

| Role | Setting | Used for | Attributes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Migrator** | `DATABASE_URL` | Boot only: provisioning the app role, applying migrations, granting privileges. | Owns the schema. Must be able to create and alter roles, unless your platform manages roles (below). |
| **App** | `FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL` | Every runtime query. | `LOGIN NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOBYPASSRLS`. |

Tenant tables have row-level security (RLS) enabled. Each request runs in a
transaction that binds the acting user, and the policies only return rows from
organizations that user belongs to. Because the app role is `NOBYPASSRLS` and does
not own the tables, that holds even if a query in the Go code forgets to filter by
organization. (The policies are enabled rather than forced, which exempts only the
table owner, the migrator, and the migrator never serves requests.) See
[Multi-tenancy](/docs/architecture/multi-tenancy) for how the policies work.

### How the API provisions the app role

Every time the API boots (and whenever you run `flagon-server migrate`), the
setup step in `api/internal/db/setup.go` does the following as the migrator:

1. Reads the role name and password from `FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL`. The name
   must be a plain SQL identifier (letters, digits, underscores, at most 63
   characters) and the URL must include a password; otherwise provisioning is
   skipped with a warning.
2. Creates the role if it does not exist, then sets its password to the one in
   the URL and pins its attributes (`NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE
   NOBYPASSRLS`). The URL is the single place the credential lives, so rotating
   the password is a config change plus a restart.
3. Applies pending migrations (below).
4. Grants the role `USAGE` on every user schema, `SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE`
   on all tables, `USAGE, SELECT` on all sequences, and matching default
   privileges so tables created by later migrations are covered automatically.

Provisioning and grants are best-effort: a failure is logged but does not stop
the boot, because readiness and the RLS self-check surface the consequence. A
migration failure is different (see below).

<Callout type="warn" title="Use a separate role for the app">

`FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL` must name a different role from `DATABASE_URL`. Setup
pins the app role to `NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS`, which is only correct for a role
that exists solely to serve requests.

</Callout>

In production mode, `flagon-server serve` refuses to start when
`FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL` is empty ("FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL is required in
production: runtime queries must use the NOBYPASSRLS app role, never the
migrator"), so a production API can never serve requests as the migrator. In
development mode an unset value defaults to the local compose app role
(`postgres://flagon_app:flagon_app@localhost:5432/flagon_api`). See
[Configuration](/docs/self-hosting/configuration) for how the mode is chosen.

`flagon-server migrate` does not require the setting. Without it, the migrator
still applies migrations but skips provisioning the app role, and logs
`FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL not set; skipping app-role provisioning and grants (the runtime never falls back to the migrator role, so serving requires it)`.

### Checking isolation

The API exposes a self-test at `GET /internal/rls-check`. It runs as the app role
against a fixture table seeded by the migrations: with organization A bound it
must see only A's row, with B only B's, and with nothing bound, nothing at all.

```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/internal/rls-check
```

```json
{"enforced":true,"org_a":["org-a"],"org_b":["org-b"],"no_org":null}
```

A `503` with `"enforced":false` means the runtime role can see across tenants
(typically because it is a superuser or has `BYPASSRLS`); fix the role before
serving users.

## Migrations

The API's schema lives in `api/internal/db/migrations/*.sql`, embedded into the
binary at build time. There is no separate migration tool and no files to ship
next to the binary.

- **Applied on boot.** `flagon-server serve` migrates before it starts
  listening. `flagon-server migrate` does the same and exits, for running it by
  hand.
- **In order, all or nothing.** Pending files are applied in filename order
  inside a single transaction, so either every pending migration applies or none
  does.
- **Safe with many instances.** The run takes a transaction-scoped Postgres
  advisory lock first, so several API instances booting at once serialize: the
  first applies, the rest wait and then find nothing to do.
- **Recorded and checksummed.** Each applied file is recorded in
  `public.schema_migrations` with a SHA-256 checksum. If a file that was already
  applied has changed, the run stops with
  `migrations are immutable once shipped`.
- **Forward-only.** There are no down migrations. See
  [Upgrading](/docs/self-hosting/upgrading).

### Why migrations run on boot

Running migrations from the serving process means a deploy is just "start the
new binary": there is no release step to forget, and the schema can never lag
the code that needs it. It also works on platforms where a one-off release
machine cannot reach the database; Fly Managed Postgres, which Flagon's hosted
instance uses, is one example.

The boot is deliberately asymmetric about failure:

| Situation | What the API does |
| --- | --- |
| Postgres unreachable (after 6 connection attempts, 2 seconds apart) | Starts **degraded**: serves, logs a warning, and `/readyz` returns `503` until the database answers. A database blip never blocks a deploy. |
| Postgres reachable but a migration fails, or an applied migration was modified | **Refuses to start**, so a broken or unknown schema is never served. |

The app's database is migrated separately by the app's own scripts
(`npm run db:migrate --workspace app`), which apply BetterAuth's schema with the
installed BetterAuth version. Flagon's hosted build runs them during the app's
build and fails the deploy if they fail.

## Managed Postgres and pgbouncer

Flagon works with managed Postgres, including providers that put a
transaction-pooling pgbouncer in front of the database. The code accounts for
it in three places:

- **Simple protocol for migrations.** The migrator connection uses pgx's simple
  query protocol, which avoids prepared statements. Transaction-pooling
  pgbouncer does not tolerate the extended protocol for DDL, and a migration can
  hang without this.
- **Transaction-scoped locks and settings.** The migration advisory lock
  (`pg_advisory_xact_lock`) and the per-request tenant binding
  (`set_config(..., true)`) are both transaction-local, so they behave correctly
  when consecutive statements land on different server connections.
- **Platform-managed roles.** Some providers manage roles themselves and reject
  `ALTER ROLE` or `GRANT` with `insufficient_privilege`. The API treats that as
  expected: it logs that the role is managed by the database and leaves it
  alone. In that case, create the app role through your provider with
  `NOBYPASSRLS`, give it read and write access to the `flagon_api` tables, and
  put its credentials in `FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL`. Then confirm with
  `/internal/rls-check`.

### TLS

The API passes its URLs to pgx, which follows the usual libpq `sslmode`
parameter. The app handles `sslmode` itself: `sslmode=disable` turns TLS off, and
**any other value** (or none) connects with full certificate verification. If
your database presents a certificate your Node runtime does not trust, the app
cannot connect until the certificate chain is trusted.

## Backups

Back up both databases. `flagon_api` holds all domain data; `flagon_app` holds
accounts, password hashes, two-factor secrets, and sessions. A `pg_dump` of each
(or your provider's snapshots) is enough. Two-factor secrets in `flagon_app` are
encrypted with the app's `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`, and SSO client secrets and SAML
keys in `flagon_api` are encrypted with the API's `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY`, so keep
both keys (separately from the dumps) with your backups. The app's own SSO
provider cache in `flagon_app` holds those credentials in plaintext, so protect
its backups accordingly.

## Related

- [Upgrading](/docs/self-hosting/upgrading)
- [Production](/docs/self-hosting/production)
- [Multi-tenancy](/docs/architecture/multi-tenancy)
- [Tenant isolation](/docs/security/tenant-isolation)
- [Self-hosting issues](/docs/troubleshooting/self-hosting-issues)

docs.title: Installation
docs.description: Install Flagon from source or with the Docker images, migrate both databases, seed a demo user, and sign in.
headings: same as: cd api && go run ./cmd/flagon-server serve
same as: npm run dev   (builds @flagon-io/ui, then runs next dev)
same as: npm run db:seed --workspace app
Run the app for production with Node
docs.body:
This page brings up a working Flagon instance: Postgres, the API, and the app,
with a demo account you can sign in with. It covers running both from source,
running the whole stack with Docker Compose, and building the API and app
images.
For what each piece does, read the [overview](/docs/self-hosting/overview) first.

The steps below target a local machine. The same commands work on a server; the
[production](/docs/self-hosting/production) page covers what changes when real
users depend on the instance (secrets, TLS, email, health checks).

## Prerequisites

| Tool | Version | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Git | any | Cloning the repository. |
| Go | 1.27.1 or newer (from `api/go.mod`) | Building and running the API from source. Not needed if you use the API's Docker image. |
| Node.js and npm | Node 24 or newer (CI runs 24; the app's Dockerfile uses 26) | Installing dependencies, building and running the app, and the app's migration and seed scripts. |
| Docker | any recent version with Compose | Running Postgres locally, and optionally the API image. |
| Postgres | 17 (the version the compose file and CI use) | Both databases. The compose file provides one. |

## Install from source

<Steps>

<Step title="Clone the repository">

```bash
git clone https://github.com/flagon-io/flagon.git
cd flagon
```

The repository is an npm workspaces monorepo plus a Go module: `app/` is the web
app, `api/` is the Go API, and `packages/ui/` is the design system the app is
built with.

</Step>

<Step title="Start Postgres">

The base `compose.yml` publishes no host ports, so it never collides with
servers you run natively. Copy the override once to publish Postgres on
`localhost:5432`, then start it:

```bash
cp compose.override.example.yml compose.override.yml
docker compose up -d postgres
```

This starts one `postgres:17-alpine` instance with the user `flagon` (password
`flagon`) and two databases: `flagon_api` for the API and `flagon_app` for the
app. The second database is created by `.docker/postgres/01-create-app-db.sql`
the first time the volume initializes.

To use your own Postgres instead, create the two databases yourself and point
the connection strings in the next steps at it. The API's migrator role must be
able to create roles; see [Database](/docs/self-hosting/database).

</Step>

<Step title="Check the API's mode">

The API chooses between **development** and **production** mode at startup.
Production refuses to start without real secrets. Unless `FLAGON_ENV` says
otherwise, a server that binds a network-reachable interface (such as
`FLAGON_HOST=0.0.0.0`) or runs on Fly.io is production, and a server bound to
loopback is development.

Run from a checkout with no configuration, the API binds `127.0.0.1`, so it is in
development mode and there is nothing to set. Every setting has a default that
points at the compose Postgres (`postgres://flagon:flagon@localhost:5432/flagon_api`
for the migrator, `postgres://flagon_app:flagon_app@localhost:5432/flagon_api` for
the runtime role), the internal token defaults to the public value
`dev-internal-token`, and stored credentials are encrypted with a public
development key. The API logs a warning for each of these. Binding to loopback
also avoids the Windows Firewall prompt.

For local overrides, put them in `api/.env`, which the API loads at startup and
git ignores. If you set `FLAGON_HOST=0.0.0.0` there, also set
`FLAGON_ENV=development`, or `make api` exits with "DATABASE_URL is required in
production (set FLAGON_ENV=development for local development)".

</Step>

<Step title="Configure the app">

The app reads `app/.env.local`. Start from the example file:

```bash
cp app/.env.example app/.env.local
```

Then fill in at least these values:

```bash
# app/.env.local
BETTER_AUTH_SECRET=<output of: openssl rand -base64 32>
BETTER_AUTH_URL=http://localhost:3000
DATABASE_URL=postgres://flagon:flagon@localhost:5432/flagon_app?sslmode=disable
FLAGON_API_URL=http://localhost:8080
FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN=dev-internal-token
```

`FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN` must match the API's value. In development both the API
and the app fall back to `dev-internal-token` when it is unset, so you can also
leave it blank; setting it explicitly makes the pairing obvious. If the two values
differ, every request from the app fails with `401` "invalid internal token".

Without `RESEND_API_KEY`, the app prints its emails (verification codes and
password resets) to its console instead of sending them, and the API writes
invitation emails, accept link included, to its log as
`[email] not sent (log mailer)`. Such an invitation reports `email_sent: false`,
and the dashboard's invite dialog shows the link with a copy button so you can
share it.

</Step>

<Step title="Install dependencies">

Run this from the repository root. The single `package-lock.json` and
`node_modules` live there, and `app` plus `packages/*` are workspaces:

```bash
npm install
```

</Step>

<Step title="Start the API">

```bash
make api
# same as: cd api && go run ./cmd/flagon-server serve
```

On boot the API connects to `flagon_api` as the migrator role, provisions the
`flagon_app` runtime role, applies every pending migration, and then serves on
`http://localhost:8080`. Check it:

```bash
curl -i http://localhost:8080/healthz   # 200 when the process is up
curl http://localhost:8080/readyz       # {"database":"ok","status":"ok"}
```

</Step>

<Step title="Migrate the app's database">

The app's auth tables are migrated separately, by the app's own scripts:

```bash
npm run db:migrate --workspace app
```

This renames any legacy BetterAuth tables to the plural names Flagon uses,
applies BetterAuth's schema with the installed version, and creates the
`user_emails` table. It is idempotent, so running it again is safe.

</Step>

<Step title="Start the app">

```bash
make app
# same as: npm run dev   (builds @flagon-io/ui, then runs next dev)
```

The app serves on `http://localhost:3000`. `make dev` does this step and the
previous API step together: it starts Postgres, then runs the API and the app in
parallel in one terminal.

</Step>

<Step title="Seed a demo user and sign in">

With the API running, create the demo account and its organization:

```bash
make seed
# same as: npm run db:seed --workspace app
```

The seed writes a pre-verified user with a static password straight into
`flagon_app`, then creates the organization through the API's `POST /orgs`, so
it exercises the real creation path. It is idempotent: re-running it resets the
password and re-verifies the email.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Email | `demo@flagon.dev` |
| Username | `demo` |
| Password | `password12345` |
| Organization | `Demo Org` at `/demo` |

Open `http://localhost:3000` and sign in; in development the login form
pre-fills the demo credentials. Override any value with `SEED_EMAIL`,
`SEED_USERNAME`, `SEED_PASSWORD`, `SEED_NAME`, `SEED_ORG_NAME`, or
`SEED_ORG_SLUG`, and set `SEED_SKIP_ORG=1` to create only the user.

<Callout type="warn" title="Development only">

The seed refuses to run when `NODE_ENV=production` unless `SEED_ALLOW_PROD=1` is
set. Never seed a static-password account into an instance other people use.

</Callout>

</Step>

</Steps>

## Run everything with Docker Compose

The compose file can run the whole stack, not only Postgres. With the override
copied (it publishes Postgres on `5432`, the API on `8080`, and the app on
`4000`):

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

This builds the `dev` targets of both Dockerfiles: the API live-reloads through
`air`, and the app runs `next dev`. The compose file sets development values on
both services (`FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN: dev-internal-token`, a development
`BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`) and sets `FLAGON_ENV: development` on the API, because a
container binds all interfaces and would otherwise start in production mode and
refuse those values. Migrate the app's database and seed the demo user as in the
steps above. Use this stack for local work only.

## Run the API with Docker

The API ships a multi-stage Dockerfile at `api/Dockerfile`. Its final stage is a
small Alpine image that runs `flagon-server serve` as a non-root user, listens on
port 8080, and declares a `HEALTHCHECK` against `/healthz`.

```bash
docker build -t flagon-api -f api/Dockerfile api
# or: make api-docker-build
```

The image sets `FLAGON_HOST=0.0.0.0` so the container binds all interfaces, and
so it runs in production mode unless you set `FLAGON_ENV=development`. Run it with the two database URLs, the internal
token, and the secrets key; without any one of them it exits at startup. The API
reaches Postgres from inside the container, so use a host name the container can
resolve (a compose service name, a Docker network alias, or your database
server's address), not `localhost`:

```bash
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 \
  -e DATABASE_URL='postgres://flagon:flagon@db.internal:5432/flagon_api?sslmode=disable' \
  -e FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL='postgres://flagon_app:<app-role-password>@db.internal:5432/flagon_api?sslmode=disable' \
  -e FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN='<a long random secret>' \
  -e FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY='<output of: openssl rand -base64 32>' \
  flagon-api
```

The image's default command is `serve`. Pass `migrate` instead to provision the
app role and apply migrations, then exit:

```bash
docker run --rm -e DATABASE_URL=... -e FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL=... flagon-api migrate
```

The `migrate` command needs only `DATABASE_URL` in production;
`FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL` tells it which runtime role to provision.

## Run the app with Docker

The app's Dockerfile builds from the **repository root**, because the npm
workspace (the app plus `packages/ui`) shares one lockfile there:

```bash
docker build -t flagon-app -f app/Dockerfile .
```

The final stage runs Next.js's standalone server (`node app/server.js`) as the
`node` user on port 3000, with `NODE_ENV=production`. Pass the app's settings at
`docker run`; in production the app requires `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN` and throws on
its first API call without it:

```bash
docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 \
  -e DATABASE_URL='postgres://flagon:flagon@db.internal:5432/flagon_app' \
  -e BETTER_AUTH_SECRET='<output of: openssl rand -base64 32>' \
  -e BETTER_AUTH_URL='https://app.example.com' \
  -e FLAGON_API_URL='http://api.internal:8080' \
  -e FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN='<the same secret as the API>' \
  flagon-app
```

The Dockerfile passes no build arguments, so an image built this way has the
Google and GitHub sign-in buttons disabled: that choice is made at build time (see
the Node section below). The image does not migrate the app's database. Run
`npm run db:migrate --workspace app` against it from a checkout (with the same
`DATABASE_URL`) before the first start and after upgrades.

## Run the app for production with Node

The app is a standard Next.js application. From the repository root:

```bash
npm ci
npm run db:migrate --workspace app   # needs DATABASE_URL (and the auth env)
npm run build                        # builds @flagon-io/ui, then the app
npm run start --workspace app        # next start, port 3000
```

Set the app's environment before `npm run build`, not only before `start`:
whether the Google and GitHub sign-in buttons are enabled is decided at build time
(in `app/next.config.ts`) from `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`/`GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` and
`GITHUB_CLIENT_ID`/`GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET`.

The app also deploys to any Next.js host. Flagon's own instance builds on Vercel
with `npm run vercel-build --workspace app`, which runs the same auth migrations
during the build and fails the deploy if a migration fails.

## Verify the install

- `GET /healthz` on the API returns `200`.
- `GET /readyz` returns `200` with `"database":"ok"`. A `503` with
  `"status":"degraded"` means the API is up but cannot reach Postgres.
- `GET /internal/rls-check` returns `200` with `"enforced":true`, which proves
  the runtime role cannot see rows outside the organization bound to its
  transaction.
- You can sign in to the app, and the dashboard lists your organization.

If any of these fail, see [Self-hosting issues](/docs/troubleshooting/self-hosting-issues).

## Related

- [Self-hosting overview](/docs/self-hosting/overview)
- [Configuration](/docs/self-hosting/configuration)
- [Database](/docs/self-hosting/database)
- [Production](/docs/self-hosting/production)
- [Self-hosting issues](/docs/troubleshooting/self-hosting-issues)

docs.title: Self-hosting overview
docs.description: What you run when you host Flagon yourself - the app, the API, two Postgres databases, and an optional AI provider - and how they connect.
docs.body:
Flagon is open source and runs entirely on your own infrastructure. A self-hosted
instance is the same code the hosted service runs: nothing about the platform
requires Flagon's own servers.

You run two processes and one or two Postgres servers. This page explains what
each piece does and how they talk to each other, so the installation and
production pages make sense before you start.

## The pieces

```text
                  Browser                         CLI, CI, MCP clients
                     │ HTTPS                      (Bearer flagon_ tokens)
                     ▼                                       │
        ┌─────────────────────────┐                          │
        │ app  (Next.js)          │                          │
        │ UI, sign-in, sessions   │                          │
        └────┬───────────────┬────┘                          │
             │               │ internal token +              │
             │               │ X-Flagon-User-* headers       │
             │               ▼                               ▼
             │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
             │  │ api  (flagon-server serve)                        │
             │  │ domain logic, permissions, agent, MCP, docs       │
             │  │ :8080 public HTTP        :9091 private /metrics   │
             │  └─────────────┬───────────────────────┬─────────────┘
             ▼                ▼                       ▼
     ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐     ┌────────────────────┐
     │ Postgres     │  │ Postgres     │     │ AI provider        │
     │ flagon_app   │  │ flagon_api   │     │ (optional)         │
     │ auth, users  │  │ domain + RLS │     │ Anthropic, OpenAI- │
     └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘     │ compatible, mock   │
                                            └────────────────────┘
```

### app

The **app** is the Next.js web UI and gateway (the `app/` directory). It renders
the dashboard, owns sign-in (email and password, two-factor, social sign-in, and
org SSO through BetterAuth), and holds the user's session. It never reads or
writes domain data itself: every request for organizations, projects, tokens, and
the rest is forwarded server-side to the API, authenticated with a shared
**internal token** plus the verified user's identity in `X-Flagon-User-Id` and
`X-Flagon-User-Email` headers. That single request path lives in
`app/src/lib/api/client.ts`.

The app also sends its own transactional email (verification codes and password
resets) through Resend when `RESEND_API_KEY` is set on the app. Invitation emails
come from the API instead, described below.

### api

The **API** is a single Go binary, `flagon-server` (`api/cmd/flagon-server`). It
is the source of truth and the only writer of domain data. It serves:

- the REST API and its generated OpenAPI spec (`/openapi.json`, `/openapi.yaml`);
- the MCP endpoint (`/mcp`), from the same tool registry the assistant uses;
- the in-product assistant (`/ai/messages`), which calls your configured model;
- the embedded docs, roadmap, and changelog (`/docs`, `/roadmap`, `/changelog`);
- health checks (`/healthz`, `/readyz`) and, on a separate private port,
  Prometheus metrics.

It also sends invitation emails itself, so an invitation made from the dashboard,
the REST API, the assistant, or MCP is delivered the same way. With
`RESEND_API_KEY` set on the API it sends through Resend; without it, it writes the
email to its log, which is fine for local development but means nobody receives
invitations in production.

The API decides at startup whether it runs in **development** or **production**
mode. Production refuses to start without the settings a real deployment needs
(the internal token, both database URLs, and the secrets key), rather than
falling back to the public development values. See
[Configuration](/docs/self-hosting/configuration).

The API applies its own schema migrations every time it boots, so there is no
separate release step. See [Database](/docs/self-hosting/database).

### The two databases

Flagon keeps two separate Postgres databases:

| Database | Owned by | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `flagon_api` | the API | Organizations, members, teams, projects, tokens, SSO configuration, audit log, notifications, AI usage. Protected by row-level security. |
| `flagon_app` | the app | BetterAuth's tables: users, sessions, accounts, verifications, two-factor secrets, rate-limit counters, and a cache of SSO provider settings. |

Locally, one Postgres instance holds both databases to keep resource use low. In
production you can run them in one instance or two; they are never joined, so
the boundary is the same either way.

The API connects to `flagon_api` with **two roles**: a migrator role that owns
the schema, and a least-privilege app role that cannot bypass row-level security
and is used for every request. That split is what makes tenant isolation hold
even if application code forgets to scope a query. See
[Database](/docs/self-hosting/database) for how the API provisions it.

### The AI provider (optional)

The assistant needs a model to do real work, but Flagon runs fine without one.
The API picks a provider from configuration: Anthropic, any OpenAI-compatible
endpoint (including a model you host yourself with Ollama or vLLM), or an
offline **mock** that matches keywords and needs no key. With nothing configured,
the API uses the mock, so the assistant panel works on a fresh install. Every
other part of Flagon works the same with or without a model.

## What is not included

A self-hosted instance runs exactly what is built today. Features that are still
on the roadmap are not available on any instance:

<Callout type="warn" title="Not available yet">

Deployments, logs and observability, packages, SCIM provisioning, and the
`flagon` CLI (a skeleton whose commands exit with code 3) are not built yet.
Billing beyond the one-free-organization limit is not built either: on the free
plan, creating or restoring a second organization you own returns
`402 Payment Required`.

</Callout>

## Where to go next

<Cards>
  <Card title="Installation" href="/docs/self-hosting/installation" description="Bring up Postgres, the API, and the app, and sign in as the demo user." />
  <Card title="Configuration" href="/docs/self-hosting/configuration" description="The handful of settings every instance needs." />
  <Card title="Production" href="/docs/self-hosting/production" description="Secrets, TLS, health checks, and running the app and API on separate hosts." />
</Cards>

## Related

- [Installation](/docs/self-hosting/installation)
- [Database](/docs/self-hosting/database)
- [Production](/docs/self-hosting/production)
- [Configuration reference](/docs/reference/configuration)
- [Self-hosting issues](/docs/troubleshooting/self-hosting-issues)

docs.title: Running in production
docs.description: Secrets, TLS, email, health checks, metrics, the dedicated MCP host, and running the app and API on separate hosts.
headings: Running the app and API on separate hosts
docs.body:
Flagon does not assume a particular host. The API is one Go binary (or the image
built from `api/Dockerfile`) backed by Postgres, and the app is a standard
Next.js application. Flagon's own instance runs the API on Fly.io and the app on
Vercel, but nothing in the code depends on either. This page covers what every
production deployment needs, wherever it runs.

## Checklist

- [ ] Both processes run behind HTTPS.
- [ ] The API runs in production mode: set `FLAGON_ENV=production` (never `development`). Unset also works in the container image or on Fly, but a binary bound to loopback behind a same-host proxy would otherwise run in development mode.
- [ ] `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN` is a long random value, identical on the app and the API.
- [ ] `DATABASE_URL` and `FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL` are set, and the app role has its own real password.
- [ ] `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY` is a random 32-byte key and backed up (rotate it with `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEYS_RETIRED`).
- [ ] `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` is random, stable, and backed up.
- [ ] `BETTER_AUTH_URL` is the app's public HTTPS URL, and the API's `FLAGON_APP_URL` matches it.
- [ ] `RESEND_API_KEY` is set on the app (verification and reset emails) and on the API (invitation emails), with `RESEND_FROM` and `FLAGON_MAIL_FROM` on a verified domain.
- [ ] If a proxy sits in front of the API, `FLAGON_CLIENT_IP_HEADER` names the header it overwrites with the client IP.
- [ ] Health checks point at `/healthz`, and readiness at `/readyz`.
- [ ] The metrics port is not reachable from the internet.
- [ ] `GET /internal/rls-check` returns `"enforced":true`.
- [ ] Both databases are backed up.

## Secrets

| Secret | Where | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN` | app and API | The app authenticates every server-side call to the API with it, and names the acting user in headers. Anyone who knows the value and can reach the API could act as any user. A production API refuses to start without it or with the public development value `dev-internal-token`, and a production app throws on its first API call without it. The API compares it in constant time. |
| `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY` | API | Encrypts stored SSO client secrets and SAML keys (AES-256-GCM). Required in production. Generate with `openssl rand -base64 32` and back it up. To change it, keep the old value in `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEYS_RETIRED` until the boot re-seal finishes; see [Rotating the encryption key](/docs/security/secrets#rotating-the-encryption-key). |
| `DATABASE_URL` (API) | API | The migrator role. It can change the schema, so only the API should hold it. |
| `FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL` | API | The runtime role. The API sets this role's password from the URL on every boot. |
| `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` | app | Signs sessions and encrypts two-factor secrets. Changing it breaks existing sessions and enrolled authenticators. |
| `DATABASE_URL` (app) | app | The app's own `flagon_app` database. |
| `RESEND_API_KEY` | app and API | Email delivery: the app sends verification and reset emails, the API sends invitation emails. Each process needs its own copy. |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `FLAGON_AI_API_KEY` | API | Only if you use a hosted model. |

The API is the only process that talks to the domain database, and the app never
needs the API's database credentials. Keep each secret on the process that uses
it.

## TLS and cookies

Terminate TLS wherever your platform does: a load balancer, a reverse proxy, or
the platform's edge. Neither process terminates TLS itself.

HTTPS is **required** for the app in production. When `NODE_ENV=production`, the
app issues its session cookie with `SameSite=None; Secure`, so browsers drop it
over plain HTTP. The `SameSite=None` part is what lets a SAML identity provider's
cross-site POST back to the app carry the session, which org SSO needs. Set
`BETTER_AUTH_URL` to the exact public HTTPS origin the browser uses.

## Running the app and API on separate hosts

The app and the API deploy independently. The app needs two settings to find the
API:

```bash
FLAGON_API_URL=https://api.example.com     # read server-side only
FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN=<same value as the API>
```

The browser never calls the API directly: every request goes to the app, and
the app's server calls the API. That gives you two options:

- **Private API.** Put the API on a private network that only the app can reach.
  Users get the full product through the app. The REST API, MCP endpoint, and
  access tokens are then unavailable to anything outside that network.
- **Public API.** Expose the API as well, so people can call it with
  [access tokens](/docs/api/authentication), connect MCP clients, and fetch the
  docs. Apart from public content (public user profiles, the docs, roadmap and
  changelog, the spec, and health checks), every operation requires a valid
  credential, and the internal path is only as strong as
  `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN`. Every route also has a request body cap
  (`FLAGON_MAX_BODY_BYTES`, 4 MiB by default, `413` beyond it) and a
  per-principal rate limit (`FLAGON_RATE_LIMIT`, 50 requests per second with a
  burst of `FLAGON_RATE_BURST`, 300, and `429` with `Retry-After` beyond it).
  `/healthz` and `/readyz` are exempt from the rate limit.

Scaling out is safe on both sides. Several API instances can boot at once
(migrations serialize on an advisory lock), and the app's sign-in rate limits
are stored in `flagon_app`, so they are shared across app instances rather than
held in one instance's memory. The API's request rate limiter is the exception:
it counts in memory on each API machine, so with several machines a caller can
make up to that many times the configured rate. The assistant's daily quota is
stored in the database and is shared.

## Client IP behind a proxy

The API records the caller's IP address in the audit log and uses it to rate
limit anonymous callers. For requests from the app, it uses the browser's address
that the app forwards (trusted only alongside the internal token). For everyone
else, it uses the TCP peer address by default, which behind a load balancer or
edge proxy is the proxy's address.

Set `FLAGON_CLIENT_IP_HEADER` to the header your proxy puts the real client IP in,
for example `Fly-Client-IP` on Fly.io. Set it **only** if every request reaches
the API through that proxy and the proxy overwrites the header; otherwise a caller
could send the header themselves and choose the IP their audit entries show. The
API never reads `X-Forwarded-For` or the app's `X-Flagon-Client-*` headers from
token callers.

## A dedicated MCP host

The MCP endpoint is always served at `POST /mcp` on the API. If you want a
separate public host name for it, such as `mcp.example.com`, point that name at
the API and set:

```bash
FLAGON_MCP_HOST=mcp.example.com
```

Requests whose `Host` header matches (compared without the port, ignoring case)
are handled by a gate in front of every other route: the MCP endpoint answers at
both `/` and `/mcp`, and every other path returns `404`. That host never exposes
the index, the OpenAPI spec, the docs routes, or any REST operation. All other
host names are unaffected and keep every route, `/mcp` included. Flagon's hosted
instance uses this for `mcp.flagon.io`.

## Health checks and readiness

| Route | Port | Returns | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /healthz` | `PORT` | `200` whenever the process is up, regardless of the database. | Liveness. Answers `GET` only, so configure checks to use `GET`, not `HEAD`. |
| `GET /readyz` | `PORT` | `200` with `{"database":"ok","status":"ok"}`, or `503` with `{"database":"unavailable","status":"degraded"}`. The database error goes to the log, not the response. | Readiness: whether the instance can serve real traffic. |
| `GET /internal/rls-check` | `PORT` | `200` when tenant isolation is enforced for the runtime role, `503` otherwise. | A post-deploy check, not a frequent probe. |

Liveness deliberately ignores the database, so a database outage does not make
your platform restart or refuse to start the API; readiness is where the outage
shows. The Docker image's `HEALTHCHECK` calls `/healthz` every 30 seconds.

These routes are registered outside the OpenAPI spec and need no credentials.

## Metrics

The API serves Prometheus metrics at `/metrics` on a **separate** listener,
`METRICS_PORT` (default `9091`). It includes HTTP request latency
(`flagon_http_request_duration_seconds`), connection-pool statistics, and the
standard Go runtime and process metrics. The listener binds the same interface
as the API (`FLAGON_HOST`), so keep the port closed to the internet and let only
your scraper reach it. If the metrics listener fails, the API keeps serving.

## Logs

The API writes structured JSON logs to stdout. Collect stdout from the process
or container. The lines to watch at boot are listed in
[Self-hosting issues](/docs/troubleshooting/self-hosting-issues#reading-the-api-log).

Every API response carries an `X-Request-Id` header. When a request fails with a
`5xx`, the response carries only a short summary, and the full cause is logged
with a `request_id` field, so ask users for the header value and search the log
for it. The app can pass its own id in `X-Request-Id` (8 to 128 letters, digits,
dots, underscores, or hyphens) to correlate a request across both services.

## Email

Two processes send email, both through Resend:

- **The app** sends verification codes and password resets. In production, a
  missing `RESEND_API_KEY` is an error, not a silent skip: the app throws
  `RESEND_API_KEY is not set: refusing to drop a transactional email in production.`
  rather than letting sign-ups wait for a code that never arrives. Set
  `RESEND_FROM` to an address on a domain you have verified with Resend.
- **The API** sends invitation emails, for invitations made from the dashboard,
  the REST API, the assistant, or MCP. Set `RESEND_API_KEY` and
  `FLAGON_MAIL_FROM` (or `RESEND_FROM`) on the API, and set `FLAGON_APP_URL` to the
  app's public URL so the accept link points at your instance (in production it
  otherwise defaults to `https://app.flagon.io`). Without a key the API uses its
  log sender and warns at boot:
  `mail provider is the LOG mailer in production: invitation emails are NOT delivered; set RESEND_API_KEY`. The invitation is
  still created and the REST response reports `email_sent: false` alongside the
  invitation `token`; the accept link is `<FLAGON_APP_URL>/invite/<token>`. The
  dashboard's invite dialog shows that link with a copy button when the email was
  not sent, so an inviter can deliver it by hand, but fix email delivery rather
  than relying on it.

## AI in production

Pin the provider instead of relying on `auto`:

```bash
FLAGON_AI_PROVIDER=anthropic
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=<key>
FLAGON_AI_DAILY_LIMIT=100
```

With `auto`, a missing or removed key falls back to the offline mock, with only
a warning in the log. With the provider pinned, a missing key stops the API at
startup (for example `FLAGON_AI_PROVIDER=anthropic requires ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`),
so you notice. A key the provider rejects (a `401` or `403` upstream) makes
assistant turns answer `503` "the AI agent is not configured". Keep a daily limit on any instance shared by people you
do not control; `0` disables the limit. See [Usage and AI limits](/docs/platform/usage).

## Related

- [Configuration](/docs/self-hosting/configuration)
- [Database](/docs/self-hosting/database)
- [Upgrading](/docs/self-hosting/upgrading)
- [Deployment topology](/docs/architecture/deployment-topology)
- [Secrets](/docs/security/secrets)

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.description: How to move a self-hosted instance to a newer version - back up, upgrade the API (which migrates itself), migrate and rebuild the app - and why there is no rollback of the schema.
headings: or, with the image: docker run --rm -e DATABASE_URL=... -e FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL=... flagon-api migrate
docs.body:
Upgrading Flagon means running newer code against your existing databases. The
API carries its schema migrations inside the binary and applies them when it
boots, so most upgrades are "back up, deploy the new API, deploy the new app".
This page explains the order, what can go wrong, and why a schema change cannot
be undone by redeploying an older version.

## How schema changes ship

- **Embedded.** The API's migrations are SQL files in
  `api/internal/db/migrations/`, compiled into the binary. Upgrading the binary
  upgrades the migrations with it.
- **Forward-only.** There are no down migrations. Each release only ever adds
  new files.
- **Immutable once applied.** The API records a SHA-256 checksum of every
  migration it applies in `public.schema_migrations`. If a shipped migration file
  is later edited, the next boot stops with
  `migrations are immutable once shipped` rather than guessing what the schema
  looks like. Fixes to a shipped migration always arrive as a new migration.
- **All or nothing.** Pending migrations run in one transaction. If any of them
  fails, none are applied and the database is left exactly as it was.

The app's auth schema is managed by BetterAuth and upgraded by the app's own
migration script (`npm run db:migrate --workspace app`), which only creates
missing tables and adds missing columns.

## Upgrade steps

<Steps>

<Step title="Read the changelog">

Check the [changelog](https://flagon.io/changelog) for the versions between yours
and the target, and look for anything that needs action beyond these steps.

</Step>

<Step title="Back up both databases">

Take a backup of `flagon_api` and `flagon_app` (a `pg_dump` of each, or your
provider's snapshots) before anything else. Because migrations are forward-only,
the backup is your rollback plan.

</Step>

<Step title="Upgrade the API">

Build or pull the new version and restart the API. On boot it takes the
migration advisory lock, applies the new migrations, and starts serving. If you
run several instances, they can restart in any order: the first one to boot
applies the migrations, and the others wait for it and find nothing left to do.

To apply migrations as a separate step first (for example, to watch the output
before shifting traffic), run the new binary with `migrate`:

```bash
flagon-server migrate
# or, with the image: docker run --rm -e DATABASE_URL=... -e FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL=... flagon-api migrate
```

Then confirm the new version is healthy: `/readyz` returns `200` and
`/internal/rls-check` returns `"enforced":true`.

<Callout type="warn" title="Check for new required settings">

A newer API can require settings an older one did not, and a production API
refuses to start without them. For example, versions that encrypt SSO secrets at
rest need `FLAGON_SECRETS_KEY`, and versions with the development/production mode
split need `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN`, `DATABASE_URL`, and `FLAGON_APP_DATABASE_URL`
set explicitly. Set them before you restart. On its first boot with a secrets key,
the API encrypts any SSO secrets still stored in plaintext and logs
`encrypted stored credentials at rest under the current key` with the number of
rows. See
[Configuration](/docs/self-hosting/configuration).

</Callout>

</Step>

<Step title="Migrate and rebuild the app">

From the new version's checkout:

```bash
npm ci
npm run db:migrate --workspace app
npm run build
```

Then restart the app. Upgrade the API before the app: the app is a client of the
API, and a newer app may call operations an older API does not have yet.

</Step>

</Steps>

## If a migration fails

When the database is reachable but a migration fails, the API refuses to start.
It exits with a non-zero status and logs `flagon exited with error`, with an
`err` field of the form
`database migration failed; refusing to start against a broken schema: apply migration <name>: <postgres error>`.
Because the run is a single transaction, nothing from that run was applied. Keep (or roll back to) the
previous version while you investigate; the previous version keeps working
against the unchanged schema. [Self-hosting issues](/docs/troubleshooting/self-hosting-issues#migration-errors)
covers the common causes.

## Rolling back

Redeploying an older API does **not** undo migrations. The older binary only
knows about the migrations it shipped with; it will start against the newer
schema, but that combination was never tested and may fail in ways that are hard
to diagnose. To truly go back:

1. Stop the API and the app.
2. Restore both databases from the backups you took before upgrading.
3. Deploy the previous versions of both.

Anything written after the backup is lost, which is why the backup comes first.

## Related

- [Database](/docs/self-hosting/database)
- [Production](/docs/self-hosting/production)
- [Installation](/docs/self-hosting/installation)
- [Self-hosting issues](/docs/troubleshooting/self-hosting-issues)
